Though Pilate pronounced him innocent, yet his soldiers, his guards, set themselves to abuse him, being swayed more by the fury of the people <hi type="italic">against him,</hi> than by their master's testimony <hi type="italic">for him;</hi> the Jewish <hi type="italic">rabble</hi> infected the Roman soldiery, or perhaps it was not so much in spite to him, as to make <hi type="italic">sport</hi> for themselves, that they thus abused him. They understood that he <hi type="italic">pretended to a crown; to taunt</hi> him with that gave them some diversion, and an opportunity to make themselves and one another merry. Note, It is an argument of a base, servile, sordid spirit, to insult over those that are in misery, and to make the calamities of any matter of sport and merriment. <div eID="gen24098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24099" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. <hi type="italic">Where</hi> this was done—in the <hi type="italic">common hall.</hi> The <hi type="italic">governor's house,</hi> which should have been a shelter to the wronged and abused, is made the theatre of this barbarity. I wonder that the governor, who was so desirous to acquit himself from the blood of this just person, would suffer this to be done in <hi type="italic">his</hi> house. Perhaps he did not order it to be done, but he <hi type="italic">connived</hi> at it; and those in authority will be accountable, not only for the wickedness which they <hi type="italic">do,</hi> or <hi type="italic">appoint,</hi> but for that which they do not restrain, when it is in the power of their hands. Masters of families should not suffer their houses to be places of abuse to any, nor their servants to make sport with the sins, or miseries, or religion, of others. <div eID="gen24099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24100" type="x-p"/> 2. <hi type="italic">Who</hi> were concerned in it. They gathered the <hi type="italic">whole band,</hi> the soldiers that were to attend the execution, would have the whole regiment (at least five hundred, some think twelve or thirteen hundred) to share in the diversion. If Christ was thus made a <hi type="italic">spectacle,</hi> let none of his followers think it strange to be so used, <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.9">1 Cor. iv. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.33">Heb. x. 33</reference>. <div eID="gen24100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24101" type="x-p"/> 3. What particular indignities were done him. <div eID="gen24101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24102" type="x-p"/> (1.) They <hi type="italic">stripped him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.27.28">v. 28</reference>. The shame of nakedness came in with sin (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.7">Gen. iii. 7</reference>); and therefore Christ, when he came to satisfy for sin, and take it away, was <hi type="italic">made naked,</hi> and submitted to <hi type="italic">that shame,</hi> that he might prepare for us <hi type="italic">white raiment, to cover us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.3.18">Rev. iii. 18</reference>. <div eID="gen24102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24103" type="x-p"/> (2.) They <hi type="italic">put on him a scarlet robe,</hi> some old red cloak, such as the Roman soldiers wore, in imitation of the <hi type="italic">scarlet robes</hi> which kings and emperors wore; thus upbraiding him with his being called <hi type="italic">a King.</hi> This <hi type="italic">sham</hi> of majesty they put upon him in his dress, when nothing but meanness and misery appeared in his countenance, only to expose him to the spectators, as the more <hi type="italic">ridiculous;</hi> yet there was something of <hi type="italic">mystery</hi> in it; this was he that was <hi type="italic">red in his apparel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.1-Isa.63.2">Isa. lxiii. 1, 2</reference>), that <hi type="italic">washed his garments in wine</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.11">Gen. xlix. 11</reference>); therefore he was dressed in a <hi type="italic">scarlet robe.</hi> Our sins were as <hi type="italic">scarlet and crimson.</hi> Christ being clad in a <hi type="italic">scarlet robe,</hi> signified his bearing our sins, to his shame, in his own body upon the tree; that we might wash our robes, and make them white, in the blood of the Lamb. <div eID="gen24103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24104" type="x-p"/> (3.) They <hi type="italic">platted a crown of thorns, and put it upon his head,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.27.29">v. 29</reference>. This was to carry on the humour of making him a <hi type="italic">mock-king;</hi> yet, had they intended it only for a <hi type="italic">reproach,</hi> they might have <hi type="italic">platted a crown of straw,</hi> or <hi type="italic">rushes,</hi> but they designed it to be painful to him, and to be <hi type="italic">literally,</hi> what crowns are said to be figuratively, lined with thorns; he that invented this abuse, it is likely, valued himself upon the wit of it; but there was a mystery in it. [1.] Thorns came in with sin, and were part of the curse that was the product of sin, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.18">Gen. iii. 18</reference>. Therefore Christ, being made a <hi type="italic">curse for us,</hi> and dying to remove the curse from us, felt the pain and smart of those thorns, nay, and <hi type="italic">binds them as a crown</hi> to him (<reference osisRef="Job.31.36">Job xxxi. 36</reference>); for his sufferings for us were <hi type="italic">his glory.</hi> [2.] Now he answered to the type of Abraham's ram that was <hi type="italic">caught in the thicket,</hi> and so offered up instead of Isaac, <reference osisRef="Gen.22.13">Gen. xxii. 13</reference>. [3.] Thorns signify afflictions, <reference osisRef="2Chr.33.11">2 Chron. xxxiii. 11</reference>. These Christ put into a <hi type="italic">crown;</hi> so much did he alter the property of them to them that are his, giving them cause to <hi type="italic">glory in tribulation,</hi> and making it to work for them a weight of glory. [4.] Christ was crowned with thorns, to show that <hi type="italic">his kingdom was not of this world,</hi> nor the glory of it worldly glory, but is attended here with bonds and afflictions, while the glory of it is <hi type="italic">to be revealed.</hi> [5.] It was the custom of some heathen nations, to bring their sacrifices to the altars, crowned with garlands; these thorns were the garlands with which this great Sacrifice was crowned. [6.] these thorns, it is likely, fetched blood from his blessed head, which trickled down his face, <hi type="italic">like the previous ointment</hi> (typifying the blood of Christ with which he consecrated himself) <hi type="italic">upon the head, which ran down upon the beard, even Aaron's beard,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.133.2">Ps. cxxxiii. 2</reference>. Thus, when he came to espouse to himself his love, his dove, his undefiled church, his <hi type="italic">head was filled with dew,</hi> and his <hi type="italic">locks with the drops of the night,</hi> <reference osisRef="Song.5.2">Cant. v. 2</reference>. <div eID="gen24104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24105" type="x-p"/> (4.) They <hi type="italic">put a reed in his right hand;</hi> this was intended for a <hi type="italic">mock-sceptre,</hi> another of the <hi type="italic">insignia</hi> of the majesty they jeered him with; as if this were a sceptre good enough for such a King, as was like <hi type="italic">a reed shaken with the wind</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.7">ch. xi. 7</reference>); like sceptre, like kingdom, both weak and wavering, and withering and worthless; but they were quite mistaken, for his throne is <hi type="italic">for ever and ever,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">sceptre of his kingdom is a right sceptre,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.45.6">Ps. xlv. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen24105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24106" type="x-p"/> (5.) <hi type="italic">They bowed the knee before him, and mocked him, saying, Hail, King of the Jews!</hi> Having made him a sham King, they thus make a jest of doing homage to him, thus ridiculing his pretensions to sovereignty, as Joseph's brethren (<reference osisRef="Gen.37.8">Gen. xxxvii. 8</reference>); <hi type="italic">Shalt thou indeed reign over us?</hi> But as they were afterward compelled to do obeisance to him, and enrich his dreams, so these here bowed the knee, in scorn to him who was, soon after this, exalted to the right hand of God, that <hi type="italic">at his name every knee might bow,</hi> or break before him; it is ill jesting with that which, sooner or later, will come in earnest. <div eID="gen24106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24107" type="x-p"/> (6.) They <hi type="italic">spit upon him;</hi> thus he had been abused in the High Priest's hall, <reference osisRef="Matt.26.67">ch. xxvi. 67</reference>. In doing homage, the subject kissed the sovereign, in token of his allegiance; thus Samuel kissed Saul, and we are bid to <hi type="italic">kiss the Son:</hi> but they, in this mock-homage, instead of kissing him, spit in his face; that blessed face which outshines the sun, and before which the angels cover theirs, was thus polluted. It is strange that the sons of men should ever do such a piece of <hi type="italic">villany,</hi> and that the Son of God should ever <hi type="italic">suffer</hi> such a piece of <hi type="italic">ignominy.</hi> <div eID="gen24107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24108" type="x-p"/> (7.) They <hi type="italic">took the reed, and smote him on the head.</hi> That which they had made the <hi type="italic">mock-ensign</hi> of his royalty, they now make the real instrument of <hi type="italic">their</hi> cruelty, and <hi type="italic">his pain.</hi> They smote him, it is probable, upon the <hi type="italic">crown of thorns,</hi> and so struck them into his head, that they might wound it the deeper, which made the more sport for them, to whom his pain was the greatest pleasure. Thus was he <hi type="italic">despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief.</hi> All this misery and shame he underwent, that he might purchase for us everlasting life, and joy, and glory. <div eID="gen24108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24109" type="x-p"/> III. The conveying of him to the place of execution. After they had mocked and abused him, as long as they thought fit, they then <hi type="italic">took the robe off from him;</hi> to signify their divesting him of all the kingly authority they had invested him with, by putting it on him; and they put his own raiment on him, because that was to fall to the soldiers' share, that were employed in the execution. They took off the robe, but no mention is made of their taking off the <hi type="italic">crown of thorns,</hi> whence it is commonly supposed (though there is no certainty of it) that he was crucified with that on his head; for as he is a Priest upon his throne, so he was a King upon his cross. Christ was led to be crucified in <hi type="italic">his own raiment,</hi> because he himself was to <hi type="italic">bear our sins in his own body upon the tree.</hi> And here, <div eID="gen24109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24110" type="x-p"/> 1. They <hi type="italic">led him away</hi> to be <hi type="italic">crucified;</hi> he was led <hi type="italic">as a lamb to the slaughter,</hi> as a sacrifice to the altar. We may well imagine how they hurried him on, and dragged him along, with all the speed possible, lest any thing should intervene to prevent the glutting of their cruel rage with his precious blood. It is probable that they now loaded him with taunts and reproaches, and treated him as the off-scouring of all things. They led him away <hi type="italic">out of the city;</hi> for Christ, that he might sanctify the people with his own blood, <hi type="italic">suffered without the gate</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.12">Heb. xiii. 12</reference>), as if he that was the glory of them that <hi type="italic">waited for redemption</hi> in Jerusalem was not worthy to live among them. To this he himself had an eye, when in the parable he speaks of his being <hi type="italic">cast out of the vineyard,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.21.39">ch. xxi. 39</reference>. <div eID="gen24110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24111" type="x-p"/> 2. They compelled Simon of Cyrene <hi type="italic">to bear his cross,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.27.32">v. 32</reference>. It seems, at first he <hi type="italic">carried the cross</hi> himself, as Isaac carried the wood for the burnt-offering, which was to burn him. And this was intended, as other things, both for pain and shame to him. But after a while they <hi type="italic">took the cross</hi> off from him, either, (1.) In compassion to him, because they saw it was too great a load for him. We can hardly think that they had any consideration of that, yet it teaches us that God <hi type="italic">considers the frame</hi> of his people, and will not <hi type="italic">suffer them to be tempted above what they are able;</hi> he gives them some breathing-time, but they must expect that the cross will return, and the lucid intervals only give them space to prepare for the next fit. But, (2.) Perhaps it was because he could not, with the cross on his back, go forward so fast as they would have him. Or, (3.) They were afraid, lest he should faint away under the load of his cross, and die, and so prevent what their malice further intended to do against him: thus even the <hi type="italic">tender mercies of the wicked</hi> (which seem to be so) <hi type="italic">are</hi> really <hi type="italic">cruel.</hi> Taking the cross off from him, they <hi type="italic">compelled</hi> one Simon of Cyrene to bear it, pressing him to the service by the authority of the governor or the priests. It was a reproach, and none would do it but by compulsion. Some think that this Simon was a disciple of Christ, at least a well-wisher to him, and that they knew it, and therefore put this upon him. Note, All that will approve themselves disciples indeed, must follow Christ, <hi type="italic">bearing his cross</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.16.24">ch. xvi. 24</reference>), <hi type="italic">bearing his reproach,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.13.13">Heb. xiii. 13</reference>. We must know the <hi type="italic">fellowship of his sufferings for us,</hi> and patiently submit to all the sufferings for him we are called out to; for those only shall <hi type="italic">reign with him,</hi> that <hi type="italic">suffer with him;</hi> shall sit with him in his kingdom, that drink of <hi type="italic">his cup,</hi> and are baptized with <hi type="italic">his baptism.</hi>
entries.033dce8278b7154abbb9e3a572464936f2a0fa87: <div eID="gen24111" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Crucifixion.</title> <div sID="gen24112" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">33</hi> And when they were come unto a place called Golgotha, that is to say, a place of a skull, <hi type="super">34</hi> They gave him vinegar to drink mingled with gall: and when he had tasted <hi type="italic">thereof,</hi> he would not drink. <hi type="super">35</hi> And they crucified him, and parted his garments, casting lots: that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet, They parted my garments among them, and upon my vesture did they cast lots. <hi type="super">36</hi> And sitting down they watched him there; <hi type="super">37</hi> And set up over his head his accusation written, THIS IS JESUS THE KING OF THE JEWS. 38 Then were there two thieves crucified with him, one on the right hand, and another on the left. <hi type="super">39</hi> And they that passed by reviled him, wagging their heads, <hi type="super">40</hi> And saying, Thou that destroyest the temple, and buildest <hi type="italic">it</hi> in three days, save thyself. If thou be the Son of God, come down from the cross. <hi type="super">41</hi> Likewise also the chief priests mocking <hi type="italic">him,</hi> with the scribes and elders, said, <hi type="super">42</hi> He saved others; himself he cannot save. If he be the King of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him. <hi type="super">43</hi> He trusted in God; let him deliver him now, if he will have him: for he said, I am the Son of God. <hi type="super">44</hi> The thieves also, which were crucified with him, cast the same in his teeth. <hi type="super">45</hi> Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land unto the ninth hour. <hi type="super">46</hi> And about the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani? that is to say, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? <hi type="super">47</hi> Some of them that stood there, when they heard <hi type="italic">that,</hi> said, This <hi type="italic">man</hi> calleth for Elias. <hi type="super">48</hi> And straightway one of them ran, and took a sponge, and filled <hi type="italic">it</hi> with vinegar, and put <hi type="italic">it</hi> on a reed, and gave him to drink. <hi type="super">49</hi> The rest said, Let be, let us see whether Elias will come to save him. <div eID="gen24112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24113" type="x-p"/> We have here the crucifixion of our Lord Jesus. <div eID="gen24113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24114" type="x-p"/> I. The place where our Lord Jesus was put to death. <div eID="gen24114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24115" type="x-p"/> 1. They came to a place called <hi type="italic">Golgotha,</hi> near adjoining to Jerusalem, probably the common place of execution. If he had had a house of his own in Jerusalem, probably, for his greater disgrace, they would have crucified him before his own door. But now in the same place where criminals were sacrificed to the justice of the government, was our Lord Jesus sacrificed to the justice of God. Some think that it was called <hi type="italic">the place of a skull,</hi> because it was the common charnel-house, where the bones and skulls of dead men were laid together out of the way, lest people should touch them, and be defiled thereby. Here lay the trophies of death's victory over multitudes of the children of men; and when by dying Christ would destroy death, he added this circumstance of honour to his victory, that he triumphed over death upon his own dunghill. <div eID="gen24115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24116" type="x-p"/> 2. There they <hi type="italic">crucified</hi> him (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.35">v. 35</reference>), nailed his hands and feet to the cross, and then reared it up, and him hanging on it; for so the manner of the Romans was to crucify. Let our hearts be touched with the feeling of that exquisite pain which our blessed Saviour now endured, and let us look upon him who was thus pierced, and mourn. Was ever sorrow like unto his sorrow? And when we behold what manner of death he died, let us in that behold with <hi type="italic">what manner of love</hi> he <hi type="italic">loved us.</hi> <div eID="gen24116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24117" type="x-p"/> II. The barbarous and abusive treatment they gave him, in which their wit and malice vied which should excel. As if death, so great a death, were not bad enough, they contrived to add to the bitterness and terror of it. <div eID="gen24117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24118" type="x-p"/> 1. By the drink they provided for him before he was nailed to the cross, <reference osisRef="Matt.27.34">v. 34</reference>. It was usual to have a cup of spiced wine for those to drink of, that were to be put to death, according to Solomon's direction (<reference osisRef="Prov.31.6-Prov.31.7">Prov. xxxi. 6, 7</reference>), <hi type="italic">Give strong drink to him that is ready to perish;</hi> but with that cup which Christ was to drink of, they mingled <hi type="italic">vinegar and gall,</hi> to make it sour and bitter. This signified, (1.) The <hi type="italic">sin of man,</hi> which is a <hi type="italic">root of bitterness, bearing gall and wormwood,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.29.18">Deut. xxix. 18</reference>. The sinner perhaps rolls it under his tongue as a sweet morsel, but to God it is <hi type="italic">grapes of gall,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.32.32">Deut. xxxii. 32</reference>. It was so to the Lord Jesus, when he bare our sins, and sooner or later it will be so to the sinner himself, <hi type="italic">bitterness at the latter end, more bitter than death,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.26">Eccl. vii. 26</reference>. (2.) It signified the <hi type="italic">wrath of God,</hi> that cup which is Father <hi type="italic">put into his hand,</hi> a bitter cup indeed, like the <hi type="italic">bitter water which caused the curse,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.5.18">Num. v. 18</reference>. This drink they offered him, as was literally foretold, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.21">Ps. lxix. 21</reference>. And, [1.] He <hi type="italic">tasted thereof,</hi> and so had the <hi type="italic">worst</hi> of it, took the bitter taste into his mouth; he let no bitter cup go by him untasted, when he was making atonement for all our sinful tasting of forbidden fruit; now he was <hi type="italic">tasting</hi> death in its full bitterness. [2.] He <hi type="italic">would not drink it,</hi> because he would not have the <hi type="italic">best of it;</hi> would have nothing like an opiate to lessen his sense of pain, for he would die so as to <hi type="italic">feel himself die,</hi> because he had so much <hi type="italic">work</hi> to <hi type="italic">do,</hi> as our High Priest, in his suffering work. <div eID="gen24118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24119" type="x-p"/> 2. By the dividing of his garments, <reference osisRef="Matt.27.35">v. 35</reference>. When they nailed him to the cross, they <hi type="italic">stripped</hi> him of his garments, at least his <hi type="italic">upper garments;</hi> for by sin we were made naked, to our shame, and thus he purchased for us white raiment to cover us. If we be at any time stripped of our comforts for Christ, let us bear it patiently; he was stripped for us. Enemies may strip us of our <hi type="italic">clothes,</hi> but cannot strip us of our <hi type="italic">best comforts;</hi> cannot take from us the <hi type="italic">garments of praise.</hi> The clothes of those that are executed are the executioner's fee: four soldiers were employed in crucifying Christ, and they must each of them have a share: his upper garment, if it were divided, would be of no use to any of them, and therefore they agreed to <hi type="italic">cast lots</hi> for it. (1.) Some think that the garment was so fine and rich, that it was worth contending for; but that agreed not with the poverty Christ appeared in. (2.) Perhaps they had heard of those that had been cured by touching the hem of his garment, and they thought it valuable for some magic virtue in it. Or, (3.) They hoped to get money of his friends for such a sacred relic. Or, (4.) Because, in derision, they would seem to put a value upon it, as royal clothing. Or, (5.) It was for diversion; to pass away the time while they waited for his death, they would play a game at dice for the clothes; but, whatever they designed, the word of God is herein accomplished. In that famous <hi type="italic">psalm,</hi> the first words of which Christ made use of upon the cross, it was said, <hi type="italic">They parted my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.22.18">Ps. xxii. 18</reference>. This was never true of David, but looks <hi type="italic">primarily</hi> at Christ, of whom David, in spirit, spoke. Then is the offence of this part of the cross ceased; for it appears to have been by the <hi type="italic">determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God.</hi> Christ stripped himself of his glories, to divide them among us. <div eID="gen24119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24120" type="x-p"/> They now <hi type="italic">sat down, and watched him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.27.36">v. 36</reference>. The chief priests were careful, no doubt, in setting this guard, lest the people, whom they still stood in awe of, should rise, and rescue him. But Providence so ordered it, that those who were appointed to <hi type="italic">watch</hi> him, thereby became unexceptionable witnesses for him; having the opportunity to see and hear that which extorted from them that noble confession (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.54">v. 54</reference>), <hi type="italic">Truly this was the Son of God.</hi> <div eID="gen24120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24121" type="x-p"/> 3. By the <hi type="italic">title</hi> set up over his head, <reference osisRef="Matt.27.37">v. 37</reference>. It was usual for the vindicating of public justice, and putting the greater shame upon malefactors that were executed, not only by a crier to proclaim before them, but by a writing also over their heads to notify what was the crime for which they suffered; so they set up over Christ's head his accusation written, to give public notice of the charge against him; <hi type="italic">This is Jesus the King of the Jews.</hi> This they designed for his reproach, but God so overruled it, that even his accusation redounded to his honour. For, (1.) Here was no crime alleged against him. It is not said that he was a pretended Saviour, or a usurping King, though they would have it thought so (<reference osisRef="John.19.21">John xix. 21</reference>); but, <hi type="italic">This is Jesus, a Saviour;</hi> surely that was no crime; and, <hi type="italic">This is the King of the Jews;</hi> nor was that a crime; for they expected that the Messiah should be so: so that, his enemies themselves being judges, he <hi type="italic">did no evil.</hi> Nay, (2.) Here was a very glorious truth asserted concerning him—that he is <hi type="italic">Jesus the King of the Jews,</hi> that King whom the Jews expected and ought to have submitted to; so that his accusation amounts to this, That he was the true Messiah and Saviour of the world; as Balaam, when he was sent for to curse Israel, blessed them all together, and that three times (<reference osisRef="Num.24.10">Num. xxiv. 10</reference>), so Pilate, instead of accusing Christ as a Criminal, proclaimed him a <hi type="italic">King,</hi> and that <hi type="italic">three times,</hi> in three inscriptions. Thus God makes men to serve <hi type="italic">his</hi> purposes, quite beyond <hi type="italic">their own.</hi> <div eID="gen24121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24122" type="x-p"/> 4. By his companions with him in suffering, <reference osisRef="Matt.27.38">v. 38</reference>. There were <hi type="italic">two thieves crucified with him</hi> at the same time, in the same place, under the same guard; two highway-men, or robbers upon the road, as the word properly signifies. It is probable that this was appointed to be <hi type="italic">execution-day;</hi> and therefore they hurried the prosecution of Christ in the morning, that they might have him ready to be executed with the other criminals. Some think that Pilate ordered it thus, that this piece of necessary justice, in executing these thieves, might atone for his injustice in condemning Christ; others, that the Jews contrived it, to add to the ignominy of the sufferings of our Lord Jesus; however it was, the scripture was fulfilled in it (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.12">Isa. liii. 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">He was numbered with the transgressors.</hi> <div eID="gen24122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24123" type="x-p"/> (1.) It was a reproach to him, that he was <hi type="italic">crucified with them.</hi> Though, while he lived, he was <hi type="italic">separate from sinners,</hi> yet <hi type="italic">in their deaths they were not divided,</hi> but he was made to partake with the vilest malefactors in their plagues, as if he had been a partaker with them in their sins; for he was made sin for us, and took upon him the <hi type="italic">likeness of sinful flesh.</hi> He was, at his death, numbered among the transgressors, and had his lot with the wicked, that we, at our death, might be <hi type="italic">numbered among the saints,</hi> and have our <hi type="italic">lot among the chosen.</hi> <div eID="gen24123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24124" type="x-p"/> (2.) It was an additional reproach, that he was crucified <hi type="italic">in the midst, between them,</hi> as if he had been the worst of the three, the principal malefactor; for among <hi type="italic">three</hi> the <hi type="italic">middle</hi> is the place for the chief. Every circumstance was contrived to his dishonour, as if the great Saviour were of all others the <hi type="italic">greatest sinner.</hi> It was also intended to ruffle and discompose him, in his last moments, with the shrieks, and groans, and blasphemies, of these malefactors, who, it is likely, made a hideous outcry when they were nailed to the cross; but thus would Christ affect himself with the miseries of sinners, when he was suffering for their salvation. Some of Christ's apostles were afterwards crucified, as Peter, and Andrew, but none of them were crucified <hi type="italic">with him,</hi> lest it should have looked as if they had been joint undertakers with him, in satisfying for man's sin, and joint purchasers of life and glory; therefore he was crucified between two malefactors, who could not be supposed to contribute any thing to the merit of his death; for he himself bare our sins <hi type="italic">in his own body.</hi> <div eID="gen24124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24125" type="x-p"/> 5. By the blasphemies and revilings with which they loaded him when he was hanging upon the cross; though we read not that they cast any reflections on the thieves that were crucified with him. One would have thought that, when they had nailed him to the cross, they had done their worst, and malice itself had been exhausted: indeed if a criminal be put into the pillory, or carted, because it is a punishment less than death, it is usually attended with such expressions of abuse; but a dying man, though an infamous man, should be treated with compassion. It is an insatiable revenge indeed which will not be satisfied with death, <hi type="italic">so great a death.</hi> But, to complete the humiliation of the Lord Jesus, and to show that, when he was dying, he was <hi type="italic">bearing iniquity,</hi> he was then <hi type="italic">loaded with reproach,</hi> and, for aught that appears, not one of his friends, who the other day cried <hi type="italic">Hosanna</hi> to him, durst be seen to show him any respect. <div eID="gen24125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24126" type="x-p"/> (1.) The common <hi type="italic">people, that passed by, reviled him.</hi> His extreme misery and exemplary patience under it, did not mollify them, or make them to relent; but they who by their outcries brought him to this, now think to justify themselves in it by their reproaches, as if they <hi type="italic">did well to condemn</hi> him. They <hi type="italic">reviled</hi> him: <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">eblasphemoun</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">they blasphemed</hi> him; and <hi type="italic">blasphemy</hi> it was, in the strictest sense, speaking evil of him who <hi type="italic">thought it not robbery to be equal with God.</hi> Observe here, <div eID="gen24126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24127" type="x-p"/> [1.] The persons that reviled him; <hi type="italic">they that passed by,</hi> the travellers that went along the road, and it was a great <hi type="italic">road,</hi> leading from Jerusalem to Gibeon; they were possessed with prejudices against him by the reports and clamours of the High Priest's creatures. It is a hard thing, and requires more application and resolution than is ordinarily met with, to keep up a good opinion of persons and things that are <hi type="italic">every where</hi> run down, and spoken against. Every one is apt to say as the most say, and to throw a stone at that which is put into an ill name. <hi type="italic">Turba Remi sequitur fortunam semper et odit damnatos—The Roman rabble fluctuate with a man's fluctuating fortunes, and fail not to depress those that are sinking.</hi> Juvenal. <div eID="gen24127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24128" type="x-p"/> [2.] The gesture they used, in contempt of him—<hi type="italic">wagging their heads;</hi> which signifies their triumph in his fall, and their insulting over him, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.22">Isa. xxxvii. 22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.18.16">Jer. xviii. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.2.15">Lam. ii. 15</reference>. The language of it was, <hi type="italic">Aha, so would we have it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.35.25">Ps. xxxv. 25</reference>. Thus they insulted over him that was the Saviour of their country, as the Philistines did over Samson the destroyer of their country. This very gesture was prophesied of (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.7">Ps. xxii. 7</reference>); <hi type="italic">They shake the head at me.</hi> And <reference osisRef="Ps.109.25">Ps. cix. 25</reference>. <div eID="gen24128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24129" type="x-p"/> [3.] The taunts and jeers they uttered. These are here recorded. <div eID="gen24129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24130" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> They upbraided him with his <hi type="italic">destroying of the temple.</hi> Though the judges themselves were sensible that what he had said of that was misrepresented (as appears <reference osisRef="Mark.14.59">Mark xiv. 59</reference>), yet they industriously spread it among the people, to bring an <hi type="italic">odium</hi> upon him, that he had a design to destroy the temple; than which nothing would more <hi type="italic">incense</hi> the people against him. And this was not the only time that the enemies of Christ had laboured to <hi type="italic">make others believe</hi> that of religion and the people of God, which they themselves have known to be <hi type="italic">false,</hi> and the charge <hi type="italic">unjust "Thou that destroyest the temple,</hi> that vast and strong fabric, try thy strength now in plucking up that <hi type="italic">cross,</hi> and drawing those <hi type="italic">nails,</hi> and so <hi type="italic">save thyself;</hi> if thou hast the power thou hast boasted of, this is a proper time to exert it, and give proof of it; for it is supposed that every man will do his utmost to <hi type="italic">save himself.</hi>" This made the cross of Christ such a <hi type="italic">stumbling-block</hi> to the Jews, that they looked upon it to be inconsistent with the <hi type="italic">power</hi> of the Messiah; he was <hi type="italic">crucified in weakness</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.13.4">2 Cor. xiii. 4</reference>), so it seemed to them; but indeed Christ crucified is the <hi type="italic">Power of God.</hi> <div eID="gen24130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24131" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> They upbraided him with his saying that he was <hi type="italic">the Son of God;</hi> If thou be so, say they, <hi type="italic">come down from the cross.</hi> Now they take the devil's words out of his mouth, with which he tempted him in the wilderness (<reference osisRef="Matt.4.3">ch. iv. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.4.6">6</reference>), and renew the same assault; <hi type="italic">If thou be the Son of God.</hi> They think that now, or never, he must prove himself to be the <hi type="italic">Son of God;</hi> forgetting that he had proved it by the miracles he wrought, particularly his raising of the dead; and unwilling to wait for the complete proof of it by his own resurrection, to which he had so often referred himself and them; which, if they had observed it, would have anticipated the offence of the cross. This comes of judging things by the present aspect of them, without a due remembrance of what is <hi type="italic">past,</hi> and a patient expectation of <hi type="italic">what may further be produced.</hi> <div eID="gen24131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24132" type="x-p"/> (2.) The <hi type="italic">chief priests and scribes,</hi> the church rulers, and the <hi type="italic">elders,</hi> the state rulers, they mocked him, <reference osisRef="Matt.27.41">v. 41</reference>. They did not think it enough to invite the rabble to do it, but gave Christ the dishonour, and themselves the diversion, or reproaching him in their own proper persons. They should have been in the temple at their devotion, for it was the first day of the feast of unleavened bread, when there was to be a <hi type="italic">holy convocation</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.7">Lev. xxiii. 7</reference>); but they were here at the place of execution, spitting their venom at the Lord Jesus. How much below the grandeur and gravity of their character was this! Could any thing tend more to make them <hi type="italic">contemptible and base before the people?</hi> One would have thought, that, though they neither feared God nor regarded man, yet common prudence should have taught them who had so great a hand in Christ's death, to keep as much as might be behind the curtain, and to play least in sight; but nothing is so mean as that malice may stick at it. Did they disparage themselves thus, to do despite to Christ, and shall we be afraid of disparaging ourselves, by joining with the multitude to <hi type="italic">do him honour,</hi> and not rather say, <hi type="italic">If this be to be vile, I will be yet more vile?</hi> <div eID="gen24132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24133" type="x-p"/> Two things the priests and elders upbraided him with. <div eID="gen24133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24134" type="x-p"/> [1.] That he could not <hi type="italic">save himself,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.27.42">v. 42</reference>. He had been before abused in his prophetical and kingly office, and now in his priestly office as a Saviour. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> They take it for granted that he <hi type="italic">could not</hi> save himself, and therefore had not the power he pretended to, when really he <hi type="italic">would not</hi> save himself, because he would die to <hi type="italic">save us.</hi> They should have argued, "He <hi type="italic">saved others,</hi> therefore he <hi type="italic">could</hi> save himself, and if he do not, it is for some good reason." But, <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> They would insinuate, that, because he did not now save himself, therefore all his pretence to save others was but sham and delusion, and was never really done; though the truth of his miracles was demonstrated beyond contradiction. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> They upbraid him with being <hi type="italic">the King of Israel.</hi> They dreamed of the external pomp and power of the Messiah, and therefore thought <hi type="italic">the cross</hi> altogether disagreeable to the King of Israel, and inconsistent with that character. Many people would like the <hi type="italic">King of Israel</hi> well enough, if he would but <hi type="italic">come down from the cross,</hi> if they could have his kingdom without the tribulation through which they must <hi type="italic">enter into</hi> it. But the matter is settled; if no cross, then no Christ, no crown. Those that would reign with him, must be willing to suffer with him, for Christ and his cross are <hi type="italic">nailed together</hi> in this world. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> They challenged him to <hi type="italic">come down from the cross.</hi> And what had become of us then, and the work of our redemption and salvation? If he had been provoked by these scoffs to <hi type="italic">come down from the cross,</hi> and so to have left his undertaking <hi type="italic">unfinished,</hi> we had been for ever <hi type="italic">undone.</hi> But his unchangeable love and resolution set him above, and fortified him against, this temptation, so that he did not <hi type="italic">fail,</hi> nor was <hi type="italic">discouraged. Fifthly,</hi> They promised that, if he would <hi type="italic">come down from the cross, they would believe him.</hi> Let him give them that proof of his being the Messiah, and they will own him to be so. When they had formerly demanded a sign, he told them that the sign he would give them, should be not his <hi type="italic">coming down from the cross,</hi> but, which was a greater instance of his power, his <hi type="italic">coming up from the grave,</hi> which they had not patience to wait two or three days for. If he had <hi type="italic">come down from the cross,</hi> they might with as much reason have said that the soldiers had juggled in nailing him to it, as they said, when he was raised from the dead, that the <hi type="italic">disciples came by night, and stole him away.</hi> But to promise ourselves that we would believe, if we had such and such means and motives of faith as we ourselves would prescribe, when we do not improve what God has appointed, is not only a gross instance of the deceitfulness of our hearts, but the sorry <hi type="italic">refuge,</hi> or <hi type="italic">subterfuge</hi> rather, of an obstinate destroying infidelity. <div eID="gen24134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24135" type="x-p"/> [2.] That God, <hi type="italic">his Father,</hi> would <hi type="italic">not save him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.43">v. 43</reference>); <hi type="italic">He trusted in God,</hi> that is, he pretended to do so; for he said, <hi type="italic">I am the Son of God.</hi> Those who call God <hi type="italic">Father,</hi> and themselves <hi type="italic">his children,</hi> thereby profess to put a confidence in him, <reference osisRef="Ps.9.10">Ps. ix. 10</reference>. Now they suggest, that he did but deceive himself and others, when he made himself so much the <hi type="italic">darling of heaven;</hi> for, if he had been the Son of God (as <hi type="italic">Job's</hi> friends argued concerning him), he would not have been <hi type="italic">abandoned to</hi> all this misery, much less <hi type="italic">abandoned in</hi> it. This was a <hi type="italic">sword in his bones,</hi> as David complains of the like (<reference osisRef="Ps.42.10">Ps. xlii. 10</reference>); and it was a <hi type="italic">two-edged</hi> sword, for it was intended, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> To <hi type="italic">vilify</hi> him, and to make the standers-by think him a deceiver and an impostor; as if his saying, that he was the <hi type="italic">Son of God,</hi> were now effectually <hi type="italic">disproved. Secondly,</hi> To <hi type="italic">terrify</hi> him, and drive him to distrust and despair of his Father's power and love; which some think, was the thing <hi type="italic">he feared, religiously feared,</hi> prayed against, and was <hi type="italic">delivered from,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.5.7">Heb. v. 7</reference>. David complained more of the endeavours of his persecutors to <hi type="italic">shake his faith,</hi> and drive him from his hope in God, than of their attempts to <hi type="italic">shake his throne,</hi> and drive him from his kingdom; their saying, There is <hi type="italic">no help for him in God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.3.2">Ps. iii. 2</reference>), and, <hi type="italic">God has forsaken him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.71.11">Ps. lxxi. 11</reference>. In this, as in other things, he was a type of Christ. Nay, these very words David, in that famous prophecy of Christ, mentions, as spoken by <hi type="italic">his enemies</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.8">Ps. xxii. 8</reference>); He <hi type="italic">trusted on the Lord that he would deliver him.</hi> Surely these priests and scribes had forgotten their psalter, or they would not have used the same words, so exactly to answer the type and prophecy: but the <hi type="italic">scriptures must be fulfilled.</hi> <div eID="gen24135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24136" type="x-p"/> (3.) To complete the reproach, the <hi type="italic">thieves also that were crucified with him</hi> were not only not reviled as he was, as if they had been saints compared with him, but, though fellow-sufferers with him, joined in with his prosecutors, and <hi type="italic">cast the same in his teeth;</hi> that is, one of them did, who said, <hi type="italic">If thou be the Christ, save thyself and us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.23.39">Luke xxiii. 39</reference>. One would think that of all people this thief had <hi type="italic">least cause,</hi> and should have had <hi type="italic">least mind,</hi> to banter Christ. Partners in suffering, though for different causes, usually commiserate one another; and few, whatever they have done before, will breathe their last in revilings. But, it seems, the greatest mortifications of the body, and the most humbling rebukes of Providence, will not of themselves mortify the corruptions of the soul, nor suppress the wickedness of the wicked, without the grace of God. <div eID="gen24136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24137" type="x-p"/> Well, thus our Lord Jesus having undertaken to satisfy the justice of God for the wrong done him in his honour by sin, he did it by suffering <hi type="italic">in his honour;</hi> not only by divesting himself of that which was due to him as the Son of God, but by submitting to the utmost indignity that could be done to the worst of men; because he was made sin for us, he was thus made a curse for us, to make reproach easy to us, if at any time we suffer it, and have all manner of evil said against us falsely, for righteousness' sake. <div eID="gen24137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24138" type="x-p"/> III. We have here the frowns of heaven, which our Lord Jesus was under, in the midst of all these injuries and indignities from men. Concerning which, observe, <div eID="gen24138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24139" type="x-p"/> 1. How this was signified—by an extraordinary and miraculous eclipse of the sun, which continued for <hi type="italic">three hours,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.27.45">v. 45</reference>. There was darkness <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">epi pasan ten gen</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">over all the earth;</hi> so most interpreters understand it, though our translation confines it to <hi type="italic">that land.</hi> Some of the ancients appealed to the annals of the nation concerning this extraordinary eclipse at the death of Christ, as a thing well known, and which gave notice to those parts of the world of something great then in doing; as the sun's going back in Hezekiah's time did. It is reported that Dionysius, at Heliopolis in Egypt, took notice of this darkness, and said, <hi type="italic">Aut Deus naturæ patitur, aut mundi machina dissolvitur—Either the God of nature is suffering, or the machine of the world is tumbling into ruin.</hi> An extraordinary light gave intelligence of the birth of Christ (<reference osisRef="Matt.2.2">ch. ii. 2</reference>), and therefore it was proper that an extraordinary darkness should notify his death, for he is the <hi type="italic">Light of the world.</hi> The indignities done to our Lord Jesus, made the <hi type="italic">heavens astonished,</hi> and <hi type="italic">horribly afraid,</hi> and even put them into disorder and confusion; such wickedness as this the sun never saw before, and therefore withdrew, and would not see this. This surprising, amazing, darkness was designed to stop the mouths of those blasphemers, who were reviling Christ as he hung on the cross; and it should seem that, for the present, it struck such a terror upon them, that though their hearts were not changed, yet they were silent, and stood doubting what this should mean, till after <hi type="italic">three hours</hi> the darkness <hi type="italic">scattered,</hi> and then (as appears by <reference osisRef="Matt.27.47">v. 47</reference>), like Pharaoh when the plague was over, they hardened their hearts. But that which was principally intended in this darkness, was, (1.) Christ's present <hi type="italic">conflict</hi> with the <hi type="italic">powers of darkness.</hi> Now the prince of this world, and his forces, the <hi type="italic">rulers of the darkness of this world,</hi> were to be cast out, to be spoiled and vanquished; and to make his victory the more illustrious, he fights them on their own ground; gives them all the advantage they could have against him by this darkness, lets them take the <hi type="italic">wind</hi> and <hi type="italic">sun,</hi> and yet baffles them, and so becomes more than a conqueror. (2.) His present want of heavenly comforts. This darkness signified that dark cloud which the human soul of our Lord Jesus was now under. God makes his sun to shine upon the just and upon the unjust; but even the light of the sun was withheld from our Saviour, when he was <hi type="italic">made sin for us. A pleasant thing it is for the eyes to behold the sun;</hi> but because now his soul was exceeding sorrowful, and the cup of divine displeasure was filled to him without mixture, even the light of the sun was suspended. When earth denied him a drop of cold water, heaven denied him a beam of light; having to deliver us from <hi type="italic">utter darkness,</hi> he did himself, in the depth of his sufferings, walk in darkness, and had no light, <reference osisRef="Isa.50.10">Isa. l. 10</reference>. During the <hi type="italic">three hours</hi> that this darkness continued, we do not find that he said <hi type="italic">one word,</hi> but passed this time in a silent retirement into his own soul, which was now in agony, wrestling with the powers of darkness, and taking in the impressions of his Father's displeasure, not against himself, but the sin of man, which he was now <hi type="italic">making his soul an offering for.</hi> Never were there three such hours since the day that God created man upon the earth, never such a dark and awful scene; the <hi type="italic">crisis</hi> of that great affair of man's redemption and salvation. <div eID="gen24139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24140" type="x-p"/> 2. How he complained of it (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.46">v. 46</reference>); <hi type="italic">About the ninth hour,</hi> when it began to clear up, after a long and silent conflict. <hi type="italic">Jesus cried, Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani?</hi> The words are related in the Syriac tongue, in which they were spoken, because worthy of double remark, and for the sake of the perverse construction which his enemies put upon them, in putting <hi type="italic">Elias</hi> for <hi type="italic">Eli.</hi> Now observe here, <div eID="gen24140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24141" type="x-p"/> (1.) Whence he borrowed this complaint—from <reference osisRef="Ps.22.1">Ps. xxii. 1</reference>. It is not probable (as some have thought) that he repeated the whole psalm; yet hereby he intimated that the whole was to be applied to him, and that David, in spirit, there spoke of his humiliation and exaltation. This, and that other word, <hi type="italic">Into thy hands I commit my spirit,</hi> he fetched from David's psalms (though he could have expressed himself in his own words), to teach us of what use the word of God is to us, to direct us in prayer, and to recommend to us the use of scripture-expressions in prayer, which will <hi type="italic">help our infirmities.</hi> <div eID="gen24141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24142" type="x-p"/> (2.) How he uttered it—<hi type="italic">with a loud voice;</hi> which bespeaks the extremity of his pain and anguish, the strength of nature remaining in him, and the great earnestness of his spirit in this expostulation. Now the scripture was fulfilled (<reference osisRef="Joel.3.15-Joel.3.16">Joel iii. 15, 16</reference>); <hi type="italic">The sun and the moon shall be darkened. The Lord shall also roar out of Zion, and utter his voice form Jerusalem.</hi> David often speaks of his <hi type="italic">crying aloud</hi> in prayer, <reference osisRef="Ps.55.17">Ps. lv. 17</reference>. <div eID="gen24142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24143" type="x-p"/> (3.) What the complaint was—<hi type="italic">My God, My God, why hast thou forsaken me?</hi> A strange complaint to come from the mouth of our Lord Jesus, who, we are sure, was <hi type="italic">God's elect, in whom his soul delighted</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.1">Isa. xlii. 1</reference>), and one in whom he was always <hi type="italic">well pleased.</hi> The Father now loved him, nay, he knew that <hi type="italic">therefore he loved him, because he laid down his life for the sheep;</hi> what, and yet forsaken of him, and in the midst of his sufferings too! Surely never sorrow was like unto that sorrow which extorted such a complaint as this from one who, being perfectly free from sin, could never be a terror to himself; but the heart knows its own bitterness. No wonder that such a complaint as this made the earth to quake, and rent the rocks; for it is enough to make both the <hi type="italic">ears of every one that hears it to tingle,</hi> and ought to be spoken of with great reverence. <div eID="gen24143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24144" type="x-p"/> Note, [1.] That our Lord Jesus was, in his sufferings, for a time, <hi type="italic">forsaken by his Father.</hi> So he saith himself, who we are sure was under no mistake concerning his own case. Not that the union between the divine and human nature was in the least weakened or shocked; no, he was <hi type="italic">now by the eternal Spirit offering himself:</hi> nor as if there were any abatement of his Father's love to him, or his to his Father; we are sure that there was upon his mind no horror of God, or despair of his favour, nor any thing of the torments of hell; but his Father forsook him; that is, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He delivered him up into the hands of his enemies, and did not appear to deliver him out of their hands. He let loose the powers of darkness against him, and suffered them to do their worst, worse than against Job. Now was that scripture fulfilled (<reference osisRef="Job.16.11">Job xvi. 11</reference>), <hi type="italic">God hath turned me over into the hands of the wicked;</hi> and no angel is sent from heaven to deliver him, no friend on earth raised up to appear for him. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He withdrew from him the present comfortable sense of his complacency in him. When <hi type="italic">his soul</hi> was first <hi type="italic">troubled,</hi> he had a <hi type="italic">voice from heaven</hi> to comfort him (<reference osisRef="John.12.27">John xii. 27, 28</reference>); when he was in his agony in the garden, there appeared an angel from heaven strengthening him; but now he had neither the one nor the other. God hid his face from him, and for awhile withdrew his rod and staff in the darksome valley. God <hi type="italic">forsook</hi> him, not as he forsook Saul, leaving him to an endless despair, but as sometimes he forsook David, leaving him to a present despondency. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> He let out upon his soul an afflicting sense of his wrath against man for sin. Christ was made <hi type="italic">Sin</hi> for us, a <hi type="italic">Curse</hi> for us; and therefore, though God loved him as a Son, he frowned upon him as a Surety. These impressions he was pleased to <hi type="italic">admit,</hi> and to <hi type="italic">waive</hi> that <hi type="italic">resistance</hi> of them which he <hi type="italic">could have made;</hi> because he would accommodate himself to this part of his undertaking, as he had done to all the rest, when it was in his power to have avoided it. <div eID="gen24144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24145" type="x-p"/> [2.] That Christ's being <hi type="italic">forsaken</hi> of his Father was the most grievous of his sufferings, and that which he complained most of. Here he laid the most doleful accents; he did not say, "Why am I scourged? And why spit upon? And why nailed to the cross?" Nor did he say to his disciples, when they turned their back upon him, <hi type="italic">Why have ye forsaken me?</hi> But when his Father stood at a distance, he cried out thus; for this as it that <hi type="italic">put wormwood and gall</hi> into the affliction and misery. This brought the <hi type="italic">waters into the soul,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.69.1-Ps.69.3">Ps. lxix. 1-3</reference>. <div eID="gen24145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24146" type="x-p"/> [3.] That our Lord Jesus, even when he was thus forsaken of his Father, kept hold of him as his God, notwithstanding; <hi type="italic">My God, my God;</hi> though forsaking me, yet <hi type="italic">mine.</hi> Christ was God's <hi type="italic">servant</hi> in carrying on the work of redemption, to him he was to make satisfaction, and by him to be carried through and crowned, and upon that account he calls him <hi type="italic">his God;</hi> for he was now <hi type="italic">doing his will.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Isa.49.5-Isa.49.9">Isa. xlix. 5-9</reference>. This supported him, and bore him up, that even in the depth of his sufferings God was his God, and this he resolves to keep fast hold of. <div eID="gen24146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24147" type="x-p"/> (4.) See how his enemies impiously bantered and ridiculed this complaint (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.47">v. 47</reference>); <hi type="italic">They said, This man calleth for Elias.</hi> Some think that this was the ignorant mistake of the Roman soldiers, who had heard talk of Elias, and of the Jews' expectation of the coming of Elias, but knew not the signification of <hi type="italic">Eli, Eli,</hi> and so made this blundering comment upon these words of Christ, perhaps not hearing the latter part of what he said, for the noise of the people. Note, Many of the reproaches cast upon the word of God and the people of God, take rise from gross mistakes. Divine truths are often corrupted by ignorance of the language and style of the scripture. Those that hear by the halves, pervert what they hear. But others think that it was the wilful mistake of some of the Jews, who knew very well what he said, but were disposed to abuse him, and make themselves and their companions merry, and to misrepresent him as one who, being forsaken of God, was driven to trust in creatures; perhaps hinting also, that he who had pretended to be himself the Messiah, would now be glad to be beholden to Elias, who was expected to be only the harbinger and forerunner of the Messiah. Note, It is no new thing for the most pious devotions of the best men to be ridiculed and abused by profane scoffers; nor are we to think it strange if what is well said in praying and preaching be misconstrued, and turned to our reproach; Christ's words were so, though he spoke as never man spoke. <div eID="gen24147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24148" type="x-p"/> IV. The cold comfort which his enemies ministered to him in this agony, which was like all the rest. <div eID="gen24148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24149" type="x-p"/> 1. Some <hi type="italic">gave him vinegar to drink</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.48">v. 48</reference>); instead of some cordial-water to revive and refresh him under this heavy burthen, they tantalized him with that which did not only add to the reproach they were loading him with, but did too sensibly represent that cup of trembling which his Father had <hi type="italic">put into his hand. One of them ran</hi> to fetch it, seeming to be officious to him, but really glad of an opportunity to abuse and affront him, and afraid lest any one should take it out of his hands. <div eID="gen24149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24150" type="x-p"/> 2. Others, which the same purpose of disturbing and abusing him, refer him to Elias (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.49">v. 49</reference>); "<hi type="italic">Let be, let us see whether Elias will come to save him.</hi> Come, let him alone, his case is desperate, neither heaven nor earth can help him; let us do nothing either to hasten his death, or to retard it; he has appealed to Elias, and <hi type="italic">to Elias let him go.</hi>"
entries.f8d19d7eca0dc0a7a3b973893e8871a9a66b5792: <div eID="gen24150" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Crucifixion; The Death of Christ.</title> <div sID="gen24151" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">50</hi> Jesus, when he had cried again with a loud voice, yielded up the ghost. <hi type="super">51</hi> And, behold, the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom; and the earth did quake, and the rocks rent; <hi type="super">52</hi> And the graves were opened; and many bodies of the saints which slept arose, <hi type="super">53</hi> And came out of the graves after his resurrection, and went into the holy city, and appeared unto many. <hi type="super">54</hi> Now when the centurion, and they that were with him, watching Jesus, saw the earthquake, and those things that were done, they feared greatly, saying, Truly this was the Son of God. <hi type="super">55</hi> And many women were there beholding afar off, which followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering unto him: <hi type="super">56</hi> Among which was Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James and Joses, and the mother of Zebedee's children. <div eID="gen24151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24152" type="x-p"/> We have here, at length, an account of the death of Christ, and several remarkable passages that attended it. <div eID="gen24152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24153" type="x-p"/> I. The <hi type="italic">manner</hi> how he breathed his last (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.50">v. 50</reference>); between the third and the sixth hour, that is, between nine and twelve o'clock, as we reckon, he was nailed to the cross, and soon after the ninth hour, that is, between three and four o'clock in the afternoon, he <hi type="italic">died.</hi> That was the time of the offering of the evening sacrifice, and the time when the paschal lamb was killed; and Christ our Passover was sacrificed for us and offered himself in the evening of the world a sacrifice to God of a sweet-smelling savour. It was at that time of the day, that the angel Gabriel delivered to Daniel that glorious prediction of the Messiah, <reference osisRef="Dan.9.21">Dan. ix. 21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.9.24">24</reference>, &c. And some think that from that very time when the angel spoke it, to this time when Christ died, was just seventy weeks, that is, four hundred and ninety years to a day, to an hour; as the departure of <hi type="italic">Israel</hi> out of Egypt was at the end of the four hundred and thirty years, <hi type="italic">even the self-same day,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.12.41">Exod. xii. 41</reference>. <div eID="gen24153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24154" type="x-p"/> Two things are here noted concerning the manner of Christ's dying. <div eID="gen24154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24155" type="x-p"/> 1. That he <hi type="italic">cried with a loud voice,</hi> as before, <reference osisRef="Matt.27.46">v. 46</reference>. Now, <div eID="gen24155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24156" type="x-p"/> (1.) This was a sign, that, after all his pains and fatigues, his life was <hi type="italic">whole</hi> in him, and nature <hi type="italic">strong.</hi> The voice of dying men is one of the first things that fails; with a panting breath and a faltering tongue, a few broken words are hardly spoken, and more hardly heard. But Christ, just before he expired, spoke like a man <hi type="italic">in his full strength,</hi> to show that his life was not forced from him, but was freely <hi type="italic">delivered</hi> by him into his Father's hands, as <hi type="italic">his own act and deed.</hi> He that had strength to cry thus when he died, could have got loose from the arrest he was under, and have bid defiance to the powers of death; but to show that <hi type="italic">by the eternal Spirit he offered himself,</hi> being the Priest as well as the Sacrifice, he <hi type="italic">cried with a loud voice.</hi> <div eID="gen24156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24157" type="x-p"/> (2.) It was significant. This <hi type="italic">loud voice</hi> shows that he attacked our spiritual enemies with an undaunted courage, and such a bravery of resolution as bespeaks him hearty in the cause and daring in the encounter. He was now <hi type="italic">spoiling principalities and powers,</hi> and in this loud voice he did, as it were, <hi type="italic">shout for mastery,</hi> as one <hi type="italic">mighty to save,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.63.1">Isa. lxiii. 1</reference>. Compare with this, <reference osisRef="Isa.62.13-Isa.62.14">Isa. lxxii. 13, 14</reference>. He now bowed himself with all his might, as Samson did, when he said, <hi type="italic">Let me die with the Philistines,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.16.30">Judg. xvi. 30</reference>. <hi type="italic">Animamque in vulnere ponit—And lays down his life.</hi> His crying with a loud voice when he died, signified that his death should be published and proclaimed to all the world; all mankind being concerned in it, and obliged to take notice of it. Christ's loud cry was like a trumpet blown over the sacrifices. <div eID="gen24157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24158" type="x-p"/> 2. That then he <hi type="italic">yielded up the ghost.</hi> This is the usual periphrasis of dying; to show that the Son of God upon the cross did truly and properly die by the violence of the pain he was put to. His <hi type="italic">soul</hi> was separated from his <hi type="italic">body,</hi> and so his body was left really and truly dead. It was certain that he <hi type="italic">did die,</hi> for it was requisite that he should die; <hi type="italic">thus it was written,</hi> both in the <hi type="italic">close rolls</hi> of the <hi type="italic">divine counsels,</hi> and in the <hi type="italic">letters patent of</hi> the <hi type="italic">divine predictions,</hi> and therefore thus <hi type="italic">it behoved him to suffer.</hi> Death being the penalty for the breach of the first covenant (<hi type="italic">Thou shalt surely die</hi>), the Mediator of the new covenant must make atonement <hi type="italic">by means of death,</hi> otherwise no remission, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.15">Heb. ix. 15</reference>. He had undertaken to make his soul an <hi type="italic">offering for sin;</hi> and he did it, when he <hi type="italic">yielded up the ghost,</hi> and voluntarily resigned it. <div eID="gen24158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24159" type="x-p"/> II. The miracles that attended his death. So many miracles being wrought <hi type="italic">by him</hi> in his life, we might well expect some to be wrought concerning him at his death, for his name was called <hi type="italic">Wonderful.</hi> Had he been fetched away as Elijah in a <hi type="italic">fiery chariot,</hi> that had itself been miracle enough; but, being sent for away by an ignominious cross, it was requisite that his humiliation should be attended with some signal emanations of the divine glory. <div eID="gen24159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24160" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">Behold, the veil of the temple was rent in twain.</hi> This relation is ushered in with <hi type="italic">Behold;</hi> "Turn aside, and see this great sight, and be astonished at it." Just as our Lord Jesus expired, at the time of the offering of the evening-sacrifice, and upon a solemn day, when the priests were officiating in the temple, and might themselves be eyewitnesses of it, <hi type="italic">the veil of the temple was rent</hi> by an invisible power; that veil which parted between the <hi type="italic">holy place</hi> and the <hi type="italic">most holy.</hi> They had condemned him for saying, <hi type="italic">I will destroy this temple,</hi> understanding it literally; now by this specimen of his power he let them know that, if he had pleased, he could have made his words good. In this, as in others of Christ's miracles, there was a mystery. <div eID="gen24160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24161" type="x-p"/> (1.) It was in correspondence with the temple of Christ's body, which was now in the dissolving. This was the true temple, in which dwelt <hi type="italic">the fulness of the Godhead;</hi> when Christ <hi type="italic">cried with a loud voice, and gave up the ghost,</hi> and so dissolved that temple, the literal temple did, as it were, echo to that cry, and answer the stroke, by <hi type="italic">rending its veil.</hi> Note, Death is the rending of the veil of flesh which interposes between us and the holy of holies; the death of Christ was so, the death of true Christians is so. <div eID="gen24161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24162" type="x-p"/> (2.) It signified the revealing and unfolding of the mysteries of the Old Testament. The veil of the temple was for concealment, as was that on the face of Moses, therefore it was called the <hi type="italic">veil of the covering;</hi> for it was highly penal for any person to see the furniture of the most holy place, except the High-Priest, and he but once a year, with great ceremony and through a cloud of smoke; all which signified the darkness of that dispensation; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.13">2 Cor. iii. 13</reference>. But now, at the death of Christ, all was laid open, the mysteries were unveiled, so that now he that runs may read the meaning of them. Now we see that the mercy-seat signified <hi type="italic">Christ</hi> the great <hi type="italic">Propitiation;</hi> the pot of <hi type="italic">manna</hi> signified Christ the Bread of life. Thus <hi type="italic">we all with open face behold, as in a glass</hi> (which helps the sight, as the veil hindered it), <hi type="italic">the glory of the Lord. Our eyes see the salvation.</hi> <div eID="gen24162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24163" type="x-p"/> (3.) It signified the uniting of Jew and Gentile, by the removing of the partition wall between them, which was the ceremonial law, by which the Jews were distinguished from all other people (as a <hi type="italic">garden enclosed</hi>), were brought near to God, while others were made to <hi type="italic">keep their distance.</hi> Christ, in his death, repealed the ceremonial law, cancelled that <hi type="italic">hand-writing of ordinances,</hi> took it out of the way, nailed it to his cross, and so <hi type="italic">broke down the middle wall of partition;</hi> and by abolishing those institutions <hi type="italic">abolished the enmity,</hi> and <hi type="italic">made in himself of twain one new man</hi> (as two rooms are made one, and that large and lightsome, by taking down the partition), so <hi type="italic">making peace,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.2.14-Eph.2.16">Eph. ii. 14-16</reference>. Christ died, to rend all dividing veils, and to make all his one, <reference osisRef="John.17.21">John xvii. 21</reference>. <div eID="gen24163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24164" type="x-p"/> (4.) It signified the consecrating and laying open of <hi type="italic">a new and living way</hi> to God. The veil kept people off from drawing near to the most holy place, where the <hi type="italic">Shechinah</hi> was. But the rending of it signified that Christ by his death opened a way to God, [1.] <hi type="italic">For himself.</hi> This was the great <hi type="italic">day of atonement,</hi> when our Lord Jesus, as the great <hi type="italic">High-Priest,</hi> not <hi type="italic">by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood, entered once for all into the holy place;</hi> in token of which the veil was rent, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.7">Heb. ix. 7</reference>, &c. Having offered his sacrifice in the outer court, the blood of it was now to be sprinkled upon the mercy-seat within the veil; wherefore <hi type="italic">lift up your heads, O ye gates,</hi> and <hi type="italic">be ye lift up, ye everlasting doors; for the King of glory,</hi> the Priest of glory, <hi type="italic">shall come in.</hi> Now was he caused to draw near, and made to approach, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.21">Jer. xxx. 21</reference>. Though he did not personally ascend into the holy place not made with hands till above forty days after, yet he immediately acquired a right to enter, and had a virtual admission. [2.] <hi type="italic">For us in him:</hi> so the apostle applies it, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.19-Heb.10.20">Heb. x. 19, 20</reference>. We have <hi type="italic">boldness to enter into the holiest, by that new and living way which he has consecrated for us through the veil.</hi> He died, to <hi type="italic">bring us to God,</hi> and, in order thereunto, to rend that veil of guilt and wrath which interposed between us and him, to take away the <hi type="italic">cherubim</hi> and <hi type="italic">flaming sword,</hi> and to open the way to <hi type="italic">the tree of life.</hi> We have free access through Christ to the throne of grace, or mercy-seat, now, and to the throne of glory hereafter, <reference osisRef="Heb.4.16">Heb. iv. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.6.20">vi. 20</reference>. The rending of the veil signified (as that ancient hymn excellently expresses it), that, <hi type="italic">when Christ had overcome the sharpness of death, he opened the kingdom of heaven to all believers.</hi> Nothing can obstruct or discourage our access to heaven, for the veil is rent; <hi type="italic">a door is opened in heaven,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.4.1">Rev. iv. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen24164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24165" type="x-p"/> 2. The <hi type="italic">earth did quake;</hi> not only mount Calvary, where Christ was crucified, but the <hi type="italic">whole land,</hi> and the adjacent countries. This earthquake signified two things. <div eID="gen24165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24166" type="x-p"/> (1.) The <hi type="italic">horrible</hi> wickedness of <hi type="italic">Christ's crucifiers.</hi> The earth, by trembling under such a load, bore its testimony to the innocency of him that was persecuted, and against the impiety of those that persecuted him. Never did the whole creation, before, groan under such a burthen as the Son of God crucified, and the guilty wretches that crucified him. The earth <hi type="italic">quaked,</hi> as if it <hi type="italic">feared to open its mouth</hi> to <hi type="italic">receive</hi> the blood of Christ, so much more precious than that of Abel, which it had received, and was <hi type="italic">cursed</hi> for it (<reference osisRef="Gen.4.11-Gen.4.12">Gen. iv. 11, 12</reference>); and as if it <hi type="italic">fain would open its mouth,</hi> to swallow up those rebels that put him to death, as it had swallowed up Dathan and Abiram for a much less crime. When the prophet would express God's great displeasure against the wickedness of the wicked, he asks, <hi type="italic">Shall not the land tremble for this?</hi> <reference osisRef="Amos.8.8">Amos viii. 8</reference>. <div eID="gen24166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24167" type="x-p"/> (2.) The <hi type="italic">glorious</hi> achievements of <hi type="italic">Christ's cross.</hi> This <hi type="italic">earthquake</hi> signified the mighty shock, nay, the fatal blow, now given to the devil's kingdom. So vigorous was the assault Christ now made upon the infernal powers, that (as of old, <hi type="italic">when he went out of Seir, when he marched through the field of Edom</hi>) the <hi type="italic">earth trembled,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.5.4">Judg. v. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.68.7-Ps.68.8">Ps. lxviii. 7, 8</reference>. God shakes all nations, when the Desire of all nations is to come; and there is a <hi type="italic">yet once more,</hi> which perhaps refers to this shaking, <reference osisRef="Hag.2.6">Hag. ii. 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hag.2.21">21</reference>. <div eID="gen24167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24168" type="x-p"/> 3. The <hi type="italic">rocks rent;</hi> the hardest and firmest part of the earth was made to feel this mighty shock. Christ had said, that if the children should cease to cry <hi type="italic">Hosanna, the stones would immediately cry out;</hi> and now, in effect, they did so, proclaiming the glory of the suffering Jesus, and themselves more sensible of the wrong done him than the hard-hearted Jews were, who yet will shortly be glad to find a <hi type="italic">hole in the rocks, and a cleft in the ragged rocks,</hi> to hide them from the face of him that sitteth on the throne. See <reference osisRef="Rev.6.16">Rev. vi. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.2.21">Isa. ii. 21</reference>. But when God's <hi type="italic">fury is poured out like fire, the rocks are thrown down by him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Nah.1.6">Nah. i. 6</reference>. Jesus Christ is <hi type="italic">the Rock;</hi> and the rending of <hi type="italic">these</hi> rocks, signified the rending of <hi type="italic">that</hi> rock, (1.) That in the clefts of it was may be <hi type="italic">hid,</hi> as Moses in the cleft of the rock at Horeb, that there we may <hi type="italic">behold the glory of the Lord,</hi> as he did, <reference osisRef="Exod.33.22">Exod. xxxiii. 22</reference>. Christ's dove is said to be <hi type="italic">hid in the clefts of the rock</hi> (<reference osisRef="Song.2.14">Cant. ii. 14</reference>), that is, as some make the allusion, sheltered in the wounds of our Lord Jesus, the Rock rent. (2.) That from the cleft of it rivers of living water may flow, and follow us in this wilderness, as from the rock which Moses <hi type="italic">smote</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.17.6">Exod. xvii. 6</reference>), and which God clave (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.15">Ps. lxxviii. 15</reference>); and <hi type="italic">that rock was Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.4">1 Cor. x. 4</reference>. When we celebrate the memorial of Christ's death, our hard and rocky hearts must be <hi type="italic">rent</hi>—the heart, and not the garments. That heart is harder than a rock, that will not <hi type="italic">yield,</hi> that will not <hi type="italic">melt,</hi> where Jesus Christ is <hi type="italic">evidently set forth crucified.</hi> <div eID="gen24168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24169" type="x-p"/> 4. The <hi type="italic">graves were opened.</hi> This matter is not related so fully as our curiosity would wish; for the scripture was not intended to gratify that; it should seem, that same earthquake that rent the rocks, <hi type="italic">opened the graves,</hi> and many bodies of <hi type="italic">saints which slept, arose.</hi> Death to the saints is but the <hi type="italic">sleep</hi> of the body, and the <hi type="italic">grave</hi> the bed it <hi type="italic">sleeps in;</hi> they awoke by the power of the Lord Jesus, and (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.53">v. 53</reference>) came <hi type="italic">out of the graves after his resurrection, and went into Jerusalem, the holy city, and appeared unto many.</hi> Now here, <div eID="gen24169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24170" type="x-p"/> (1.) We may raise many enquiries concerning it, which we cannot resolve: as, [1.] <hi type="italic">Who</hi> these <hi type="italic">saints</hi> were, that <hi type="italic">did arise.</hi> Some think, the <hi type="italic">ancient patriarchs,</hi> that were in such care to be buried in the land of Canaan, perhaps in the believing foresight of the advantage of this early resurrection. Christ had lately proved the doctrine of the resurrection from the instance of the patriarchs (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.32">ch. xxii. 32</reference>), and here was a speedy confirmation of his argument. Others think, these that arose were <hi type="italic">modern saints,</hi> such as had been Christ in the flesh, but died before him; as his father Joseph, Zecharias, Simeon, John Baptist, and others, that had been known to the disciples, while they lived, and therefore were the fitter to be witnesses to them in an <hi type="italic">apparition</hi> after.
