What if we should suppose that they were the <hi type="italic">martyrs,</hi> who in the Old-Testament times had sealed the truths of God with their blood, that were thus <hi type="italic">dignified</hi> and <hi type="italic">distinguished?</hi> Christ particularly points at them as his forerunners, <reference osisRef="Matt.23.35">ch. xxiii. 35</reference>. And we find (<reference osisRef="Rev.20.4-Rev.20.5">Rev. xx. 4, 5</reference>), that those who were <hi type="italic">beheaded for the testimony of Jesus,</hi> arose <hi type="italic">before the rest of the dead.</hi> Sufferers with Christ shall <hi type="italic">first</hi> reign with him. [2.] It is uncertain whether (as some think) they arose to life, now at the death of Christ, and disposed of themselves elsewhere, but did not <hi type="italic">go into the city</hi> till after his resurrection; or whether (as others think), though <hi type="italic">their sepulchres</hi> (which the <hi type="italic">Pharisees</hi> had <hi type="italic">built</hi> and <hi type="italic">varnished,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.23.29">ch. xxiii. 29</reference>), and so made remarkable, were shattered now by the earthquake (so little did God regard that hypocritical respect), yet they did not <hi type="italic">revive</hi> and <hi type="italic">rise</hi> till after the resurrection; only, for brevity-sake, it is mentioned here, upon the mention of the <hi type="italic">opening of the graves,</hi> which seems more probable. [3.] Some think that they arose only to bear witness of Christ's resurrection to those to whom they appeared, and, having finished their testimony, retired to their graves again. But it is more agreeable, both to Christ's honour and theirs, to <hi type="italic">suppose,</hi> though we cannot <hi type="italic">prove,</hi> that they arose as Christ did, to <hi type="italic">die no more,</hi> and therefore ascended with him to glory. Surely on them who did partake of his first resurrection, a <hi type="italic">second</hi> death had no power. [4.] To whom they appeared (not <hi type="italic">to all the people</hi> it is certain, but to <hi type="italic">many</hi>), whether enemies or friends, in what manner they appeared, how often, what they said and did, and how they disappeared, are secret things which belong not to us; we must not covet to be <hi type="italic">wise above what is written.</hi> The relating of this matter so briefly, is a plain intimation to us, that we must not look that way for a confirmation of our faith; we have a more sure word of prophecy. See <reference osisRef="Luke.16.31">Luke xvi. 31</reference>. <div eID="gen24170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24171" type="x-p"/> (2.) Yet we may learn many good lessons from it. [1.] That even those who lived and died before the death and resurrection of Christ, had saving benefit thereby, as well as those who have lived since; for he <hi type="italic">was</hi> the same <hi type="italic">yesterday</hi> that he is <hi type="italic">to-day,</hi> and will be <hi type="italic">for ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.13.8">Heb. xiii. 8</reference>. [2.] That Jesus Christ, by dying, conquered, disarmed, and disabled, death. These saints that arose, were the present trophies of the victory of Christ's cross over the powers of <hi type="italic">death,</hi> which he thus <hi type="italic">made a show of openly.</hi> Having by death destroyed him that had the power of death, he thus <hi type="italic">led captivity captive,</hi> and gloried in these <hi type="italic">re-taken prizes,</hi> in them fulfilling that scripture, <hi type="italic">I will ransom them from the power of the grave.</hi> [3.] That, in virtue of Christ's resurrection, the bodies of all the saints shall, in the fulness of time, <hi type="italic">rise again.</hi> This was an earnest of the general resurrection at the last day, when <hi type="italic">all that are in the graves shall hear the voice of the Son of God.</hi> And perhaps Jerusalem is <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> called here the <hi type="italic">holy city,</hi> because the saints, at the general resurrection, shall enter into the <hi type="italic">new Jerusalem;</hi> which will be indeed what the other was in name and type only, the <hi type="italic">holy city,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.21.2">Rev. xxi. 2</reference>. [4.] That all the saints do, by the influence of Christ's death, and in conformity to it, rise from the <hi type="italic">death of sin</hi> to the <hi type="italic">life of righteousness.</hi> They are <hi type="italic">raised up with him</hi> to a divine and spiritual life; they go <hi type="italic">into the holy city,</hi> become <hi type="italic">citizens</hi> of it, have their conversation in it, and <hi type="italic">appear to many,</hi> as persons not of this world. <div eID="gen24171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24172" type="x-p"/> III. The conviction of his enemies that were employed in the execution (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.54">v. 54</reference>), which some make no less than another miracle, all things considered. Observe, <div eID="gen24172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24173" type="x-p"/> 1. The persons convinced; <hi type="italic">the centurion, and they that were with him watching Jesus;</hi> a captain and his company, that were set on the guard on this occasion. (1.) They were <hi type="italic">soldiers,</hi> whose profession is commonly hardening, and whose breasts are commonly not so susceptible as some others of the impressions either of fear or pity. But there is no spirit too big, too bold, for the power of Christ to break and humble. (2.) They ware <hi type="italic">Romans, Gentiles,</hi> who knew not the scriptures which were now fulfilled; yet they only were convinced. A sad presage of the <hi type="italic">blindness</hi> that should <hi type="italic">happen to Israel,</hi> when the gospel should be sent to the Gentiles, to open their eyes. Here were the Gentiles <hi type="italic">softened,</hi> and the Jews <hi type="italic">hardened.</hi> (3.) They were the persecutors of Christ, and those that but just before had reviled him, as appears <reference osisRef="Luke.23.36">Luke xxiii. 36</reference>. How soon can God, by the power he has over men's consciences, alter their language, and fetch confessions of his truths, to his own glory, out of the mouths of those that have <hi type="italic">breathed</hi> nothing but <hi type="italic">threatenings, and slaughter,</hi> and blasphemies! <div eID="gen24173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24174" type="x-p"/> 2. The means of their conviction; they perceived <hi type="italic">the earthquake,</hi> which frightened them, and saw the other <hi type="italic">things that were done.</hi> These were designed to assert the honour of Christ in his sufferings, and had their end on these soldiers, whatever they had on others. Note, The dreadful appearances of God in his providence sometimes work strangely for the conviction and awakening of sinners. <div eID="gen24174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24175" type="x-p"/> 3. The expressions of this conviction, in two things. <div eID="gen24175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24176" type="x-p"/> (1.) The <hi type="italic">terror</hi> that was <hi type="italic">struck</hi> upon them; they <hi type="italic">feared greatly;</hi> feared lest they should have been buried in the darkness, or swallowed up in the earthquake. Note, God can easily frighten the most daring of his adversaries, and make them know themselves to be but men. Guilt puts men into fear. He that, when iniquity abounds, doth not <hi type="italic">fear always,</hi> with a fear of <hi type="italic">caution,</hi> when judgments are abroad, cannot but <hi type="italic">fear greatly,</hi> with a fear of <hi type="italic">amazement;</hi> whereas there are those who will not fear, <hi type="italic">though the earth be removed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.46.1-Ps.46.2">Ps. xlvi. 1, 2</reference>. <div eID="gen24176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24177" type="x-p"/> (2.) The <hi type="italic">testimony</hi> that was <hi type="italic">extorted</hi> from them; they said, <hi type="italic">Truly this was the Son of God;</hi> a noble confession; Peter was blessed for it, <reference osisRef="Matt.16.16-Matt.16.17">ch. xvi. 16, 17</reference>. It was the great matter now in dispute, the point upon which he and his enemies had <hi type="italic">joined issue,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.26.63-Matt.26.64">ch. xxvi. 63, 64</reference>. His disciples believed it, but at this time durst not confess it; our Saviour himself was tempted to question it, when he said, <hi type="italic">Why hast thou forsaken me?</hi> The Jews, now that he was dying upon the cross, looked upon it as plainly determined against him, that he was not the Son of God, because he did not come down from the cross. And yet now this centurion and the soldiers make this voluntary confession of the Christian faith, <hi type="italic">Truly this was the Son of God.</hi> The best of his disciples could not have said more at any time, and at this time they had not faith and courage enough to say thus much. Note, God can maintain and assert the honour of a truth then when it seems to be crushed, and run down; for <hi type="italic">great is the truth, and will prevail.</hi> <div eID="gen24177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24178" type="x-p"/> IV. The attendance of his friends, that were witnesses of his death, <reference osisRef="Matt.27.55-Matt.27.56">v. 55, 56</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen24178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24179" type="x-p"/> 1. Who they were; <hi type="italic">many women who followed him from Galilee.</hi> Not his apostles (only elsewhere we find John by the cross, <reference osisRef="John.19.26">John xix. 26</reference>), their hearts failed them, they durst not appear, for fear of coming under the same condemnation. But here were a company of women, some would have called them <hi type="italic">silly</hi> women, that <hi type="italic">boldly</hi> stuck to Christ, when the rest of his disciples had basely deserted him. Note, Even those of the weaker sex are often, by the grace of God, made strong in faith, that Christ's strength may be made perfect in weakness. There have been women martyrs, famous for courage and resolution in Christ's cause. Now of these women it is said, (1.) That they had <hi type="italic">followed Jesus from Galilee,</hi> out of the great love they had to him, and a desire to hear him preach; otherwise, the males only were obliged to come up, to worship at the feast. Now having followed him such a long journey as from Galilee to Jerusalem, eighty or a hundred miles, they resolved not to forsake him now. Note, Our former services and sufferings for Christ should be an argument with us, faithfully to persevere to the end in our attendance on him. Have we followed him <hi type="italic">so far</hi> and so long, done so much, and laid out so much for him, and shall we forsake him now? <reference osisRef="Gal.3.3-Gal.3.4">Gal. iii. 3, 4</reference>. (2.) That they <hi type="italic">ministered to him</hi> of their substance, for his necessary subsistence. How gladly would they have ministered to him now, if they might have been admitted! But, being forbidden that, they resolved to <hi type="italic">follow him.</hi> Note, When we are restrained from doing what we <hi type="italic">would,</hi> we must do what we can, in the service of Christ. Now that he is <hi type="italic">in heaven,</hi> though he is out of the reach of our <hi type="italic">ministration,</hi> he is not out of the reach of our <hi type="italic">believing views.</hi> (3.) Some of them are particularly named; for God will <hi type="italic">honour</hi> those that <hi type="italic">honour</hi> Christ. They were such as we have several times met with <hi type="italic">before,</hi> and it was their praise, that we meet with them <hi type="italic">to the last.</hi> <div eID="gen24179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24180" type="x-p"/> 2. What they did; they were <hi type="italic">beholding afar off.</hi> <div eID="gen24180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24181" type="x-p"/> (1.) They stood <hi type="italic">afar off.</hi> Whether their own fear or their enemies' fury kept them at a distance, is not certain; however, it was an aggravation of the sufferings of Christ, that his <hi type="italic">lovers and friends stood aloof from his sore,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.38.11">Ps. xxxviii. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.19.13">Job xix. 13</reference>. Perhaps they might have come nearer, if they would; but good people, when they are in sufferings, must not think it strange, if some of their best friends be shy of them. When Paul's danger was imminent, <hi type="italic">no man stood by him,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.16">2 Tim. iv. 16</reference>. If we be thus looked strangely upon, remember, our Master was so before us. <div eID="gen24181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24182" type="x-p"/> (2.) They were there <hi type="italic">beholding,</hi> in which they showed a concern and kindness for Christ; when they were debarred from doing any other office of love to him, they looked a look of love toward him. [1.] It was a <hi type="italic">sorrowful</hi> look; they looked unto him who was now pierced, and <hi type="italic">mourned;</hi> and no doubt, were <hi type="italic">in bitterness</hi> for him. We may well imagine how it cut them to the heart, to see him in this torment; and what floods of tears it fetched from their eyes. Let us with an eye of faith behold Christ and him crucified, and be affected with that great love wherewith he loved us. But, [2.] It was no more than a look; they beheld him, but they could not <hi type="italic">help him.</hi> Note, When Christ was in his sufferings, the best of his friends were but spectators and lookers on, even the <hi type="italic">angelic guards stood trembling by,</hi> saith Mr. Norris, for he <hi type="italic">trod the wine-press alone,</hi> and of the people there was none with him; so <hi type="italic">his own arm wrought salvation.</hi>
entries.ebdc69c8bde0f3ed37f3fbecdebfbc27a57b41ae: <div eID="gen24182" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Burial of Christ.</title> <div sID="gen24183" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">57</hi> When the even was come, there came a rich man of Arimathæa, named Joseph, who also himself was Jesus' disciple: 58 He went to Pilate, and begged the body of Jesus. Then Pilate commanded the body to be delivered. <hi type="super">59</hi> And when Joseph had taken the body, he wrapped it in a clean linen cloth, 60 And laid it in his own new tomb, which he had hewn out in the rock: and he rolled a great stone to the door of the sepulchre, and departed. <hi type="super">61</hi> And there was Mary Magdalene, and the other Mary, sitting over against the sepulchre. <hi type="super">62</hi> Now the next day, that followed the day of the preparation, the chief priests and Pharisees came together unto Pilate, <hi type="super">63</hi> Saying, Sir, we remember that that deceiver said, while he was yet alive, After three days I will rise again. <hi type="super">64</hi> Command therefore that the sepulchre be made sure until the third day, lest his disciples come by night, and steal him away, and say unto the people, He is risen from the dead: so the last error shall be worse than the first. 65 Pilate said unto them, Ye have a watch: go your way, make <hi type="italic">it</hi> as sure as ye can. <hi type="super">66</hi> So they went, and made the sepulchre sure, sealing the stone, and setting a watch. <div eID="gen24183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24184" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of Christ's <hi type="italic">burial,</hi> and the manner and circumstances of it, concerning which observe, 1. The <hi type="italic">kindness</hi> and <hi type="italic">good will</hi> of his friends that <hi type="italic">laid him in the grave.</hi> 2. The <hi type="italic">malice</hi> and <hi type="italic">ill will</hi> of his enemies that were very solicitous to keep him there. <div eID="gen24184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24185" type="x-p"/> I. His friends gave him a <hi type="italic">decent burial.</hi> Observe, <div eID="gen24185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24186" type="x-p"/> 1. In general, that Jesus Christ was <hi type="italic">buried;</hi> when his precious soul was gone to paradise, his blessed body was deposited in the chambers of the grave, that he might answer the type of Jonas, and fulfil the prophecy of Isaias; he <hi type="italic">made his grave with the wicked.</hi> Thus in all things he must be made <hi type="italic">like unto his brethren,</hi> sin only excepted, and, like us, unto dust <hi type="italic">he must return.</hi> He was buried, to make his death the more certain, and his resurrection the more illustrious. Pilate would not deliver his body to be buried, till he was well assured that he was really dead; while the witnesses lay <hi type="italic">unburied,</hi> there were some hopes concerning them, <reference osisRef="Rev.11.8">Rev. xi. 8</reference>. But Christ, the great Witness, is as one <hi type="italic">free among the dead, like the slain that lie in the grave.</hi> He was <hi type="italic">buried,</hi> that he might take off the terror of the grave, and make it easy to us, might warm and perfume that cold noisome bed for us, and that we might be <hi type="italic">buried with him.</hi> <div eID="gen24186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24187" type="x-p"/> 2. The particular circumstances of his burial here related. <div eID="gen24187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24188" type="x-p"/> (1.) The time <hi type="italic">when</hi> he was buried; <hi type="italic">when the evening was come;</hi> the same evening that he died, before sun-set, as is usual in burying malefactors. It was not deferred till the next day, because it was <hi type="italic">the sabbath;</hi> for burying the dead is not proper work either for a day of rest or for a day of rejoicing, as the sabbath is. <div eID="gen24188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24189" type="x-p"/> (2.) The person that took care of the funeral was Joseph of Arimathea. The apostles had all fled, and none of them appeared to show this respect to their Master, which the disciples of John <hi type="italic">showed</hi> to him after he was beheaded, who <hi type="italic">took up his body, and buried it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.14.12">ch. xiv. 12</reference>. The women that followed him durst not move in it; then did God stir up this good man to do it; for what work God has to do, he will find out instruments to do it. Joseph was a fit man, for, [1.] He had wherewithal to do it, being a <hi type="italic">rich man.</hi> Most of Christ's disciples were poor men, such were most fit to go about the country to preach the gospel; but here was one that was a <hi type="italic">rich man,</hi> ready to be employed in a piece of service which required <hi type="italic">a man of estate.</hi> Note, Worldly wealth, though it is to many an objection in religion's way, yet, in some services to be done for Christ, it is an advantage and an opportunity, and it is well for those who have it, if withal they have a heart to use it for God's glory. [2.] He was well affected to our Lord Jesus, for he was himself <hi type="italic">his disciple,</hi> believed in him, though he did not openly profess it. Note, Christ has more secret disciples than we are aware of; seven thousand in Israel, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.4">Rom. xi. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen24189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24190" type="x-p"/> (3.) The grant of the dead body procured from Pilate, <reference osisRef="Matt.27.58">v. 58</reference>. Joseph <hi type="italic">went to</hi> Pilate, the proper person to be applied to on this occasion, who had the disposal of the body; for in things wherein the power of the magistrate is concerned, due regard must be had to that power, and nothing done to break in upon it. What we do that is good, must be done peaceably, and not tumultuously. Pilate was willing to give the body to one that would inter it decently, that he might do something towards atoning for the guilt his conscience charged him with in condemning an innocent person. In Joseph's petition, and Pilate's ready grant of it, <hi type="italic">honour</hi> was done to Christ, and a testimony borne to his <hi type="italic">integrity.</hi> <div eID="gen24190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24191" type="x-p"/> (4.) The dressing of the body in its grave-clothes (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.59">v. 59</reference>); though he was an honourable counsellor, yet he himself <hi type="italic">took the body,</hi> as it should seem, into his own arms, from the infamous and accursed tree (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.29">Acts xiii. 29</reference>); for where there is true love to Christ, no service will be thought too mean to stoop to for him. Having taken it, he wrapped it in a <hi type="italic">clean linen cloth;</hi> for burying in linen was then the common usage, which Joseph complied with. Note, Care is to be taken of the dead bodies of good men, for there is a glory intended for them at the resurrection, which we must hereby testify our belief of, and wind up the dead body as designed for a better place. This common act of humanity, if done after a <hi type="italic">godly sort,</hi> may be made an acceptable piece of Christianity. <div eID="gen24191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24192" type="x-p"/> (5.) The depositing of it in the sepulchre, <reference osisRef="Matt.27.60">v. 60</reference>. Here there was nothing of that pomp and solemnity with which the grandees of the world are <hi type="italic">brought to the grave, and laid in the tomb,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.21.32">Job xxi. 32</reference>. A private funeral did best befit him whose kingdom came not with observation. <div eID="gen24192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24193" type="x-p"/> [1.] He was laid in a <hi type="italic">borrowed</hi> tomb, in Joseph's burying place; as he had not a house of his own, wherein to <hi type="italic">lay his head</hi> while he lived, so he had not a grave of his own, wherein to <hi type="italic">lay his body</hi> when he was dead, which was an instance of his poverty; yet in this there might be somewhat of a mystery. The grave is the peculiar heritage of a <hi type="italic">sinner,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.24.19">Job xxiv. 19</reference>. There is nothing we can truly call our own but our sins and our graves; he <hi type="italic">returneth to his earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.146.4">Psalm cxlvi. 4</reference>. When we go to the grave, we go to our own place; but our Lord Jesus, who had no sin of his own, had no grave of his own; dying under imputed sin, it was fit that he should be buried in a <hi type="italic">borrowed</hi> grave; the Jews designed that he should have <hi type="italic">made his grave with the wicked,</hi> should have been buried with the thieves with whom he was crucified, but God over-ruled it, so as that he should make it <hi type="italic">with the rich in his death,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.53.9">Isa. liii. 9</reference>. <div eID="gen24193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24194" type="x-p"/> [2.] He was laid in a <hi type="italic">new tomb,</hi> which Joseph, it is likely, designed <hi type="italic">for himself;</hi> it would, however, be <hi type="italic">never the worse</hi> for <hi type="italic">his</hi> lying in it, who was to rise so quickly, but a <hi type="italic">great deal the better</hi> for <hi type="italic">his</hi> lying in it, who has altered the property of the grave, and made it <hi type="italic">anew</hi> indeed, by turning it into a <hi type="italic">bed of rest,</hi> nay into a <hi type="italic">bed of spices,</hi> for all the saints. <div eID="gen24194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24195" type="x-p"/> [3.] In a tomb that was <hi type="italic">hewn out of a rock;</hi> the ground about Jerusalem was generally rocky. Shebna had his sepulchre hewn out thereabouts <hi type="italic">in a rock,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.22.16">Isa. xxii. 16</reference>. Providence ordered it that Christ's sepulchre should be in a solid entire rock, that no room might be left to suspect his disciples had access to it by some underground passage, or broke through the back wall of it, to steal the body; for there was no access to it but by the door, which was watched. <div eID="gen24195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24196" type="x-p"/> [4.] A <hi type="italic">great stone was rolled to the door of his sepulchre;</hi> this also was according to the custom of the Jews in burying their dead, as appears by the description of the grave of Lazarus (<reference osisRef="John.11.38">John xi. 38</reference>), signifying that those who are dead, are <hi type="italic">separated</hi> and <hi type="italic">cut off from all the living;</hi> if the grave were his prison, now was the prison-door locked and bolted. The rolling of the stone to the grave's mouth, was with them as filling up the grave is with us, it completed the funeral. Having thus in silence and sorrow deposited the previous body of our Lord Jesus in the grave, the house <hi type="italic">appointed for all living,</hi> they <hi type="italic">departed</hi> without any further ceremony. It is the most melancholy circumstance in the funerals of our Christian friends, when we have laid their bodies in the dark and silent grave, to go home, and leave them behind; but alas, it is not we that <hi type="italic">go home,</hi> and <hi type="italic">leave them behind,</hi> no, it is they that are gone to the better home, and have left us behind. <div eID="gen24196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24197" type="x-p"/> (6.) The company that attended the funeral; and that was very <hi type="italic">small</hi> and <hi type="italic">mean.</hi> Here were none of the relations in mourning, to follow the corpse, no formalities to grace the solemnity, but some good women that were true mourners—<hi type="italic">Mary Magdalene, and the other Mary,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.27.56">v. 56</reference>. These, as they had attended him <hi type="italic">to the cross,</hi> so they followed him to <hi type="italic">the grave;</hi> as if they composed themselves to sorrow, they <hi type="italic">sat over against the sepulchre,</hi> not so much to fill their eyes with the sight of what was done, as to empty them in rivers of tears. Note, True love to Christ will carry us through, to the utmost, in following him. Death itself cannot quench that divine fire, <reference osisRef="Song.8.6-Song.8.7">Cant. viii. 6, 7</reference>. <div eID="gen24197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24198" type="x-p"/> II. His enemies did what they could to prevent his resurrection; what they did herein was <hi type="italic">the next day that followed the day of the preparation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.27.62">v. 62</reference>. That was the seventh day of the week, the Jewish <hi type="italic">sabbath,</hi> yet not expressly called so, but described by this periphrasis, because it was now shortly to give way to the Christian sabbath, which began the day after. Now, 1. All that day, Christ lay dead in the grave; having for six days laboured and done all his work, on the seventh day he <hi type="italic">rested,</hi> and was <hi type="italic">refreshed.</hi> 2. On that day, the <hi type="italic">chief priests and Pharisees,</hi> when they should have been at their devotions, asking pardon for the sins of the week past, were dealing with Pilate about securing the sepulchre, and so <hi type="italic">adding rebellion to their sin.</hi> They that had so often quarrelled with Christ for works of the greatest mercy on that day, were themselves busied in a work of the greatest malice. Observe here, <div eID="gen24198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24199" type="x-p"/> (1.) Their address to <hi type="italic">Pilate;</hi> they were vexed that the body was given to one that would bury it decently; but, since it must be so, they desire a guard may be set on the sepulchre. <div eID="gen24199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24200" type="x-p"/> [1.] Their petition sets forth, that <hi type="italic">that deceiver</hi> (so they call him who is truth itself) <hi type="italic">had said, After three days I will rise again.</hi> He had said so, and his disciples <hi type="italic">remembered</hi> those very words for the confirmation of their faith, but his persecutors remember them for the provocation of their rage and malice. Thus the same word of Christ to the one was a savour of life unto life, to the other of death unto death. See how they compliment Pilate with the title of <hi type="italic">Sir,</hi> while they reproach Christ with the title of <hi type="italic">Deceiver.</hi> Thus the most malicious slanderers of <hi type="italic">good men</hi> are commonly the most sordid flatterers of <hi type="italic">great men.</hi> <div eID="gen24200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24201" type="x-p"/> [2.] It further sets forth their jealousy; <hi type="italic">lest his disciples come by night, and steal him away, and say, He is risen.</hi> <div eID="gen24201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24202" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That which <hi type="italic">really</hi> they were afraid of, was, his <hi type="italic">resurrection;</hi> that which is most Christ's honour and his people's joy, is most the terror of his enemies. That which exasperated Joseph's brethren against him, was the presage of his rise, and of his having dominion over them (<reference osisRef="Gen.37.8">Gen. xxxvii. 8</reference>); and all they aimed at, in what they did against him, was, to prevent that. Come, say they, let us <hi type="italic">slay him,</hi> and see <hi type="italic">what will become of his dreams.</hi> So the chief priests and Pharisees laboured to defeat the predictions of Christ's resurrection, saying, as David's enemies of him (<reference osisRef="Ps.41.8">Ps. xli. 8</reference>), <hi type="italic">Now that he lieth, he shall rise up no more;</hi> if he should rise, that would break all their measures. Note, Christ's enemies, even when they have gained their point, are still in fear of losing it again. Perhaps the priests were surprised at the respect shown to Christ's dead body by Joseph and Nicodemus, two honourable counsellors, and looked upon it as an ill presage; nor can they forget his raising Lazarus from <hi type="italic">the dead,</hi> which so confounded them. <div eID="gen24202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24203" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That which they took on them to be afraid of, was, lest <hi type="italic">his disciples should come by night, and steal him away,</hi> which was a very improbable thing; for, 1. They had not the courage to own him while he lived, when they might have done him and themselves real service; and it was not likely that his death should put courage into such cowards. 2. What could they promise themselves by stealing away his body, and making people believe he was risen; when, if he should not rise, and so prove himself a deceiver, his disciples, who had left all for him in this world, in dependence upon a recompence in the other world, would of all others suffer most by the imposture, and would have had reason to throw the first stone at his name? What good would it do them, to carry on a cheat upon themselves, to steal away his body, and say, <hi type="italic">He is risen;</hi> when, if he were not risen, their faith was vain, and they were <hi type="italic">of all men the most miserable?</hi> The chief priests apprehend that if the doctrine of Christ's resurrection be once preached and believed, the <hi type="italic">last error will be worse than the first;</hi> a proverbial expression, intimating no more than this, that we shall all be routed, all undone. They think it was <hi type="italic">their error,</hi> that they had so long connived at his preaching and miracles, which <hi type="italic">error</hi> they thought they had <hi type="italic">rectified</hi> by putting him to death; but if people should be persuaded of his resurrection, that would <hi type="italic">spoil all</hi> again, his interest would revive with him, and theirs must needs sink, who had so barbarously murdered him. Note, Those that opposed Christ and his kingdom, will see not only their attempts baffled, but themselves miserably <hi type="italic">plunged</hi> and <hi type="italic">embarrassed,</hi> their errors each worse than other, and the last worst of all, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.4-Ps.2.5">Ps. ii. 4, 5</reference>. <div eID="gen24203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24204" type="x-p"/> [3.] In consideration hereof, they humbly move to have a guard set upon the sepulchre till the third day; <hi type="italic">Command that the sepulchre be made sure.</hi> Pilate must still be their drudge, his civil and military power must both be engaged to serve their malice; one would think that death's prisoners needed no other guard, and that the grave were <hi type="italic">security</hi> enough to itself; but what will not those fear, who are conscious to themselves both of <hi type="italic">guilt</hi> and <hi type="italic">impotency,</hi> in opposing the Lord and his anointed? <div eID="gen24204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24205" type="x-p"/> (2.) Pilate's answer to this address (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.65">v. 65</reference>); <hi type="italic">He have a watch, make it sure, as sure as you can.</hi> He was ready to gratify Christ's friends, in allowing them the body, and his enemies, in setting a guard upon it, being desirous to please all sides, while perhaps he laughed in his sleeve at both for making such ado, <hi type="italic">pro</hi> and <hi type="italic">con,</hi> about the dead body of a man, looking upon the hopes of one side and the fears of the other to be alike ridiculous. <hi type="italic">Ye have a watch;</hi> he means the constant guard that was kept in the tower of Antonia, out of which the allows them to detach as many as they pleased for that purpose, but, as if ashamed to be himself seen in such a thing, he leaves the management of it wholly to them. Methinks that word, <hi type="italic">Make it as sure as you can,</hi> looks like a banter, either, [1.] Of their <hi type="italic">fears;</hi> "Be sure to set a strong guard upon the dead man;" or rather, [2.] Of their <hi type="italic">hopes;</hi> "Do your worst, try your wit and strength to the utmost; but if he be of God, he will rise, in spite of you and all your guards." I am apt to think, that by this time Pilate had had some talk with the centurion, his own officer, of whom he would be apt to enquire how that <hi type="italic">just man</hi> died, whom he had condemned with such reluctance; and that he gave him such an account of those things as made him conclude that <hi type="italic">truly he was the Son of God;</hi> and Pilate would give more credit to him than to a thousand of those spiteful priests that called him a <hi type="italic">Deceiver;</hi> and if so, no marvel that he tacitly derides their project, in thinking to secure the sepulchre upon him who had so lately rent the rocks, and made the earth to quake. Tertullion, speaking of Pilate, saith, <hi type="italic">Ipse jam pro su&#226; conscienti&#226; Christianus—In his conscience he was a Christian;</hi> and it is possible that he might be under such convictions at this time, upon the centurion's report, and yet never be thoroughly persuaded, any more than Agrippa or Felix was, to be a Christian. <div eID="gen24205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24206" type="x-p"/> (3.) The wonderful care they took, hereupon, to secure the sepulchre (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.66">v. 66</reference>); <hi type="italic">They sealed the stone;</hi> probably with the great seal of their <hi type="italic">sanhedrim,</hi> whereby they interposed their authority, for who durst break the public seal? But not trusting too much to that, withal they <hi type="italic">set a watch,</hi> to keep <hi type="italic">his disciples</hi> from coming to <hi type="italic">steal him away,</hi> and, if possible, to hinder <hi type="italic">him</hi> from coming out of the grave. So they intended, but God brought this good out of it, that they who were set to <hi type="italic">oppose</hi> his resurrection, thereby had an opportunity to observe it, and did so, and told the chief priests what they observed, who were thereby rendered the more inexcusable. Here was all the power of earth and hell combined to keep Christ a prisoner, but all in vain, when his hour was come; death, and all those sons and heirs of death, could then no longer hold him, no longer have dominion over him. To guard the sepulchre against the poor weak disciples, was folly, because <hi type="italic">needless;</hi> but to think to guard it against the power of God was folly, because <hi type="italic">fruitless</hi> and to no purpose; and yet they thought they had <hi type="italic">dealt wisely.</hi>  <chapter eID="Matt.27"/> <div eID="gen24206" type="x-p"/>

entries.6a5847d61f817dc893b2346793b94a61496c2d28: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13820"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 27</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.27.1-Matt.27.10">Mt 27:1-10</reference>. Jesus Led Away to Pilate--Remorse and Suicide of Judas. ( =</title> <div sID="gen26523" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Mark.15.1">Mr 15:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.23.1">Lu 23:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.18.28">Joh 18:28</reference>).<div eID="gen26523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26524" type="x-p"/> Jesus Led Away to Pilate (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.1">Mt 27:1</reference>, 2).<div eID="gen26524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26525" type="x-p"/> For the exposition of this portion, see on <reference osisRef="John.18.28">Joh 18:28</reference>, &c.<div eID="gen26525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26526" type="x-p"/> Remorse and Suicide of Judas (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.3-Matt.27.10">Mt 27:3-10</reference>).<div eID="gen26526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26527" type="x-p"/> This portion is peculiar to Matthew. On the progress of guilt in the traitor, see on <reference osisRef="Mark.14.1-Mark.14.11">Mr 14:1-11</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.13.21-John.13.30">Joh 13:21-30</reference>.<div eID="gen26527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26528" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13820"/><hi type="bold">3. Then Judas, which had betrayed him, when he saw that he was condemned--</hi>The condemnation, even though not unexpected, might well fill him with horror. But perhaps this unhappy man expected, that, while he got the bribe, the Lord would miraculously escape, as He had once and again done before, out of His enemies' power: and if so, his remorse would come upon him with all the greater keenness.<div eID="gen26528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26529" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">repented himself--</hi>but, as the issue too sadly showed, it was "the sorrow of the world, which worketh death" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.7.10">2Co 7:10</reference>).<div eID="gen26529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26530" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and brought again the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders--</hi>A remarkable illustration of the power of an awakened conscience. A short time before, the promise of this sordid pelf was temptation enough to his covetous heart to outweigh the most overwhelming obligations of duty and love; now, the possession of it so lashes him that he cannot use it, cannot even keep it! <div eID="gen26530" type="x-p"/>
entries.e6d1bfd12651b2f1662de8a2653316f2ed305bf2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13821"/><div sID="gen26531" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13821"/><hi type="bold">4. Saying, I have sinned in that I have betrayed the innocent blood--</hi>What a testimony this to Jesus! Judas had been with Him in all circumstances for three years; his post, as treasurer to Him and the Twelve (<reference osisRef="John.12.6">Joh 12:6</reference>), gave him peculiar opportunity of watching the spirit, disposition, and habits of his Master; while his covetous nature and thievish practices would incline him to dark and suspicious, rather than frank and generous, interpretations of all that He said and did. If, then, he could have fastened on one questionable feature in all that he had so long witnessed, we may be sure that no such speech as this would ever have escaped his lips, nor would he have been so stung with remorse as not to be able to keep the money and survive his crime.<div eID="gen26531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26532" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And they said, What is that to us? see thou to that--</hi>"Guilty or innocent is nothing to us: We have Him now--begone!" Was ever speech more hellish uttered? <div eID="gen26532" type="x-p"/>
entries.9de2d4689ed0551930db8d7c54c436273223f678: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13822"/><div sID="gen26533" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13822"/><hi type="bold">5. And he cast down the pieces of silver--</hi>The sarcastic, diabolical reply which he had got, in place of the sympathy which perhaps he expected, would deepen his remorse into an agony.<div eID="gen26533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26534" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the temple--</hi>the temple proper, commonly called "the sanctuary," or "the holy place," into which only the priests might enter. How is this to be explained? Perhaps he flung the money in after them. But thus were fulfilled the words of the prophet--"I cast them to the potter in the house of the Lord" (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.13">Zec 11:13</reference>).<div eID="gen26534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26535" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and departed, and went and hanged himself--</hi>For the details, see on <reference osisRef="Acts.1.18">Ac 1:18</reference>. <div eID="gen26535" type="x-p"/>
entries.1bf6a05d9418e410b5d5a608d965fb8d9a6c4165: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13823"/><div sID="gen26536" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13823"/><hi type="bold">6. And the chief priests took the silver pieces, and said, It is not lawful for to put them into the treasury--</hi>"the Corban," or chest containing the money dedicated to sacred purposes (see on <reference osisRef="Matt.15.5">Mt 15:5</reference>).<div eID="gen26536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26537" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because it is the price of blood--</hi>How scrupulous now! But those punctilious scruples made them unconsciously fulfil the Scripture. <div eID="gen26537" type="x-p"/>
entries.aea4d54d897558fec4ba651df6ad746c32a20787: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13824"/><div sID="gen26538" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13824"/><hi type="bold">9. Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by Jeremy the prophet, saying--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Zech.11.12">Zec 11:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.11.13">13</reference>). Never was a complicated prophecy, otherwise hopelessly dark, more marvellously fulfilled. Various conjectures have been formed to account for Matthew's ascribing to Jeremiah a prophecy found in the book of Zechariah. But since with this book he was plainly familiar, having quoted one of its most remarkable prophecies of Christ but a few chapters before (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.4">Mt 21:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.21.5">5</reference>), the question is one more of critical interest than real importance. Perhaps the true explanation is the following, from Lightfoot: "Jeremiah of old had the first place among the prophets, and hereby he comes to be mentioned above all the rest in <reference osisRef="Matt.16.14">Mt 16:14</reference>; because he stood first in the volume of the prophets (as he proves from the learned David Kimchi) therefore he is first named. When, therefore, Matthew produceth a text of Zechariah under the name of Jeremy, he only cites the words of the volume of the prophets under his name who stood first in the volume of the prophets. Of which sort is that also of our Saviour (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.41">Lu 24:41</reference>), 'All things must be fulfilled which are written of Me in the Law, and the Prophets, and the Psalms,' or the Book of Hagiographa, in which the Psalms were placed first."<div eID="gen26538" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.27.11-Matt.27.26">Mt 27:11-26</reference>. Jesus Again before Pilate--He Seeks to Release Him but at Length Delivers Him to Be Crucified. ( = <reference osisRef="Mark.15.1-Mark.15.15">Mr 15:1-15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.23.1-Luke.23.25">Lu 23:1-25</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.18.28-John.18.40">Joh 18:28-40</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen26539" type="x-p"/> For the exposition, see on <reference osisRef="Luke.23.1-Luke.23.25">Lu 23:1-25</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.18.28-John.18.40">Joh 18:28-40</reference>.<div eID="gen26539" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.27.27-Matt.27.33">Mt 27:27-33</reference>. Jesus Scornfully and Cruelly Entreated of the Soldiers, Is Led Away to Be Crucified. ( = <reference osisRef="Mark.15.16-Mark.15.22">Mr 15:16-22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.23.26-Luke.23.31">Lu 23:26-31</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.19.2">Joh 19:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.19.17">17</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen26540" type="x-p"/> For the exposition, see on <reference osisRef="Mark.15.16-Mark.15.22">Mr 15:16-22</reference>.<div eID="gen26540" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.27.34-Matt.27.50">Mt 27:34-50</reference>. Crucifixion and Death of the Lord Jesus. ( = <reference osisRef="Mark.15.25-Mark.15.37">Mr 15:25-37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.23.33-Luke.23.46">Lu 23:33-46</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.19.18-John.19.30">Joh 19:18-30</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen26541" type="x-p"/> For the exposition, see on <reference osisRef="John.19.18-John.19.30">Joh 19:18-30</reference>.<div eID="gen26541" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.27.51-Matt.27.66">Mt 27:51-66</reference>. Signs and Circumstances Following the Death of the Lord Jesus--He Is Taken Down from the Cross, and Buried--The Sepulchre Is Guarded. ( = <reference osisRef="Mark.15.38-Mark.15.47">Mr 15:38-47</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.23.47-Luke.23.56">Lu 23:47-56</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.19.31-John.19.42">Joh 19:31-42</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen26542" type="x-p"/> The Veil Rent (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.51">Mt 27:51</reference>). <div eID="gen26542" type="x-p"/>
entries.bdd091e6e60ec239ab33b1ad179b5ea4063b1552: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13825"/><div sID="gen26543" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13825"/><hi type="bold">51. And, behold, the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom--</hi>This was the thick and gorgeously wrought veil which was hung between the "holy place" and the "holiest of all," shutting out all access to the presence of God as manifested "from above the mercy seat and from between the cherubim"--"the Holy Ghost this signifying, that the way into the holiest of all was not yet made manifest" (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.8">He 9:8</reference>). Into this holiest of all none might enter, not even the high priest, save once a year, on the great day of atonement, and then only with the blood of atonement in his hands, which he sprinkled "upon and before the mercy seat seven times" (<reference osisRef="Lev.16.14">Le 16:14</reference>)--to signify that access for sinners to a holy God is only through atoning blood. But as they had only the blood of bulls and of goats, which could not take away sins (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.4">He 10:4</reference>), during all the long ages that preceded the death of Christ the thick veil remained; the blood of bulls and of goats continued to be shed and sprinkled; and once a year access to God through an atoning sacrifice was vouchsafed--in a picture, or rather, was dramatically represented, in those symbolical actions--nothing more. But now, the one atoning Sacrifice being provided in the precious blood of Christ, access to this holy God could no longer be denied; and so the moment the Victim expired on the altar, that thick veil which for so many ages had been the dread symbol of separation between God and guilty men was, without a hand touching it, mysteriously "rent in twain from top to bottom"--"the Holy Ghost this signifying, that the way into the holiest of all was NOW made manifest!" How emphatic the statement, from top to bottom; as if to say, Come boldly now to the Throne of Grace; the veil is clean gone; the mercy seat stands open to the gaze of sinners, and the way to it is sprinkled with the blood of Him--"who through the eternal Spirit hath offered Himself without spot to God!" Before, it was death to go in, now it is death to stay out. See more on this glorious subject on He 10. 19-22.<div eID="gen26543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26544" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">An Earthquake--</hi>The Rocks Rent--The Graves Opened, that the Saints Which Slept in Them Might Come Forth after Their Lord's Resurrection (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.51-Matt.27.53">Mt 27:51-53</reference>). <div eID="gen26544" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13826"/><div sID="gen26545" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13826"/><hi type="bold">51. and the earth did quake--</hi>From what follows it would seem that this earthquake was local, having for its object the rending of the rocks and the opening of the graves.<div eID="gen26545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26546" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and the rocks rent--</hi>"were rent"--the physical creation thus sublimely proclaiming, at the bidding of its Maker, the concussion which at that moment was taking place in the moral world at the most critical moment of its history. Extraordinary rents and fissures have been observed in the rocks near this spot. <div eID="gen26546" type="x-p"/>
entries.00bea2688bd4b2b8a0081b8703b23501b51f276d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13827"/><div sID="gen26547" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13827"/><hi type="bold">52. And the graves were opened; and many bodies of the saints which slept arose--</hi>These sleeping saints (see on <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.14">1Th 4:14</reference>) were Old Testament believers, who--according to the usual punctuation in our version--were quickened into resurrection life at the moment of their Lord's death, but lay in their graves till His resurrection, when they came forth. But it is far more natural, as we think, and consonant with other Scriptures, to understand that only the graves were opened, probably by the earthquake, at our Lord's death, and this only in preparation for the subsequent exit of those who slept in them, when the Spirit of life should enter into them from their risen Lord, and along with Him they should come forth, trophies of His victory over the grave. Thus, in the opening of the graves at the moment of the Redeemer's expiring, there was a glorious symbolical proclamation that the death which had just taken place had "swallowed up death in victory"; and whereas the saints that slept in them were awakened only by their risen Lord, to accompany Him out of the tomb, it was fitting that "the Prince of Life ... should be the First that should rise from the dead" (<reference osisRef="Acts.26.23">Ac 26:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.20">1Co 15:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.23">23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.1.18">Col 1:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.1.5">Re 1:5</reference>).<div eID="gen26547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26548" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and went into the holy city--</hi>that city where He, in virtue of whose resurrection they were now alive, had been condemned.<div eID="gen26548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26549" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and appeared unto many--</hi>that there might be undeniable evidence of their own resurrection first, and through it of their Lord's. Thus, while it was not deemed fitting that He Himself should appear again in Jerusalem, save to the disciples, provision was made that the fact of His resurrection should be left in no doubt. It must be observed, however, that the resurrection of these sleeping saints was not like those of the widow of Nain's son, of Jairus' daughter, of Lazarus, and of the man who "revived and stood upon his feet," on his dead body touching the bones of Elisha (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.13.21">2Ki 13:21</reference>)--which were mere temporary recallings of the departed spirit to the mortal body, to be followed by a final departure of it "till the trumpet shall sound." But this was a resurrection once for all, to life everlasting; and so there is no room to doubt that they went to glory with their Lord, as bright trophies of His victory over death.<div eID="gen26549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26550" type="x-p"/> The Centurion's Testimony (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.54">Mt 27:54</reference>). <div eID="gen26550" type="x-p"/>
entries.ae502b55199329304aef0caab0b49e6993afc135: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13828"/><div sID="gen26551" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13828"/><hi type="bold">54. Now when the centurion--</hi>the military superintendent of the execution.<div eID="gen26551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26552" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and they that were with him watching Jesus, saw the earthquake--</hi>or felt it and witnessed its effects.<div eID="gen26552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26553" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and those things that were done--</hi>reflecting upon the entire transaction.<div eID="gen26553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26554" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they feared greatly--</hi>convinced of the presence of a Divine Hand.<div eID="gen26554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26555" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">saying, Truly this was the Son of God--</hi>There cannot be a reasonable doubt that this expression was used in the Jewish sense, and that it points to the claim which Jesus made to be the Son of God, and on which His condemnation expressly turned. The meaning, then, clearly is that He must have been what He professed to be; in other words, that He was no impostor. There was no medium between those two. See, on the similar testimony of the penitent thief--"This man hath done nothing amiss"--Luke 23. 41.<div eID="gen26555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26556" type="x-p"/> The Galilean Women (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.55">Mt 27:55</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.27.56">56</reference>). <div eID="gen26556" type="x-p"/>
entries.f009ed6131f9bc57d7ca8ccd6e0d8ea56a2e2715: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13829"/><div sID="gen26557" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13829"/><hi type="bold">55. And many women were there beholding afar off, which followed Jesus--</hi>The sense here would be better brought out by the use of the pluperfect, "which had followed Jesus."<div eID="gen26557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26558" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from Galilee, ministering unto him--</hi>As these dear women had ministered to Him during His glorious missionary tours in Galilee (see on <reference osisRef="Luke.8.1-Luke.8.3">Lu 8:1-3</reference>), so from this statement it should seem that they accompanied him and ministered to His wants from Galilee on His final journey to Jerusalem. <div eID="gen26558" type="x-p"/>
entries.d8690ddc1d58475dd31ff3babd6f02e596a1e45d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13830"/><div sID="gen26559" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13830"/><hi type="bold">56. Among which was Mary Magdalene--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Luke.8.2">Lu 8:2</reference>).<div eID="gen26559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26560" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and Mary the mother of James and Joses--</hi>the wife of Cleophas, or rather Clopas, and sister of the Virgin (<reference osisRef="John.19.25">Joh 19:25</reference>). See on <reference osisRef="Matt.13.55">Mt 13:55</reference>,<reference osisRef="Matt.13.56">56</reference>.<div eID="gen26560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26561" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and the mother of Zebedee's children--</hi>that is, Salome: compare <reference osisRef="Mark.15.40">Mr 15:40</reference>. All this about the women is mentioned for the sake of what is afterwards to be related of their purchasing spices to anoint their Lord's body.<div eID="gen26561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26562" type="x-p"/> The Taking Down from the Cross and the Burial (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.57-Matt.27.60">Mt 27:57-60</reference>).<div eID="gen26562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26563" type="x-p"/> For the exposition of this portion, see on <reference osisRef="John.19.38-John.19.42">Joh 19:38-42</reference>.<div eID="gen26563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26564" type="x-p"/> The Women Mark the Sacred Spot that They Might Recognize It on Coming Thither to Anoint the Body (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.61">Mt 27:61</reference>). <div eID="gen26564" type="x-p"/>
entries.171387c5606d10f900ff736ed9c04a019170f4d3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13831"/><div sID="gen26565" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13831"/><hi type="bold">61. And there was Mary Magdalene, and the other Mary--</hi>"the mother of James and Joses," mentioned before (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.56">Mt 27:56</reference>).<div eID="gen26565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26566" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sitting over against the sepulchre--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Mark.16.1">Mr 16:1</reference>).<div eID="gen26566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26567" type="x-p"/> The Sepulchre Guarded (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.62-Matt.27.66">Mt 27:62-66</reference>). <div eID="gen26567" type="x-p"/>
entries.072338163954f219b12d4501b4a257663ebf5013: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13832"/><div sID="gen26568" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13832"/><hi type="bold">62. Now the next day, that followed the day of the preparation--</hi>that is, after six o'clock of our Saturday evening. The crucifixion took place on the Friday and all was not over till shortly before sunset, when the Jewish sabbath commenced; and "that sabbath day was an high day" (<reference osisRef="John.19.31">Joh 19:31</reference>), being the first day of the feast of unleavened bread. That day being over at six on Saturday evening, they hastened to take their measures. <div eID="gen26568" type="x-p"/>
entries.da220fdc12a26f439709aa1ddef9d4f34c996a3a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13833"/><div sID="gen26569" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13833"/><hi type="bold">63. Saying, Sir, we remember that that deceiver--</hi>Never, remarks Bengel, will you find the heads of the people calling Jesus by His own name. And yet here there is betrayed a certain uneasiness, which one almost fancies they only tried to stifle in their own minds, as well as crush in Pilate's, in case he should have any lurking suspicion that he had done wrong in yielding to them.<div eID="gen26569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26570" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">said, while he was yet alive--</hi>Important testimony this, from the lips of His bitterest enemies, to the reality of Christ's death; the corner-stone of the whole Christian religion.<div eID="gen26570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26571" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">After three days--</hi>which, according to the customary Jewish way of reckoning, need signify no more than "after the commencement of the third day."<div eID="gen26571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26572" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I will rise again--</hi>"I rise," in the present tense, thus reporting not only the fact that this prediction of His had reached their ears, but that they understood Him to look forward confidently to its occurring on the very day named. <div eID="gen26572" type="x-p"/>
entries.5dbc3fcfe05780ed1ae8ffef9e6ec764bffabaa4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13834"/><div sID="gen26573" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13834"/><hi type="bold">64. Command therefore that the sepulchre be made sure--</hi>by a Roman guard.<div eID="gen26573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26574" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">until the third day--</hi>after which, if He still lay in the grave, the imposture of His claims would be manifest to all.<div eID="gen26574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26575" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and say unto the people, he is risen from the dead--</hi>Did they really fear this?<div eID="gen26575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26576" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">so the last error shall be worse than the first--</hi>the imposture of His pretended resurrection worse than that of His pretended Messiahship. <div eID="gen26576" type="x-p"/>
entries.1dd6ff5e2aebe77fd48c3d37ff574df2a4c6760c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13835"/><div sID="gen26577" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13835"/><hi type="bold">65. Pilate said unto them, Ye have a watch--</hi>The guards had already acted under orders of the Sanhedrim, with Pilate's consent; but probably they were not clear about employing them as a night watch without Pilate's express authority.<div eID="gen26577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26578" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">go your way, make it as sure as ye can--</hi>as ye know how, or in the way ye deem securest. Though there may be no irony in this speech, it evidently insinuated that if the event should be contrary to their wish, it would not be for want of sufficient human appliances to prevent it. <div eID="gen26578" type="x-p"/>
entries.db51bb926af9fe5a87beeba84ffc1ac2bcadd768: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13836"/><div sID="gen26579" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13836"/><hi type="bold">66. So they went, and made the sepulchre sure, sealing the stone--</hi>which Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.16.4">Mr 16:4</reference>) says was "very great."<div eID="gen26579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26580" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and setting a watch--</hi>to guard it. What more could man do? But while they are trying to prevent the resurrection of the Prince of Life, God makes use of their precautions for His own ends. Their stone-covered, seal-secured sepulchre shall preserve the sleeping dust of the Son of God free from all indignities, in undisturbed, sublime repose; while their watch shall be His guard of honor until the angels shall come to take their place. <chapter eID="Matt.27"/>

entries.cdeb46c1afb5cd9a078451217b223bc85e0eab29: <div eID="gen38838" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen38839" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen38840" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen38840" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen38839" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen38841" type="x-p"/> In the morning, Christ is bound and delivered to Pontius Pilate, <reference osisRef="Mat.27.1">Mat 27:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.27.2">Mat 27:2</reference>. Judas, seeing his Master condemned, repents, acknowledges his transgression to the chief priests, attests Christ's innocence, throws down the money, and goes and hangs himself, <reference osisRef="Mat.27.3-Mat.27.5">Mat 27:3-5</reference>. They buy the potter's field with the money, <reference osisRef="Mat.27.6-Mat.27.10">Mat 27:6-10</reference>. Christ, questioned by Pilate, refuses to answer, <reference osisRef="Mat.27.11-Mat.27.14">Mat 27:11-14</reference>. Pilate, while inquiring of the Jews whether they would have Jesus or Barabbas released, receives a message from his wife to have nothing to do in this wicked business, <reference osisRef="Mat.27.15-Mat.27.19">Mat 27:15-19</reference>. The multitude, influenced by the chief priests and elders, desire Barabbas to be released, and Jesus to be crucified, <reference osisRef="Mat.27.20-Mat.27.23">Mat 27:20-23</reference>. Pilate attests his innocence, and the people make themselves and their posterity responsible for his blood, <reference osisRef="Mat.27.24">Mat 27:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.27.25">Mat 27:25</reference>. Barabbas is released, and Christ is scourged, <reference osisRef="Mat.27.26">Mat 27:26</reference>. The soldiers strip him, clothe him with a scarlet robe, crown him with thorns, mock, and variously insult him, <reference osisRef="Mat.27.27-Mat.27.31">Mat 27:27-31</reference>. Simon compelled to bear his cross, <reference osisRef="Mat.27.32">Mat 27:32</reference>. They bring him to Golgotha, give him vinegar mingled with gall to drink, crucify him, and cast lots for his raiment, <reference osisRef="Mat.27.33-Mat.27.36">Mat 27:33-36</reference>. His accusation, <reference osisRef="Mat.27.37">Mat 27:37</reference>. Two thieves are crucified with him, <reference osisRef="Mat.27.38">Mat 27:38</reference>. He is mocked and insulted while hanging on the cross, <reference osisRef="Mat.27.39-Mat.27.44">Mat 27:39-44</reference>. The awful darkness, <reference osisRef="Mat.27.45">Mat 27:45</reference>. Jesus calls upon God, is offered vinegar to drink, expires, <reference osisRef="Mat.27.46-Mat.27.50">Mat 27:46-50</reference>. Prodigies that accompanied and followed his death, <reference osisRef="Mat.27.51-Mat.27.53">Mat 27:51-53</reference>. He is acknowledged by the centurion, <reference osisRef="Mat.27.54">Mat 27:54</reference>. Several women behold the crucifixion, <reference osisRef="Mat.27.55">Mat 27:55</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.27.56">Mat 27:56</reference>. Joseph of Arimathea begs the body of Pilate, and deposites it in his own new tomb, <reference osisRef="Mat.27.57-Mat.27.60">Mat 27:57-60</reference>. The women watch the sepulchre, <reference osisRef="Mat.27.61">Mat 27:61</reference>. The Jews consult with Pilate how they may prevent the resurrection of Christ, <reference osisRef="Mat.27.62-Mat.27.64">Mat 27:62-64</reference>. He grants them a guard for the sepulchre, and they seal the stone that stopped the mouth of the tomb where he was laid, <reference osisRef="Mat.27.65">Mat 27:65</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.27.66">Mat 27:66</reference>. <div eID="gen38841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38842" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen38842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38843" type="x-p"/> When the morning was come - As soon as it was light - took counsel against Jesus. They had begun this counsel the preceding evening, see <reference osisRef="Mat.26.59">Mat 26:59</reference>. But as it was contrary to all forms of law to proceed against a person's life by night, they seem to have separated for a few hours, and then, at the break of day, came together again, pretending to conduct the business according to the forms of law. <div eID="gen38843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38844" type="x-p"/> To put him to death - They had already determined his death, and pronounced the sentence of death on him; <reference osisRef="Mat.26.66">Mat 26:66</reference>. And now they assemble under the pretense of reconsidering the evidence, and deliberating on it, to give the greater appearance of justice to their conduct. They wished to make it appear that "they had taken ample time to consider of it, and, from the fullest conviction, by the most satisfactory and conclusive evidence, they had now delivered him into the hands of the Romans, to meet that death to which they had adjudged him."
entries.37c67a3a092f8fc23bbeb67d8d419ec0524d30d2: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen38844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38845" type="x-p"/> They - delivered him to Pontius Pilate - The Sanhedrin had the power of life and death in their own hands in every thing that concerned religion; but as they had not evidence to put Christ to death because of false doctrine, they wished to give countenance to their conduct by bringing in the civil power, and therefore they delivered him up to Pilate as one who aspired to regal dignities, and whom he must put to death, if he professed to be Caesar's friend. Pontius Pilate governed Judea ten years under the Emperor Tiberius; but, having exercised great cruelties against the Samaritans, they complained of him to the emperor, in consequence of which he was deposed, and sent in exile to Vienna, in Dauphiny, where he killed himself two years after.
entries.46b05a61d226ce651d5b0d6daf9aa51c18bd6dec: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen38845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38846" type="x-p"/> Judas - when he saw that he was condemned, repented - There is much of the wisdom and goodness of God to be seen in this part of Judas's conduct. Had our Lord been condemned to death on the evidence of one of his own disciples, it would have furnished infidels with a strong argument against Christ and the Christian religion. "One of his own disciples, knowing the whole imposture, declared it to the Jewish rulers, in consequence of which he was put to death as an impostor and deceiver." But the traitor, being stung with remorse, came and acknowledged his crime, and solemnly declared the innocence of his Master, threw back the money which they gave him to induce him to do this villainous act; and, to establish the evidence which he now gave against them and himself, in behalf of the innocence of Christ, hanged himself, or died through excessive grief and contrition. Thus the character of Christ was rescued from all reproach; infidelity deprived of the power to cry "imposture!" and the Jewish rulers overwhelmed with eternal infamy. If it should ever be said, "One who knew him best delivered him up as an impostor," - to this it may be immediately answered, "The same person, struck with remorse, came and declared his own guilt, and Christ's innocence; accused and convicted the Jewish rulers, in the open council, of having hired him to do this iniquitous action, threw them back the bribe they had given him, and then hanged himself through distress and despair, concluding his iniquity in this business was too great to be forgiven." Let him who chooses, after this plenary evidence to the innocence of Christ, continue the objection, and cry out imposture! take heed that he go not and do Likewise. Caiaphas, Pilate, and Judas have done so already, and I have known several, who have called Christ an impostor, who have cut their own throats, shot, drowned, or hanged themselves. God is a jealous God, and highly resents every thing that is done and said against that eternal truth that came to man through Jesus Christ, by the Holy Spirit. Indeed, there is one class of Deists, viz. those who are vicious in their lives, and virulent in their opposition to Christianity, who generally bring themselves to an untimely end.
entries.4094970ee58c6e929755b7c3c8969a84090cfba2: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen38846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38847" type="x-p"/> Innocent blood - Αιμα αθωον, a Hebraism, for an innocent man. But instead of αθωον, innocent, two ancient MSS., Syriac, Vulgate, Sahidic, Armenian, and all the Itala; Origen, Cyprian, Lucifer, Ambrose, Leo, read δικαιον, righteous, or just. <div eID="gen38847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38848" type="x-p"/> What is that to us? - What is it? - A great deal. You should immediately go and reverse the sentence you have pronounced, and liberate the innocent person. But this would have been justice, and that would have been a stranger at their tribunal.
entries.06c558bd0ae5cf8d6234fb3e6d4e09e61a42ab4a: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen38848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38849" type="x-p"/> In the temple - Ναος signifies, properly, the temple itself, into which none but the priests were permitted to enter; therefore εν τῳ ναῳ must signify, near the temple, by the temple door, where the boxes stood to receive the free-will offerings of the people, for the support and repairs of the sacred edifice. See this amply proved by Kypke. <div eID="gen38849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38850" type="x-p"/> Hanged himself - Or was strangled - απηγξατο. Some eminent critics believe that he was only suffocated by excessive grief, and thus they think the account here given will agree with that in <reference osisRef="Act.1.18">Act 1:18</reference>. Mr. Wakefield supports this meaning of the word with great learning and ingenuity. I have my doubts - the old method of reconciling the two accounts appears to me quite plausible - he went and strangled himself, and the rope breaking, he fell down, and by the violence of the fall his body was bursted, and his bowels gushed out. I have thought proper, on a matter of such difficulty, to use the word strangled, as possessing a middle meaning between choking or suffocation by excessive grief, and hanging, as an act of suicide. See the note on <reference osisRef="Mat.10.4">Mat 10:4</reference>. Dr. Lightfoot is of opinion that the devil caught him up into the air, strangled him, and threw him down on the ground with violence, so that his body was burst, and his guts shed out! This was an ancient tradition.
entries.66215913e845e67d22b50f3a8eb5daf700b990f2: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen38850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38851" type="x-p"/> The treasury - Κορβαναν - the place whither the people brought their free-will offerings for the service of the temple, so called from the Hebrew קרבן korban, An Offering, from קרב karab, he drew nigh, because the person who brought the gift came nigh to that place where God manifested his glory between the cherubim, over the mercy-seat in the most holy place. It is from this idea that the phrase to draw nigh to God is taken, which is so frequently used in the sacred writings. <div eID="gen38851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38852" type="x-p"/> Because it is the price of blood - "What hypocrites, as one justly exclaims, to adjudge an innocent man to death, and break the eternal laws of justice and mercy without scruple, and to be, at the same time, so very nice in their attention to a ceremonial direction of the law of Moses! Thus it is that the devil often deludes many, even among the priests, by a false and superstitious tenderness or conscience in things indifferent, while calumny, envy, oppression of the innocent, and a conformity to the world, give them no manner of trouble or disturbance." See Quesnel.
entries.0002597da6e342dc7241592ed5e07dc820a1db10: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen38852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38853" type="x-p"/> To bury strangers in - Τοις ξενοις, the strangers, probably meaning, as some learned men conjecture, the Jewish strangers who might have come to Jerusalem, either to worship, or on some other business, and died there during their stay. See here, the very money for which the blessed Jesus was sold becomes subservient to the purpose of mercy and kindness! The bodies of strangers have a place of rest in the field purchased by the price at which his life was valued, and the souls of strangers and foreigners have a place of rest and refuge in his blood which was shed as a ransom price for the salvation of the whole world.
entries.9ecc714654b5d7c241d32a6e68e6be636dc1f187: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen38853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38854" type="x-p"/> The field of blood - In vain do the wicked attempt to conceal themselves; God makes them instrumental in discovering their own wickedness. Judas, by returning the money, and the priests, by laying it out, raise to themselves an eternal monument - the one of his treachery, the others of their perfidiousness, and both of the innocence of Jesus Christ. As, long as the Jewish polity continued, it might be said, "This is the field that was bought from the potter with the money which Judas got from the high priests for betraying his Master; which he, in deep compunction of spirit, brought back to them, and they bought this ground for a burial-place for strangers: for as it was the price of the blood of an innocent man, they did not think proper to let it rest in the treasury of the temple where the traitor had thrown it, who afterwards, in despair, went and hanged himself." What a standing proof must this have been of the innocence of Christ, and of their perfidy!
entries.7ad9502b39b67d9e043fd38482a5c2685b315917: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen38854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38855" type="x-p"/> Jeremy the prophet - The words quoted here are not found in the Prophet Jeremiah, but in <reference osisRef="Zac.11.13">Zac 11:13</reference>. But St. Jerome says that a Hebrew of the sect of the Nazarenes showed him this prophecy in a Hebrew apocryphal copy of Jeremiah; but probably they were inserted there only to countenance the quotation here. <div eID="gen38855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38856" type="x-p"/> One of Colbert's, a MS. of the eleventh century, has Ζαχαριου, Zechariah; so has the later Syriac in the margin, and a copy of the Arabic quoted by Bengel. In a very elegant and correct MS. of the Vulgate, in my possession, written in the fourteenth century, Zachariam is in the margin, and Jeremiam in the text, but the former is written by a later hand. Jeremiah is wanting in two MSS., the Syriac, later Persic, two of the Itala, and in some other Latin copies. It is very likely that the original reading was δια τοι προφητου, and the name of no prophet mentioned. This is the more likely, as Matthew often omits the name of the prophet in his quotations. See <reference osisRef="Mat.1.22">Mat 1:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mat.2.5">Mat 2:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.2.15">Mat 2:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mat.13.35">Mat 13:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mat.21.4">Mat 21:4</reference>. Bengel approves of the omission. <div eID="gen38856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38857" type="x-p"/> It was an ancient custom among the Jews, says Dr. Lightfoot, to divide the Old Testament into three parts: the first beginning with the law was called The Law; the second beginning with the Psalms was called The Psalms; the third beginning with the prophet in question was called Jeremiah: thus, then, the writings of Zechariah and the other prophets being included in that division that began with Jeremiah, all quotations from it would go under the name of this prophet. If this be admitted, it solves the difficulty at once. Dr. Lightfoot quotes Baba Bathra, and Rabbi David Kimchi's preface to the prophet Jeremiah, as his authorities; and insists that the word Jeremiah is perfectly correct as standing at the head of that division from which the evangelist quoted, and which gave its denomination to all the rest. But Jeremiah is the reading in several MSS. of the Coptic. It is in one of the Coptic Dictionaries in the British Museum, and in a Coptic MS. of Jeremiah, in the library of St. Germain. So I am informed by the Rev. Henry Tattam, Rector of St Cuthbert's, Bedford.
entries.570a7996eb985b45d3559850231684ac897cef26: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen38857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38858" type="x-p"/> Before the governor - My old MS. English Bible translates ηγημων Meyr cheef justyse, Presedent. <div eID="gen38858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38859" type="x-p"/> Art thou the King of the Jews? - The Jews had undoubtedly delivered him to Pilate as one who was rising up against the imperial authority, and assuming the regal office. See on <reference osisRef="Mat.27.2">Mat 27:2</reference> (note).
