Though the perception of the flesh would have led him to dread destruction, still in his heart faith remained firm, by which he beheld the presence of God, of whose absence he complains. We have explained elsewhere how the Divine nature gave way to the weakness of the flesh, so far as was necessary for our salvation, that Christ might accomplish all that was required of the Redeemer. We have likewise pointed out the distinction between the sentiment of nature and the knowledge of faith; and, there ore, the perception of God’s estrangement from him, which Christ had, as suggested by natural feeling, did not hinder him from continuing to be assured by faith that God was reconciled to him. This is sufficiently evident from the two clauses of the complaint; for, before stating the temptation, he begins by saying that he betakes himself to God as <hi type="italic">his God, </hi>and thus by the shield of faith he courageously expels that appearance of <hi type="italic">forsaking </hi>which presented itself on the other side. In short, during this fearful torture his faith remained uninjured, so that, while he complained of being forsaken, he still relied on the aid of God as at hand.<div eID="gen102987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen102988" type="x-p"/>That this expression eminently deserves our attention is evident from the circumstance, that the Holy Spirit, in order to engrave it more deeply on the memory of men, has chosen to relate it in the Syriac language; <note n="286"> <div sID="gen102989" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">A voulu qu’il fust escrit et enregistré en langue Syrienne, de la quelle on usoit lors communément au pays</foreign>;” — “determined that it should be written and recorded in the Syrian language, which was then commonly used in the country.”<div eID="gen102989" type="x-p"/> </note> for this has the same effect as if he made us hear Christ himself repeating the very words which then proceeded from his mouth. So much the more detestable is the indifference of those who lightly pass by, as a matter of jesting, the deep sadness and fearful trembling which Christ endured. No one who considers that Christ undertook the office of Mediator on the condition of suffering our condemnation, both in his body and in his soul, will think it strange that he maintained a struggle with the sorrows of death, as if an offended God had thrown him into a whirlpool of afflictions.<div eID="gen102988" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.27.46" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen102984" osisID="Matt.27.46" type="section"/>
entries.70c4e79eec11a66cc62c340d4b45748b914b3198: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.27.47" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.27.47" sID="gen102990" type="section"/> <div sID="gen102991" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">47.</hi> <hi type="italic">He calleth Elijah. </hi>Those who consider this as spoken by the soldiers, ignorant and unskilled in the Syriac language, and unacquainted with the Jewish religion, and who imagine that the soldiers blundered through a resemblance of the words, are, in my opinion, mistaken. I do not think it at all probable that they erred through ignorance, but rather that they deliberately intended to mock Christ, and to turn his prayer into an occasion of slander. For Satan has no method more effectual for ruining the salvation of the godly, than by dissuading them from calling on God. For this reason, he employs his agents to drive off from us, as far as he can, the desire to pray. Thus he impelled the wicked enemies of Christ basely to turn his prayer into derision, intending by this stratagem to strip him of his chief armor. And certainly it is a very grievous temptation, when prayer appears to be so far from yielding any advantage to us, that God exposes his name to reproaches, instead of lending a gracious car to our prayers. This ironical language, therefore — or rather this barking of dogs — amounts to saying that Christ has no access to God, because, by imploring <hi type="italic">Elijah, </hi>he seeks relief in another quarter. Thus we see that he was tortured on every hand, in order that, overwhelmed with despair, he might abstain from calling on God, which was, to abandon salvation. But if the hired brawlers of Antichrist, as well as wicked men existing in the Church, are now found to pervert basely by their calumnies what has been properly said by us, let us not wonder that the same thing should happen to our Head. Yet though they may change <hi type="italic">God </hi>into <hi type="italic">Elijah, </hi>when they have ridiculed us to their heart’s content, God will at length listen to our groanings, and will show that he vindicates his glory, and punishes base falsehood.<div eID="gen102991" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.27.47" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen102990" osisID="Matt.27.47" type="section"/>
entries.fd73f1b5c3e835086686531bb61f8d90045701f2: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.27.48" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.27.48" sID="gen102992" type="section"/> <div sID="gen102993" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">48.</hi> <hi type="italic">And immediately one ran. </hi>As Christ had once refused to drink, it may be conjectured with probability, that it was repeatedly offered to him for the sake of annoyance; though it is also not improbable that <hi type="italic">the vinegar </hi>was held out to him in a cup before he was raised aloft, and that <hi type="italic">a sponge </hi>was afterwards applied to his mouth, while he was hanging on the cross.<div eID="gen102993" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.27.48" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen102992" osisID="Matt.27.48" type="section"/>
entries.ef52235460d397263c459469736508e9ba2934dc: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.27.50" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.27.50" sID="gen102996" type="section"/> <div sID="gen102997" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.27.50">Matthew 27:50</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">Jesus having again cried with a loud voice. </hi>Luke, who makes no mention of the former complaint, repeats the words of this second <hi type="italic">cry, </hi>which Matthew and Mark leave out. He says that Jesus cried, <hi type="italic">Father, into thy hands I commit my spirit; </hi>by which he declared that, though he was fiercely attacked by violent temptations, still his faith was unshaken, and always kept its ground unvanquished. For there could not have been a more splendid triumph than when Christ boldly expresses his assurance that God is the faithful guardian of his soul, which all imagined to be lost. But instead of speaking to the deaf, he betook himself directly to God, and committed to his bosom the assurance of his confidence. He wished, indeed, that men should hear what he said; but though it might be of no avail to men, he was satisfied with having God alone as his witness. And certainly there is not a stronger or more decided testimony of faith than when a pious man—perceiving himself attacked on every hand:, so that he finds no consolation on the part of men—despises the madness of the whole world, discharges his sorrows and cares into the bosom of God, and rests in the hope of his promises.<div eID="gen102997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen102998" type="x-p"/>Though this form of prayer appears to be borrowed from <reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.31.5">Psalm 31:5</reference>, yet I have no doubt that he applied it to his immediate object, according to present circumstances; as if he had said, “I see, indeed, O Father, that by the universal voice I am destined to destruction, and that <hi type="italic">my soul </hi>is, so to speak, hurried to and fro; but though, according to the flesh, I perceive no assistance in thee, yet this will not hinder me from committing my spirit into thy hands, and calmly relying on the hidden safeguard of thy goodness.” Yet it ought to be observed, that David, in the passage which I have quoted, not only prayed that his soul, received by the hand of God, might continue to be safe and happy after death, but committed his life to the Lord, that, guarded by his protection, he might prosper both in life and in death. He saw himself continually besieged by many deaths; nothing, therefore, remained but to commit himself to the invincible protection of God. Having made God the guardian of his soul, he rejoices that it is safe from all danger; and, at the same time, prepares to meet death with confidence, whenever it shall please God, because the Lord guards the souls of his people even in death. No as the former was taken away from Christ, to commit his soul to be protected by the Father during the frail condition of the earthly life, he hastens cheerfully to death, and desires to be preserved beyond the world; for the chief reason why God receives our souls into his keeping is, that our faith may rise beyond this transitory life.<div eID="gen102998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen102999" type="x-p"/>Let us now remember that it was not in reference to himself alone that Christ committed his soul to the Father, but that he included, as it were, in one bundle all the souls of those who believe in him, that they may be preserved along with his own; and not only so, but by this prayer he obtained authority to save all souls, so that not only does the heavenly Father, for his sake, deign to take them into his custody, but, giving up the authority into his hands, commits them to him to be protected. And therefore Stephen also, when dying, resigns his soul into his hands, saying, <hi type="italic">Lord Jesus, receive my spirit,</hi> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Acts.7.59">Acts 7:59</reference>.) Every one who, when he comes to die, following this example, shall believe in Christ, will not breathe his soul at random into the air, but will resort to a faithful guardian, who keeps in safety whatever has been delivered to him by the Father.<div eID="gen102999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen103000" type="x-p"/>The <hi type="italic">cry </hi>shows also the intensity of the feeling; for there can be no doubt that Christ, out of the sharpness of the temptations by which he was beset, not without a painful and strenuous effort, broke out into this <hi type="italic">cry. </hi>And yet he likewise intended, by this loud and piercing exclamation, to assure us that his soul would be safe and uninjured by death, in order that we, supported by the same confidence, may cheerfully depart from the frail hovel of our flesh.<div eID="gen103000" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.27.50" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen102996" osisID="Matt.27.50" type="section"/>
entries.764ee144e13cac4c0e7c787b676d4ea2d47b2062: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.27.51" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.27.51" sID="gen103001" type="section"/> <div sID="gen103002" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">51.</hi> <hi type="italic">And, lo, the veil of the temple was rent. </hi>When Luke blends <hi type="italic">the rending of the veil </hi>with the eclipse of the sun, he inverts the order; for the Evangelists, as we have frequently seen, are not careful to mark every hour with exactness. Nor was it proper that the <hi type="italic">veil </hi>should be <hi type="italic">rent, </hi>until the sacrifice of expiation had been completed; for then Christ, the true and everlasting Priest, having abolished the figures of the law, opened up for us by his blood the way to the heavenly sanctuary, that we may no longer stand at a distance within the porch, but may freely advance into the presence of God. For so long as the shadowy worship lasted, <note n="287"> <div sID="gen103003" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Cependant que le service, qui avoit les ombres de la Loy, a duré</foreign>;” — “so long as the service, which contained the shadows of the Law, lasted.”<div eID="gen103003" type="x-p"/> </note> a <hi type="italic">veil </hi>was hung up before the earthly sanctuary, in order to keep the people not only from entering but from seeing it, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Exod.26.33">Exodus 26:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:2Chr.3.14">2 Chronicles 3:14</reference>.) Now Christ, by<div eID="gen103002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen103004" type="x-p"/>blotting out the handwriting which was opposed to us,<lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Col.2.14">Colossians 2:14</reference>,)<div eID="gen103004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen103005" type="x-p"/>removed every obstruction, that, relying on him as Mediator, we may all be <hi type="italic">a royal priesthood, </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:1Pet.2.9">1 Peter 2:9</reference>.) Thus the <hi type="italic">rending </hi>of the <hi type="italic">veil </hi>was not only an abrogation of the ceremonies which existed under the law, but <hi type="italic">was, </hi>in some respects, an opening of heaven, that God may now invite the members of his Son to approach him with familiarity.<div eID="gen103005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen103006" type="x-p"/>Meanwhile, the <hi type="italic">Jews </hi>were informed that the period of abolishing outward sacrifices had arrived, and that the ancient priesthood would be of no farther use; that though the building of the temple was left standing, it would not be necessary to worship God there after the ancient custom; but that since the substance and truth of the shadows had been fulfilled, the figures of the law were changed into spirit. For though Christ offered a visible sacrifice, yet, as the Apostle tells us (<reference osisRef="Bible:Heb.9.14">Hebrews 9:14</reference>) it must be viewed spiritually, that we may enjoy its value and its fruit. But it was of no advantage to those wretched men that the outward sanctuary was laid bare by <hi type="italic">the rending of the veil, </hi>because the inward <hi type="italic">veil </hi>of unbelief, which was in their hearts, <note n="288"> <div sID="gen103007" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Qui estoit en leurs cœurs</foreign>.”<div eID="gen103007" type="x-p"/> </note> hindered them from beholding the saving light.<div eID="gen103006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen103008" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And the earth trembled, and the rocks were split. </hi>What Matthew adds about the earthquake and the <hi type="italic">splitting oft he rocks, </hi>I think it probable, took place at the same time. In this way not only did the earth bear the testimony to its Creator, but it was even called as a witness against the hard-heartedness of a perverse nation; for it showed how monstrous that obstinacy must have been on which neither the <hi type="italic">earthquake </hi>nor <hi type="italic">the splitting of the rocks </hi>made any impression.<div eID="gen103008" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.27.51" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen103001" osisID="Matt.27.51" type="section"/>
entries.9a4365e5223ab9fd684cb4d2ac655f7d9b195c62: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.27.52" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.27.52" sID="gen103009" type="section"/> <div sID="gen103010" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">52</hi> <hi type="italic"> And graves were opened. </hi>This was also a striking miracle, by which God declared that his Son entered into the prison of death, not to continue to be shut up there, but to bring out all who were held captive. For at the very time when the despicable weakness of the flesh was beheld in the person of Christ, the magnificent and divine energy of his death penetrated even to hell. This is the reason why, when he was about to be shut up in a sepulcher, other sepulchers <hi type="italic">were opened </hi>by him. Yet it is doubtful if this <hi type="italic">opening of the graves </hi>took place before his resurrection; for, in my opinion, <hi type="italic">the resurrection of the saints, </hi>which is mentioned immediately afterwards, was subsequent to the resurrection of Christ. There is no probability in the conjecture of some commentators that, after having received life and breath, they remained three days concealed in their graves. I think it more probable that, when Christ died, the <hi type="italic">graves </hi>were immediately <hi type="italic">opened: </hi>and that, when he rose, some of the godly, having received life, <hi type="italic">went out of their graves, and were seen </hi>in the city. For Christ is called<hi type="italic"> the first-born from the dead,</hi> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Col.1.18">Colossians 1:18</reference>,) and <hi type="italic">the first-fruits of those who rise, </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:1Cor.15.20">1 Corinthians 15:20</reference>,) because by his death he commenced, and by his resurrection he completed, a new life; not that, when he died, the dead were immediately raised, but because his death was the source and commencement of life. This reason, therefore, is fully applicable, since the opening of the graves was the presage of a new life, that the fruit or result appeared three days afterwards, because Christ, in rising from the dead, brought others along with him out of their graves as his companions. Now by this sign it was made evident, that he neither died nor rose again in a private capacity, but in order to shed the odor of life on all believers.<div eID="gen103010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen103011" type="x-p"/>But here a question arises. Why did God determine that only some should arise, since a participation in the resurrection of Christ belongs equally to all believers? I reply: As the time was not fully come when the whole body of the Church should be gathered to its Head, he exhibited in a few persons an instance of the new life which all ought to expect. For we know that Christ was received into heaven on the condition that the <hi type="italic">life </hi>of his members should still <hi type="italic">be hid, </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:Col.3.3">Colossians 3:3</reference>,) until it should be manifested by his coming. But in order that the minds of believers might be more quickly raised to hope, it was advantageous that the resurrection, which was to be common to all of them, should be tasted by a few.<div eID="gen103011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen103012" type="x-p"/>Another and more difficult question is, What became of those saints afterwards? For it would appear to be absurd to suppose that, after having been once admitted by Christ to the participation of a new life, they again returned to dust. But as this question cannot be easily or quickly answered, so it is not necessary to give ourselves much uneasiness about a matter which is not necessary to be known. That they continued long to converse with men is not probable; for it was only necessary that they should be <hi type="italic">seen </hi>for a short time, that in them, as in a mirror or resemblance, the power of Christ might plainly appear. As God intended, by their persons, to confirm the hope of the heavenly life among those who were then alive, there would be no absurdity in saying that, after having performed this office, they again rested in their graves. But it is more probable that the life which they received was not afterwards taken from them; for if it had been a mortal life, it would not have been a proof of a perfect resurrection. Now, though the whole world will rise again, and though Christ will raise up the wicked to judgment, as well as believers to salvation, yet as it was especially for the benefit of his Church that he rose again, so it was proper that he should bestow on none but <hi type="italic">saints </hi>the distinguished honor of rising along with him.<div eID="gen103012" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.27.52" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen103009" osisID="Matt.27.52" type="section"/>
entries.b36eaff3971f8a77248ec6dbe5edac7ab483d754: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.27.53" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.27.53" sID="gen103013" type="section"/> <div sID="gen103014" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">53.</hi> <hi type="italic">And</hi> <hi type="italic">went into the holy city. </hi>When Matthew bestows on Jerusalem the honorable designation of <hi type="italic">the holy city, </hi>he does not intend to applaud the character of its inhabitants, for we know that it was at that time full of all pollution and wickedness, so that it was rather <hi type="italic">a den of robbers, </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:Jer.7.11">Jeremiah 7:11</reference>.) But as it had been chosen by God, its <hi type="italic">holiness, </hi>which was founded on God’s adoption, could not be effaced by any corruptions of men, till its rejection was openly declared. Or, to express it more briefly, on the part of man it was profane, and on the part of God it was <hi type="italic">holy, </hi>till the destruction or pollution of the temple, which happened not long after the crucifixion of Christ.<div eID="gen103014" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.27.53" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen103013" osisID="Matt.27.53" type="section"/>
entries.9345deb46fd454df20a533c616932d9354d077df: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.27.54" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.27.54" sID="gen103015" type="section"/> <div sID="gen103016" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">54.</hi> <hi type="italic">Now the centurion. </hi>As Luke mentions the <hi type="italic">lamentation </hi>of the people, <hi type="italic">the centurion </hi>and his soldiers were not the only persons who acknowledged Christ to be <hi type="italic">the Son of God; </hi>but the Evangelists mention this circumstance respecting him for the purpose of heightening their description: for it is wonderful that an irreligious man, who had not been instructed in the Law, and was ignorant of true religion, should form so correct a judgment from the signs which he beheld. This comparison tends powerfully to condemn the stupidity of the city; for it was an evidence of shocking madness, that when the fabric of the world <hi type="italic">shook and trembled, </hi>none of the Jews were affected by it except the despised rabble. And yet, amidst such gross blindness, God did not permit the testimonies which he gave respecting his Son to be buried in silence. Not only, therefore, did true religion open the eyes of devout worshippers of God to perceive that from heaven God was magnifying the glory of Christ, but natural understanding compelled foreigners, and even soldiers, to confess what they had not learned either from the law or from any instructor.<div eID="gen103016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen103017" type="x-p"/>When Mark says that <hi type="italic">the centurion </hi>spoke thus, because Christ, <hi type="italic">when he had uttered a loud voice, expired, </hi>some commentators think that he intends to point out the unwonted strength which remained unimpaired till death; and certainly, as the body of Christ was almost exhausted of blood, it could not happen, in the ordinary course of things, that the sides and the lungs should retain sufficient rigor for uttering so loud a cry. Yet I rather think that <hi type="italic">the centurion </hi>intended to applaud the unshaken perseverance of Christ in calling on the name of God. Nor was it merely the <hi type="italic">cry of </hi>Christ that led <hi type="italic">the centurion </hi>to think so highly of him, but this confession was extorted from him by perceiving that his extraordinary strength harmonized with heavenly miracles.<div eID="gen103017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen103018" type="x-p"/>The words, <hi type="italic">he feared God,</hi> <note n="289"> <div sID="gen103019" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Quand il est dit <hi type="italic">qu’il craignit Dieu</hi></foreign>;” — “when it is said <hi type="italic">that he feared God.</hi>” Calvin does not quote in this instance the exact words of Scripture. Of<hi type="italic"> the centurion and those who were with him,</hi> Matthew says, (<foreign xml:lang="el">ἐφοζήθησαν σφόδρα</foreign>,) <hi type="italic">they were greatly terrified;</hi> and of the <hi type="italic">centurion</hi> Luke says, (<foreign xml:lang="el">ἐδόξασε τὸν Θεόν</foreign>,) <hi type="italic">he glorified God.</hi>—<hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen103019" type="x-p"/> </note> must not be so explained as if he had fully repented. <note n="290"> <div sID="gen103020" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Il ne faut pas entendre qu’il ait esté entierement converti</foreign>;” — “we must not understand them to mean that he was fully converted.”<div eID="gen103020" type="x-p"/> </note> It was only a sudden and transitory impulse, as it frequently happens, that men who are thoughtless and devoted to the world are struck with the fear of God, when he makes an alarming display of his power; but as they have no living root, indifference quickly follows, and puts an end to that feeling. <hi type="italic">The centurion </hi>had not undergone such a change as to dedicate himself to God for the remainder of his life, but was only for a moment the herald of the divinity of Christ.<div eID="gen103018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen103021" type="x-p"/>When Luke represents him as saying no more than <hi type="italic">certainly this was a righteous man, </hi>the meaning is the same as if he had plainly said that he was <hi type="italic">the Son of God, </hi>as it is expressed by the other two Evangelists. For it had been universally reported that Christ was put to death, because he declared himself to be the Son of God. Now when <hi type="italic">the centurion </hi>bestows on him the praise of <hi type="italic">righteousness, </hi>and pronounces him to be innocent, he likewise acknowledges him to be <hi type="italic">the Son of God; </hi>not that he understood distinctly how Christ was begotten by God the Father, but because he entertains no doubt that there is some divinity in him, and, convinced by proofs, holds it to be certain that Christ was not an ordinary man, but had been raised up by God.<div eID="gen103021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen103022" type="x-p"/>As to <hi type="italic">the multitudes, </hi>by <hi type="italic">striving their breasts, </hi>they expressed the dread of punishment for a public crime, because they felt that public guilt had been contracted by an unjust and shocking murder. <note n="291"> <div sID="gen103023" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Elles ont lamenté, craignans que malheur n’adveint sur tout le pays pour punition de ce qu’ils avoyent tous consenti à la condamnation et mort inique de Christ</foreign>.” — “They lamented, fearing that something unhappy would befall their country, as a punishment for their having all consented to the condemnation and unjust death of Christ.”<div eID="gen103023" type="x-p"/> </note> But as they went no farther, their lamentation was of no avail, unless, perhaps, in some persons it was the commencement or preparation of true repentance. And since nothing more is described to us than the lamentation which God drew from them to the glory of his Son, let us learn by this example, that it is of little importance, or of no importance at all, if a man is struck with terror, when he sees before his eyes the power of God, until, after the astonishment has been abated, the fear of God remains calmly in his heart.<div eID="gen103022" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.27.54" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen103015" osisID="Matt.27.54" type="section"/>
entries.e219500bceb5341b9e90b61bb7a3c3733de82a53:
55. And there were also many women there. I consider this to have been added in order to inform us that, while the disciples had fled and were scattered in every direction, still some of their company were retained by the Lord as witnesses. Now though the Apostle John did not depart from the cross, yet no mention is made of him; but praise is bestowed on the women alone, who accompanied Christ till death, because their extraordinary attachment to their Master was the more strikingly displayed, when the men fled trembling. For they must have been endued with extraordinary strength of attachment, since, though they could render him no service, they did not cease to treat him with reverence, even when exposed to the lowest disgrace. And yet we learn fromLuke that all the men had not fled; for he says that all his acquaintances stood at a distance. But not without reason do the Evangelists bestow the chief praise on the women, for they deserved the preference above the men. In my opinion, the implied contrast suggests a severe reproof of the apostles. I speak of the great body of them; for since only one remained, the three Evangelists, as I mentioned a little ago, take no notice of him. It was in the highest degree disgraceful to chosen witnesses to withdraw from that spectacle on which depended the salvation of the world. Accordingly, when they afterwards proclaimed the gospel, they must have borrowed from women the chief portion of the history. But if a remedy had not been miraculously prepared by Providence against a great evil, they would have deprived themselves, and us along with them, of the knowledge of redemption.
At first sight, we might think that the testimony of the women does not possess equal authority; but if we duly consider by what power of the Spirit they were supported against that temptation, we shall find that there is no reason why our faith should waver, since it rests on God, who is the real Author of their testimony.
“Qui est à la verité l’Autheur de ce tesmoignage des femmes;” — “who is in reality the Author of this testimony of the women.”
Yet let us observe, that it proceeded from the inconceivable goodness of God, that even to us should come that gospel which speaks of the expiation by which God has been reconciled to us. For during the general desertion of those who ought to have run before others, God encouraged some, out of the midst of the flock, who, recovering from the alarm, should be witnesses to us of that history, without the belief of which we cannot be saved. Of the women themselves, we shall presently have another opportunity of saying something. At present, it may be sufficient to take a passing notice of one point, that their eagerness for instruction led them to withdraw from their country, and constantly to learn from the lips of Christ, and that they spared neither toil nor money, provided that they might enjoy his saving doctrine.
MATTHEW 27:57-61; MARK 15:42-47; LUKE 23:50-56
Matthew 27:57-61
Mark 15:42-47
Luke 23:50-56
57. And when the evening was come, there came a rich man from Arimathea, named Joseph, who himself was a disciple of Jesus. 58. He went to Pilate, and requested the body of Jesus; then Pilate commanded the body to be delivered. 59. And Joseph, having received the body, wrapped it in a clean linen cloth. 60. And laid it in his own new tomb, which he had hewn out in the rock, and having rolled a great stone to the door of the tomb, he departed. 61. And Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were there, sitting opposite to the sepulcher. 
42. And when it was now evening, (because it was the preparation,
“Le jour de la preparation:” — “the day of the preparation.”
which goes before the Sabbath,) 43. Joseph of Arimathea, an honorable counselor, who was also himself waiting for the kingdom of God, came and boldly went in to Pilate, and asked the body of Jesus. 44. And Pilate wondered if he were already dead; and having called to him the centurion, he asked him if he had been long dead. 45. And having ascertained it from the centurion, he gave the body to Joseph. 46. And he, having brought a linen cloth, took him down (from the cross,
“De la croix.”
) and wrapped him in the linen cloth, and laid him in the tomb which had been hewn out of the rock; and rolled a stone to the door of the tomb. 47. And Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of Joses, saw where he was laid.
50. And, lo, a man named Joseph, a counselor, a good and righteous man, 51. Who had not consented to their decision, and to their deed; a native of Arimathea, a city of the Jews, who also himself waited for the kingdom of God. 52. He came to Pilate, and requested the body of Jesus. 53. And he took him down, and wrapped him in a linen cloth, and laid him in a tomb which had been hewn out in the rock, in which no man had ever been laid. 54. And it was the day of the preparation, and the Sabbath was approaching. 55. And the women who had come with him from Galilee followed, and saw the tomb, and how the body was laid. 56. And they returned, and prepared spices and ointments, and rested on the Sabbath, according to the commandment.
 
The burial of Christ is now added, as an intermediate transition from the ignominy of the cross to the glory of the resurrection. True, indeed, God determined, for another reason, that Christ should be buried, that it might be more fully attested that he suffered real death on our account. But yet it ought to be regarded as the principal design, that in this manner the cursing, which he had endured for a short time, began to be removed; for his body was not thrown into a ditch in the ordinary way, but honorably laid in a hewn sepulcher. Although at that time the weakness of the flesh was still visible, and the divine power of the Spirit was not clearly seen before his resurrection; yet God determined by this, as a sort of preparation, to shadow out what he was shortly afterwards to do, that he might exalt gloriously above the heavens his Son, the conqueror of death.
entries.936d1ae942e2debca561de64202cd95d8c305eb5: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.27.57" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.27.57" sID="gen103040" type="section"/> <div sID="gen103041" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.27.57">Matthew 27:57</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">And when the evening was come. </hi>Let it be understood that <hi type="italic">Joseph </hi>did not come in the dusk of <hi type="italic">the evening, </hi>but before sunset, that he might perform this office of kindness to his Master, without violating <hi type="italic">the Sabbath; </hi>for the <hi type="italic">Sabbath </hi>commenced in the evening, and therefore it was necessary that Christ should be laid in the grave before night came on. Now from the time that Christ died until <hi type="italic">the Sabbath </hi>began to be observed, there were three free days. And though John does not mention <hi type="italic">Joseph </hi>only, but joins <hi type="italic">Nicodemus </hi>as his companion, (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.19.39">19:39</reference>;) yet as he alone undertook the business at first, and as <hi type="italic">Nicodemus </hi>did no more than follow and join him, the three: Evangelists satisfied themselves with relating in a brief narrative what was done by Joseph alone.<div eID="gen103041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen103042" type="x-p"/>Now though this affection of <hi type="italic">Joseph </hi>deserved uncommon praise, still we ought first to consider the providence of God, in subduing a man of high and honorable rank among his countrymen, to wipe away the reproach of the cross by the honor of burial. And, indeed, as he exposed himself to the dislike and hatred of the whole nation, and to great dangers, there can be no doubt that this singular courage arose from a secret movement of the Spirit; for though he had formerly been one of Christ’s <hi type="italic">disciples, </hi>yet he had never ventured to make a frank and open profession of his faith. When the death of Christ now presents to him a spectacle full of despair, and fitted to break the strongest minds, how comes he suddenly to acquire such noble courage that, amidst the greatest terrors, he feels no dread, and hesitates not to advance farther than he had ever done, when all was in peace? Let us know then that, when the Son of God was buried by the hand of Joseph, it was the work of God.<div eID="gen103042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen103043" type="x-p"/>To the same purpose must also be referred the circumstances which are here detailed. <hi type="italic">Joseph’s </hi>piety and integrity of life are commended, that in the servant of God we may learn to recognize the work of God. The Evangelists relate that he was <hi type="italic">rich, </hi>in order to inform us that his amazing magnanimity of mind enabled him to rise superior to the obstruction which would otherwise have compelled him to retire. For <hi type="italic">rich men, </hi>being naturally proud, find nothing more difficult than to expose themselves voluntarily to the contempt of the people. Now we know how mean and disgraceful an act it was to receive from the hand of the executioner the body of a crucified man. Besides, as men devoted to riches are wont to avoid everything fitted to excite prejudice, the more eminent he was for wealth, the more cautious and timid he would have been, unless a holy boldness <note n="295"> <div sID="gen103044" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Une saincte hardiesse</foreign>.”<div eID="gen103044" type="x-p"/> </note> had been imparted to him from heaven. The dignity of his rank is likewise mentioned, that he was a <hi type="italic">counselor, </hi>or <hi type="italic">senator, </hi>that in this respect also the power of God may be displayed; for it was not one of the lowest of the people that was employed to bury the body of Christ in haste and in concealment, but from a high rank of honor he was raised up to discharge this office. For the less credible it was that such an office of kindness should be performed towards Christ, the more clearly did it appear that the whole of this transaction was regulated by the purpose and hand of God.<div eID="gen103043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen103045" type="x-p"/>We are taught by this example, that the rich are so far from being excusable, when they deprive Christ of the honor due to him: that they must be held to be doubly criminal, for turning into obstructions those circumstances which ought to have been excitements to activity. It is too frequent and customary, I acknowledge, for those who think themselves superior to others, to withdraw from the yoke, and to become soft and effeminate through excessive timidity and solicitude about their affairs. But we ought to view it in a totally different light; for if riches and honors do not aid us in the worship of God, we utterly abuse them. The present occurrence shows how easy it is for God to correct wicked fears by hindering us from doing our duty; since formerly <hi type="italic">Joseph </hi>did not venture to make an open profession of being a disciple of Christ, when matters were doubtful, but now, when the rage of enemies is at its height, and when their cruelty abounds, he gathers courage, and does not hesitate to incur manifest danger. We see then how the Lord in a moment forms the hearts to new feelings, and raises up by a spirit of fortitude those who had previously fainted. But if, through a holy desire to honor Christ, Joseph assumed such courage, while Christ was hanging on the cross, woe to our slothfulness, <note n="296"> <div sID="gen103046" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Mandite soit nostre lascheté</foreign>;” — “accursed be our sloth.”<div eID="gen103046" type="x-p"/> </note> if, now that he has risen from the dead, an equal zeal, at least, to glorify him do not burn in our hearts.<div eID="gen103045" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.27.57" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen103040" osisID="Matt.27.57" type="section"/>
entries.679eeb80aa0fa768f6ee112ae9d2d99a04d9df85: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.27.59" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.27.59" sID="gen103051" type="section"/> <div sID="gen103052" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.27.59">Matthew 27:59</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">And having taken the body. </hi>The three Evangelists glance briefly at the burial; and therefore they say nothing about the aromatic ointments which John alone mentions, (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.19.39">19:39</reference>) only they relate that <hi type="italic">Joseph purchased a clean linen cloth; </hi>from which we infer, that Christ was honorably buried. And, indeed, there could be no doubt that <hi type="italic">a rich man, </hi>when he gave up his <hi type="italic">sepulcher </hi>to our Lord, made provision also, in other respects, for suitable magnificence and splendor. And this, too, was brought about by the secret providence of God, rather than by the premeditated design of men, that a new sepulcher, <hi type="italic">in which no man had ever yet been laid, </hi>was obtained by our Lord, who is <hi type="italic">the first-born from the dead,</hi> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Col.1.18">Colossians 1:18</reference>,) and <hi type="italic">the first-fruits of them that rise,</hi> (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Cor.15.20">1 Corinthians 15:20</reference>.) God intended, therefore, by this Mark to distinguish his Son from the remainder of the human race, and to point out by the <hi type="italic">sepulcher </hi>itself his newness of life.<div eID="gen103052" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.27.59" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen103051" osisID="Matt.27.59" type="section"/>
entries.6f0222bf8d54786dba89de099d01292a959f9dc3:
61. And Mary Magdalene, and the other Mary, were there. Matthew and Mark relate only that the women looked at what was done, and marked the place where the body was laid. But Luke states, at the same time, their resolution, which was, that they returned to the city, and prepared spices and ointments, that two days afterwards they might render due honor to the burial. Hence we learn that their minds were filled with a better odor, which the Lord breathed into his death, that he might bring them to his grave, and exalt them higher.
MATTHEW 27:62-66
Matthew 27:62-66
62. And the next day, which is after the preparation,
“Qui est apres preparation du Sabbath;” — “which is after the preparation of the Sabbath.”
the chief priests and Pharisees came to Pilate, 63. Saying, Sir, we remember that that impostor said, while he was still alive, After three days I shall rise again. 64. Command, therefore, that the sepulcher be made secure till the third day, lest perhaps his disciples come by night to steal him, and say to the people, He is risen from the dead; and the last error shall be worse than the first. 65. Pilate saith to them, You have a guard; go, make it as secure as you can. 66. And they went and made the sepulcher secures sealing the stone, and posting guards.
entries.b5b83ac9ccd224681d211de2c942834870c3caae: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.27.62" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.27.62" sID="gen103061" type="section"/> <div sID="gen103062" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.27.62">Matthew 27:62</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">And the next day. </hi>In this narrative Matthew did not so much intend to show with what determined rage the scribes and priests pursued Christ, as to exhibit to us, as in a mirror, the amazing providence of God in proving the resurrection of his Son. Cunning men, practiced at least in fraud and treachery, plot among themselves, and contrive a method by which they may extinguish the memory of a dead man; for they see that they have gained nothing, if they do not destroy the certainty of the resurrection. But while they are attempting to do this, they appear rather as if they had expressly intended to bring it forth to the light, that it might be known. The resurrection of Christ would undoubtedly have been less manifest, or, at least, they would have had more plausible grounds for denying it, if they had not taken pains to station witnesses at the sepulcher. We see then how the Lord not only <hi type="italic">disappointeth the crafty,</hi> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Job.5.12">Job 5:12</reference>,) but employs even their own schemes as snares for holding them fast, that he may draw and compel them to render obedience to him. The enemies of Christ were indeed unworthy of having his resurrection made known to them; but it was proper that their insolence should be exposed, and every occasion of slander taken away from them, and that even their consciences should be convinced, so that they might not be held excusable for ignorance. Yet let us observe that God, as if he had hired them for the purpose, employed their services for rendering the glory of Christ more illustrious, because no plausible ground for lying, in order to deny it, was left to them when they found the grave empty; not that they desisted from their wicked rage, but with all persons of correct and sober judgment it was a sufficient testimony that Christ was risen, since his body, which had been placed in a grave, and protected by guards who surrounded it on all sides, was not to be found.<div eID="gen103062" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.27.62" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen103061" osisID="Matt.27.62" type="section"/>
entries.13524ea8f5eb29d51891484bed03a619b3af22cd: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.27.63" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.27.63" sID="gen103063" type="section"/> <div sID="gen103064" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">63.</hi> We <hi type="italic">remember that that impostor said. </hi>This thought was suggested to them by divine inspiration, not only that the Lord might execute upon them just vengeance for their wickedness, (as he always punishes bad consciences by secret torments,) but chiefly in order to restrain their unholy tongues. Yet we again perceive what insensibility seizes on wicked men, when they are bewitched by Satan. They go so far as to call him an <hi type="italic">impostor, </hi>whose divine power and glory were lately manifested by so many miracles. This certainly was not to defy the clouds, but to spit in the face of God, so to speak, by ridiculing the brightness of the sun. Such examples show us that we ought, with pious and modest thoughtfulness, to direct our attention early to the glory of God when it is presented to our view, that our hardness of heart may not lead us to brutal and dreadful blindness. Now though it may appear strange and absurd for wicked men to indulge in such wicked mockery over Christ when dead, that our minds may not be rendered uneasy by this licentiousness, we ought always to consider wisely the purpose to which the Lord turns it. Wicked men imagine that they will overwhelm the whole of the doctrine of Christ, together with his miracles, by that single blasphemy, which they haughtily vomit out; but God employs no other persons than themselves for vindicating his Son from all blame of <hi type="italic">imposture. </hi>Whenever these wicked men shall labor to overturn everything by their calumnies, and shall launch out into unmeasured slander, let us wait with composure and tranquillity of mind until God bring light out of darkness.<div eID="gen103064" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.27.63" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen103063" osisID="Matt.27.63" type="section"/>
entries.6e47c5947aecece787e3ffdd57492039e8ce5dab:
65. You have a guard. By these words, Pilate means that he grants their request by permitting them to post soldiers to keep watch. This, permission bound them more firmly, so that they could not escape by any evasion; for though they were not ashamed to break out against Christ after his resurrection, yet with Pilate’s signet they as truly shut their own mouths as they shut up the sepulcher.
MATTHEW 28:1-7; MARK 16:1-7; LUKE 24:1-8
Matthew 28:1-7
Mark 16:1-7
Luke 24:1-8
1. Now in the evening of the Sabbaths,
“Ou, au bout du Sabbaths, comme le jour apparoissoit pour luire pour le premier de la semaine;” — “or, at the end of the Sabbath, as the day began to dawn for the first of the week.”
which began to dawn towards the first of the Sabbaths, came Mary Magdalene, and the other Mary, to see the sepulcher. 2. And lo, there was a great earthquake; for the angel of the Lord came down from heaven, and approached, and rolled away the stone from the door, and sat upon it. 3. And his countenance was like lightning, and his raiment was white as snow. 4. And through fear of him the guards trembled, and became as dead men. 5. But the angel answering, said to the women, Fear not; for I know that you seek Jesus, who was crucified. 6. He is not here; for he is risen, as he said. Come, see the place where the Lord lay: 7. And go quickly, and tell his disciples that he is risen from the dead; and, lo, he goeth before you into Galilee; there shall you see him: lo, I have told you.
1. And when the Sabbath was past, Mary Magdalene, and Mary, the wife of James, and Salome, bought spices to come and anoint him. 2. And very early in the morning of the first day of the Sabaths,
“Le premier des Sabbaths; ou, jour de la semaine;”—the first of the Sabbaths, or day of the week.”
They come to the tomb at the rising of the sun.
“Le soleil estant ja levé; ou, commençant à se lever, ou, n’estant encore levé;” — “the sun having already risen; or beginning to rise, or not having yet risen.”
3. And they said among themselves, Who shall roll away the stone for us from the door of the tomb? 4. And having looked, they saw that the stone was rolled away; for it was very great. 5. And entering the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right side, clothed in a white robe; and they were afraid. 6. But he saith to them, Be not terrified: you seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified; he is risen, he is not here: lo, the place where they laid him. 7. But go away, tell his disciples and Peter, that he goeth before you into Galilee; there shall you see him, as he said to you.
1. And on the first day of the Sabbaths, very early in the morning, they came to the tomb, carrying the spices which they had prepared, and some women with them. 2. And they found the stone rolled away from the tomb. 3. And having entered, they found not the body of the Lord Jesus. 4. And it happened, while they were in consternation on this account, lo, two men stood near them in shining garments. 5. And when the women were terrified, and bowed their face to the earth, they said to them, Why do you seek the living among the dead? 6. He is not here, but is risen: remember how he told you, while he was still in Galilee, 7. Saying, that the Son of man must be delivered into the hands of the wicked men, and be crucified and rise again on the third day. 8. And they remembered his words.

entries.30f3e22b3cae104208c93110a5c2af571c2044cd:
<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="27" type="chapter">
               <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:271" />
               <ns0:head>CHAP. XXVII.</ns0:head>
               <ns0:p n="1">1 WHen the morning was come, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Luk. 22.66.</ns0:note> all the chief priests and elders of the people, took councel against Jesus, to put him to death.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">2 And when they had bound him, they led <ns0:hi>him</ns0:hi> away, and delivered him to Pontius Pilate the go<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vernour.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Mark Ch.</ns0:hi> 15.1. saith. <ns0:hi>And straightway in the Morning, the Chief Priests held a Consultation with the Elders and Scribes, and the whole Councel, and bound Iesus, and carried him away, and delivered him to Pilate, Luke</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 23.1. <ns0:hi>And the whole multitude of them arose, and led hhm to Pilate, Iohn, Ch.</ns0:hi> 18.28. saith, <ns0:hi>Then led they Iesus from Caiphas, unto the Hall of Iudgment, and it was early, and they themselves went <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ot into the Iudgment Hall, lest they should be defiled, but that they might eat the Passover.</ns0:hi> If any ask why, having con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />demned Christ, they did not put him to Death. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> tells us, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 31. <ns0:hi>It was not Lawful for them, to put any one to Death.</ns0:hi> They had already out of their Malice to Christ broken several of their own <ns0:hi>Canons,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Rules</ns0:hi> observed in ordinary Capital Causes, <ns0:hi>Sitting in the Night-time,</ns0:hi> and upon a <ns0:hi>Festival day.</ns0:hi> They must have notoriously broken another, if they had themselves on that day put him to Death. It should seem by their <ns0:hi>stoning Stephen, Acts</ns0:hi> 7.59. They had a Power in some Cases to put Persons to Death, but Christ was to be <ns0:hi>Crucified,</ns0:hi> and as to that kind of Death they had no Power, see <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 18.32. Besides that we must con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sider it was the <ns0:hi>Passover-day,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Stoning</ns0:hi> any Man to Death, required a Concourse of People to throw Stones, and they were afraid of <ns0:hi>Tumults.</ns0:hi> The Roman Governour had the <ns0:hi>Militia</ns0:hi> in his Power, and could better prevent, and suppress Tumults than they could do: Finally, Christ was by his Death to give Testimony to his <ns0:hi>Kingly Office</ns0:hi>; and the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> as we shall hear, had this to Charge him with, That he made himself a King, this was a Civil Cause, and to be adjudged by <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Roman Governour</ns0:hi> amongst them. In the Morning therefore, Consul<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ting how to put Christ to Death, they delivered him to <ns0:hi>Pontius Pilate,</ns0:hi> having first bound him, (for tho he was bound upon his first Apprehension, yet it is probable, that they had loosed him, when he came in the Hall of the <ns0:hi>High Priest,</ns0:hi> and now bind him a second time, when they carried him before <ns0:hi>Pilate) Iohn</ns0:hi> tells us, that they would not themselves go into the <ns0:hi>Iudg<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment Hall, lest they should be defiled, but that they might eat the Passover,</ns0:hi> which Words have in them a Difficulty, and also give us an Account, of a most inaccountable <ns0:hi>Superstition.</ns0:hi> For the <ns0:hi>Passover,</ns0:hi> they had eaten it the Night before. But we must know, that not the <ns0:hi>Paschal Lamb</ns0:hi> only, but all the Sacrifices offered any of the seven days, were also called the <ns0:hi>Passover, Deut.</ns0:hi> 16.1.2. &c. It was now the <ns0:hi>First day of unleavened Bread,</ns0:hi> but there were to be Offerings this day, of which they were to Eat, which in a large Sense are called the <ns0:hi>Passover.</ns0:hi> But how inaccountable was the Superstition of these Hypocrites. They made no Conscience, when they had eaten the <ns0:hi>Paschal Lamb</ns0:hi> in the Evening, to spend the whole Night in consulting how to shed innocent Blood, and condemning of Christ, but they pretend now <ns0:hi>Conscience,</ns0:hi> that they will not go into a <ns0:hi>Pagans</ns0:hi> house in the Morning, for that was the Defilement they feared, having nothing to do to sit in Judgment with him.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 Then Judas who had betrayed him, when he saw that he was condemned, repented himself, and brought again the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests, and elders.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 Saying, I have sinned in that I have betrayed the innocent blood; and they said, What <ns0:hi>is that</ns0:hi> to us? see thou <ns0:hi>to that.</ns0:hi>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 And he cast down the pieces of silver in the temple, and departed and went and hanged himself <ns0:note place="margin">Acts 1.18.</ns0:note>.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> (who alone reports this piece of History) inter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rupteth his Relation of our Saviours Tryal before <ns0:hi>Pilate,</ns0:hi> with an Account of <ns0:hi>Iudas</ns0:hi> his end. We must not interpret <ns0:hi>Then,</ns0:hi> strictly, so as to think <ns0:hi>Iudas</ns0:hi> did thi<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> at the time, when <ns0:hi>Christ</ns0:hi> was carried before <ns0:hi>Pilate,</ns0:hi> but some short time after; for they went immediately from the <ns0:hi>High Priests Hall, to the Iudgment Hall,</ns0:hi> and staid there until <ns0:hi>Christ</ns0:hi> was condemned by <ns0:hi>Pilate,</ns0:hi> be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore they returned to come into the <ns0:hi>Temple.</ns0:hi> But possibly it was that day, after <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> had condemned him, or within some short time after, that <ns0:hi>Iudas</ns0:hi> (as it is said) <ns0:hi>Repented himself.</ns0:hi> That is, began to be terrifyed in his Conscience, for what he had done. The Consciences of the worst of Men, will not always digest Mire and Dirt, but sometimes throw it up, yea tho it hath first incurably poisoned them, sin is sweet in the Mouth, but bitter in the Belly. All Repentance is not saving. Nor doth all <ns0:hi>Con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fession</ns0:hi> of sin obtain <ns0:hi>Remission. Iudas</ns0:hi> here repents, and Confesseth he <ns0:hi>had Sinned,</ns0:hi> and his <ns0:hi>particular</ns0:hi> sin, in betraying an <ns0:hi>innocent Person</ns0:hi>; yet he findeth no Mercy, he hath not an Heart <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> beg Forgiveness, nor to apply himself to Christ for Remedy. But the Answer of the chief <ns0:hi>Priests</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Elders,</ns0:hi> is very remarka<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble. <ns0:hi>What is that to us, look thou to that?</ns0:hi> Wretched <ns0:hi>Iudas</ns0:hi>! He had been the Servant of these wicked Mens Lusts, and for a poor Wages served them, in the highest Act of <ns0:hi>Villany.</ns0:hi> He falls into a distress of Conscience for what he had done. What mi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />serable Comforters do they prove? Tempters never make good Comforters. Those who are the Devils Instruments, to Com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mand here, Entice, or allure Men to sin, will afford them no re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lief when they come to be troubled, for what they have done: Nor will it now satisfie the Conscience of <ns0:hi>Iudas,</ns0:hi> to remember that he had a <ns0:hi>Warrant</ns0:hi> for apprehending Christ, and acted Mi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nisterially. The <ns0:hi>Priests</ns0:hi> will not take the Money, he throws <ns0:hi>it down in the Temple,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>goes and hangs himself.</ns0:hi> How great is the Power of Conscience, smiting for the Guilt of sin? <ns0:hi>Iudas</ns0:hi> could have no hope of a better Life, so as all his Happiness lay in the time of this present Life. Yet, he is not able to allow himself that. The Devil that entred into his Heart, to Tempt him, now entreth again to perswade him, to put an end to his Misery in this Life, by hastning himself to an Eternal Misery. Let all Apostates turning <ns0:hi>Persecutors</ns0:hi> of innocent Persons, read this, and Tremble. There is a Difficulty of reconciling this Text, to that of <ns0:hi>Luke, Acts</ns0:hi> 1.18. where it is said of him, <ns0:hi>That he falling Head-long burst asunder in the midst, and all his Bowels gushed out.</ns0:hi> That which is usually said, is, that he fell from the place where he hanged himself, and with the fall burst himself: I know there are some others, who think that the Word <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, need not be translated, he hanged himself; but he was <ns0:hi>Suffocated</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Strangled.</ns0:hi> Some think the Devil strangled him, and threw him down a Precipice. Others, that he was <ns0:hi>Suffocated</ns0:hi> by some Disease, which caused a Rupture of his Body. Others think (as we translate it) that he hanged himself, and <ns0:hi>Swelling</ns0:hi> his Body brake, and his Bowels gushed out: Concerning the manner of his Death, we can determine nothing, but that he was <ns0:hi>Strangled,</ns0:hi> and his <ns0:hi>Bowels gushed out,</ns0:hi> both these the Scripture asserts, but how it was, we cannot certainly tell.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 And the chief priests took the silver pieces and said, It is not lawful for to put them into the treasury, because it is the price of blood.<ns0:note place="bottom">God, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 23.18. had forbidden <ns0:hi>to bring the Price</ns0:hi> of a <ns0:hi>Whore,</ns0:hi> or a <ns0:hi>Dog, into the Temple,</ns0:hi> This, they had interpreted of all <ns0:hi>filthy Gain</ns0:hi>: Upon which they thus determine, that it was not Lawful for them, to put the Money they had given <ns0:hi>Iudas,</ns0:hi> for so sordid a Service as that, of <ns0:hi>betraying his Master,</ns0:hi> into the Chest, or place which they had, where they kept the Monies given for the Repairs of the <ns0:hi>Temple</ns0:hi>; and in this they were right enough, perhaps, but in this they shewed them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves stupidly blind Hypocrites, that they saw not it was much less Lawful for them, who had hired him to this sordid Action, to be imployed in the Service of the Temple, for <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 52.11. those that <ns0:hi>bear the Vessels of the Lord,</ns0:hi> ought to <ns0:hi>be Holy.</ns0:hi> Thus to justifie our Saviours words, they <ns0:hi>strain at a</ns0:hi> Gnat, and swallow a Camel.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 And they took councel, and bought with them the potters field, to bury strangers in.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 Wherefore that field was called The <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Acts 1.19.</ns0:note> field of blood to this day.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 Then was fulfilled, that which was spoken by Jeremiah the prophet, saying, And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him that was <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>whom they bought of the Chil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dren of</ns0:hi> Israel.</ns0:note> va<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lued, whom they of the children of Israel did value.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 And gave them for the potters field, as the Lord appointed me.<ns0:note place="bottom">They at last resolve what to do with the Money, which was no great Sum (for as we Noted before, it exceeded not three pounds and fifteen Shillings) they would not turn it to their own private use, for (probably) it was before taken out of the Treasury, neither would they again return it into the Treasury, because it had been made use of as the <ns0:hi>Hire of Blood.</ns0:hi> They therefore agree to buy with it a piece of Ground, ordinarily known by the Name of the <ns0:hi>Potters Field,</ns0:hi> probably because some Potter had Digged Earth, and thrown the wast of his Pot-kilnes there, so as it was of no great value. This Field the Vulgar upon this purchase of it by the Priests, called many Years after. <ns0:hi>The Field of the Blood. Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by</ns0:hi> Jeremy <ns0:hi>the Prophet.</ns0:hi> The <ns0:hi>Evangelists</ns0:hi> use this Term <ns0:hi>fulfilled,</ns0:hi> as I have be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore Noted, in very different Senses. 1. Sometimes to express the Accomplishment of a Prophesy. 2. Sometimes to express the fulfilling of a Type or answering it by the <ns0:hi>Antitype.</ns0:hi> 3. Sometimes to express an Allusion to some other Scripture, men<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tioning some matter of Fact, of a like Nature. For the Text here quoted, we have no such Text in the Writing of the Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phet <ns0:hi>Ieremy,</ns0:hi> which are upon sacred <ns0:hi>Record. Ieremy</ns0:hi> indeed did buy a Field by order from God, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 32.9. to declare his Faith in Gods promises, for the return of the Jews out of Captivity, but he bought it of his Uncle <ns0:hi>Hananeel,</ns0:hi> and for seventeen pieces of <ns0:hi>Silver,</ns0:hi> and that he was a <ns0:hi>Potter,</ns0:hi> or that the <ns0:hi>Field</ns0:hi> was called by that Name, we do not Read. The nearest place in the <ns0:hi>Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />p<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ets</ns0:hi> to this Text is <ns0:hi>Zechar.</ns0:hi> 11.12, 13. <ns0:hi>And I said unto them, if you think good, give me my price, so they weighed for my p<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ice thirty pieces of Silver, and the Lord said unto me, cast it unto the Potters, a goodly price, that I was prized at of t<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>em. And I took the thirty pieces of Silver, and I cast t<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>em to the Potter in the House of the Lord.</ns0:hi> It is a very hard Text as it lies in the Prophet to give a just account of. The P<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ophet was one of them who Prophesied after the Captivity of <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> yet <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 6. he plainly Prophesieth after Gods Destructi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on of the Jews and of <ns0:hi>Ierusalem.</ns0:hi> Which Destruction being (af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter that of the <ns0:hi>Caldeans</ns0:hi>) to what it should refer, but to the last Destruction of the Jews by the <ns0:hi>Romans,</ns0:hi> I cannot understand. <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 7. he saith, <ns0:hi>I will feed the Flock of <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>he Slaughter,</ns0:hi> that is, the Flock designed for the Slaughter, or drawing near to the Slaugh<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter, <ns0:hi>even you, O poor of the Flock</ns0:hi>! Christ came in Person to feed the Church of the Jews, but they also abhorred him, so that he abhorred them, and resolved to cast them quite off. <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 8, 9. so he broke first his <ns0:hi>Staff</ns0:hi> called <ns0:hi>Beauty,</ns0:hi> took away all the Glo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry and Beauty of that Church. Then as it were in Indignati<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on, he saith, <ns0:hi>If you think good give me my price.</ns0:hi> What Requi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tal will you give me for my Labour amongst you? <ns0:hi>So they weighed for my price thirty pieces of Silver.</ns0:hi> Their selling of Christ to a Traytor for so much, signified their High Con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tempt of him. <ns0:hi>And the Lord said, Cast it unto the Potter, a goodly price that I was prized at of them, and I took the thirty pieces of Silver, and cast them to the Potter, in the House of the Lord.</ns0:hi> The <ns0:hi>Evangelist</ns0:hi> indeed doth not quote the very Words of the Prophet, but the substance of them. And for my part I think, that the Evangelist here by <ns0:hi>fulfilling,</ns0:hi> mean<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth <ns0:hi>the Accomplishment of the Prophesy in</ns0:hi> Zechariah. For I know not what other Tolerable Sense to make of the Prophesy, if we do not say the <ns0:hi>prophet</ns0:hi> spake in the Person of Chri<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>t, fore<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />telling his own coming among<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>t them, their Rejection, and Co<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>tempt of him, and his utter Rejection of them, and Prophesi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing as a piece of their Contempt and <ns0:hi>Rejection of him,</ns0:hi> their selling him to <ns0:hi>Iudas</ns0:hi> for <ns0:hi>thirty pieces of Silver</ns0:hi> (a most Con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />temptible price) and God so ordering it by his Providence, that this Money should again be brought them, and this <ns0:hi>Potters Field</ns0:hi> should be bought with it. So as I think, that Text was fulfil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led here, more than by <ns0:hi>Allusion,</ns0:hi> or as it was <ns0:hi>Typical</ns0:hi> to this Act, and that this <ns0:hi>Act</ns0:hi> was the very thing which there is <ns0:hi>prophesied,</ns0:hi> and here fulfilled. But how <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>This was spoken by</ns0:hi> Jeremy <ns0:hi>the Prophet</ns0:hi> is an harder Knot. It is observable that <ns0:hi>Zechariah</ns0:hi> hath many things found in <ns0:hi>Ieremy,</ns0:hi> and it is not im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />probable, that the very same thing was Prophesied by <ns0:hi>Ieremy,</ns0:hi> tho afterward repeated by <ns0:hi>Zechariah,</ns0:hi> and only in the Writings of <ns0:hi>Zechariah</ns0:hi> left upon sacred Record. <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> having now given us an account of the fate of <ns0:hi>Iudas,</ns0:hi> returned to our Savi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />our, carryed (as we heard) before Pilate.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:272" />11 And Jesus stood before the governour, and the governour asked him, saying, Art thou the king of the Jews? And Jesus said unto him <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Tim. 6.13.</ns0:note> Thou say<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />est.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> hath the same, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 15.2. so hath <ns0:hi>Luke, Ch.</ns0:hi> 23.3. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> relates it more di<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>tinctly, <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 18.29. Pilate <ns0:hi>then went out unto them, and said, What Accusation bring you against this Man? They answered and said, If he were not a Male<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />factor we would not have delivered him up to thee. Then said</ns0:hi> Pilate <ns0:hi>unto them. Take him and Iudge him according to your Law. The Iews therefore said unto him, It is not lawful for us to put any Man to Death. That the saying of Iesus might be fu<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>filled, which he spake signifying what Death he should Dye.</ns0:hi> The other Evangelists seem to have given us the Story of this our Saviours first appearance before <ns0:hi>Pilate,</ns0:hi> Summarily<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                     <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> seems to have gi<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>en us it more orderly, and particularly, It is the course of all Judicaturs to require the Accusers to speake fir<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>t. <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> therefore asketh <ns0:hi>what Accusation they had brought against him</ns0:hi>? Their Answer was very Malapert. <ns0:hi>If he had not <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>een a Malefactor,</ns0:hi> &c. what was this to the purpose? Sup<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />po<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>e him never so great a Malefactor? Mu<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>t it not appear he is so before a Judge Condemns him? These Accusers (as it seem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth) were of the same mind that the <ns0:hi>Papists</ns0:hi> are, that the <ns0:hi>Ci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vil Magistrate,</ns0:hi> is to be <ns0:hi>Executioner</ns0:hi> to the <ns0:hi>Church,</ns0:hi> and when the Ecclesiastical power hath Condemned a Man for Heresy or Blasphemy, the Civil Magistrate hath nothing to do, but with<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />out his own hearing the Cause to put the Person to Death. But they met with a more equal Judge, tho he were an Heathen. Say ye so, saith he, <ns0:hi>Take him then, and Iudge him according to <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>our Law.</ns0:hi> This he either speaks as deriding them, and scorn<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing what they would have put him upon: or else not thinking he had deserved any thing worthy of Death, knowing they might without him Scourge him, or inflict some lighter punishments. They reply<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                     <ns0:hi>It is not lawful for us to put any Man to Death.</ns0:hi> It is very Questionable in what Sense they spake this. Those that affirm that the Power of Judging, and determining in <ns0:hi>Capital Causes,</ns0:hi> was be<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ore this time taken from the Jews, must affirm that <ns0:hi>Stephen</ns0:hi> was put to Death in a Popular Tumult, for he was after this <ns0:hi>Stone<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                     </ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>Deat<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                     </ns0:hi> by the Jews, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 7.59. which is not probable, con<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>idering what we Read of him, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 6.13.15. called before the <ns0:hi>Counci<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                     </ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Witnesses used against him,</ns0:hi> and have no <ns0:hi>Record</ns0:hi> of any notice the Civil Magistrate took of the Fact as a Disorder. I therefore rather think their meaning was, This is with us a <ns0:hi>Feast-Day,</ns0:hi> on which it is not lawful for us to put a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ny to Death without thy Consent. Or, it is not lawful for us to put any to Death, <ns0:hi>for any Civil Cause,</ns0:hi> for saying, he is <ns0:hi>our King,</ns0:hi> for it is manifest by the Question which <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> first put to him, upon his second coming into the H<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ll, mentioned <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 18.33. in which all the other three Evangelists agree, that they had charged him with saying, that <ns0:hi>he was the King of the Iews,</ns0:hi> to which all that he replyed, which is Recorded by <ns0:hi>Matthew, Mark</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Luke,</ns0:hi> is <ns0:hi>Thou sayest it.</ns0:hi> I am not bound to accuse my self, who Witnesses this against me? But <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> saith<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> That <ns0:hi>our Saviour said, sayest thou this thing of thy self, or did o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thers tell it thee of me</ns0:hi>? Pilate <ns0:hi>answered, Am I a Iew? thy own Nation, and the Chief Priests have delivered thee to me. What hast thou done? Iesus answered, and said. My King<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom is not of this World, if my Kingdom were of this World, then would my Servants Fight, that I should not be delivered to the Iews, but now is not my Kingdom from hence.</ns0:hi> Our Savi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />our by this Answer to <ns0:hi>Pilates</ns0:hi> Question, seems to vindicate his Right not to be Condemned without Witness, which if others had told <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> this, they were bound to have produced. <ns0:hi>Pi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />late</ns0:hi> tells him, He had it not of himself, he was no <ns0:hi>Iew,</ns0:hi> but they were those of his own Nation, who had delivered him to him, and therefore asketh him what he had done. Then our Sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />viour openeth himself, not denying that he was <ns0:hi>the King of the Iews,</ns0:hi> but telling him he was no <ns0:hi>King of this World,</ns0:hi> his King<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom was a Spiritual Kingdom, and he might know what <ns0:hi>King</ns0:hi> he was, by his <ns0:hi>Retinue,</ns0:hi> and those who took his part, for if he had laid Claim to any secular Kingdom, he should have had some appearing to take his part, and to Fight for him to deliver him from his Enemies, but he saw he had none. <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> laying hold of his Words, replys, <ns0:hi>Art thou a King? Iesus answered, Thou sayest that I am a King, to this end was I Born, and for this Cause came I into the World, that I should bear Wit<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness to the Truth. Every one that is of the Truth, heareth my Voice.</ns0:hi> Pilate <ns0:hi>saith unto him, What is Truth?</ns0:hi> Our Saviour still useth Prudence, and keeps himself upon a close Guard. It had been dangerous for him, directly to have owned himself a King. He therefore only tells <ns0:hi>Pilate,</ns0:hi> That he said he was a King, and that he came into the World to bear Testimony to the Truth, and further adds, <ns0:hi>That every one who was of the Truth, did hear his Voice.</ns0:hi> This poseth <ns0:hi>Pilate,</ns0:hi> who had no Notion of that <ns0:hi>Truth,</ns0:hi> which Christ spake of, he goes out as it were deriding him, saying, <ns0:hi>what is Truth</ns0:hi>? Presently he go<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth out to the Jews, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 38. and tells them, <ns0:hi>he found in him no fault at all,</ns0:hi> and offers to release him, but this we shall meet with in our Evangelist by and by, the passages hereto menti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />oned are only related by <ns0:hi>Iohn.</ns0:hi> Excepting only the <ns0:hi>Question,</ns0:hi> Art thou <ns0:hi>the King of the Iews</ns0:hi>? and our Saviours Answer, <ns0:hi>Thou sayest it.</ns0:hi> which is reported by all.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 And when he was accused of the chief priests, and elders, he answered nothing.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 Then saith Pilate unto him: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>p. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 span">
                        <ns0:desc>〈…〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> Hearest thou not how many things they witness against thee?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 And he answered him to never a word, insomuch that the governour marvelled great<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> saith much the same, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 15.3, 4, 5.
