These things were before <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> went out to the People, and told them, that he found no fault in him at all: and offered to release <ns0:hi>Barab<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bas</ns0:hi> unto them. Then seemeth to me to follow in order, what we have in <ns0:hi>Luke,</ns0:hi> 23. from the 5<ns0:hi>th. v.</ns0:hi> to the 17<ns0:hi>th.</ns0:hi> in these Words. <ns0:hi>And they were the more fierce, saying, He stirreth up the People, Teaching from all Iewry beginning from</ns0:hi> Galilee <ns0:hi>to this place.</ns0:hi> The constant charge which we shall observe, was laid upon all the Ministers of the Gospel from Christs time, <ns0:hi>Tertullus</ns0:hi> the Roman Advocate, thus charged <ns0:hi>Paul, &c. when</ns0:hi> Pilate <ns0:hi>heard of</ns0:hi> Galilee, <ns0:hi>he asked whether the Man were a</ns0:hi> Galilean. <ns0:hi>And as soon as he knew that he belonged to</ns0:hi> Herods <ns0:hi>Iurisdiction, he sent him to</ns0:hi> Herod, <ns0:hi>who himself was also at</ns0:hi> Jerusalem <ns0:hi>at that time.</ns0:hi> After the Death of <ns0:hi>Herod the great,</ns0:hi> who dyed soon after our Saviour was Born (as we heard be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore) <ns0:hi>The Scepter departed from</ns0:hi> Judah, there were no more Kings. The Government of Jewry was turned into a <ns0:hi>Tetrachy,</ns0:hi> divided into four Provinces, each of which had a Governour, who was called the <ns0:hi>Tetrarch</ns0:hi> of that Providence. You have the Division, and the Names of the <ns0:hi>Tetrarchs, Luke</ns0:hi> 3.1. where you will find that <ns0:hi>Herod</ns0:hi> was <ns0:hi>Tetrarch</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>Galilee.</ns0:hi> Our Sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />viour being taken within the Jurisdiction of <ns0:hi>Pilate,</ns0:hi> it seemeth not to have been necessary for <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> to have sent him to <ns0:hi>He<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rod,</ns0:hi> but a Complement to satisfy his Curiosity. For (saith <ns0:hi>Luke.) When</ns0:hi> Herod <ns0:hi>saw Iesus, he was exceeding glad, for he was desirous to see him</ns0:hi> of a <ns0:hi>long Season, because he had heard many things of him, and he hoped to have seen some Miracle done by him. Then he questioned with him in ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ny Words, but he answered him nothing. And the Chief Priests, and Scribes stood, and Vehemently accused him. And</ns0:hi> He<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rod <ns0:hi>with his Men of War, set him at nought, and mocked him, and arrayed him in a Gorgeous Robe, and sent him again to</ns0:hi> Pilate. <ns0:hi>And the same Day</ns0:hi> Pilate <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> Herod, <ns0:hi>were made Friends together<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> for before they were at Enmity between themselves.</ns0:hi> This is now all Historical, and hath in it nothing difficult. Christ had spent most of his time in <ns0:hi>Galilee</ns0:hi> (which was <ns0:hi>Herods Tetrarchy</ns0:hi>) tho <ns0:hi>Herod</ns0:hi> had not seen him, yet he had heard much of him, and had the Curiosity to desire to see him, hoping that our Saviour would have wrought some Miracle before him. But he failed in his Expectation. He propounds several Questions to him. Our Saviour being not before a proper Judge, answereth him nothing. So as there was nothing done, only the <ns0:hi>Chief Priests, and Scribes</ns0:hi> followed him with Incessant Clamours. <ns0:hi>Herod</ns0:hi> and his Guard, Vilify and mock him, put him on a Gorgeous Robe, and send him back to <ns0:hi>Pilate.</ns0:hi> All the effect of this was, <ns0:hi>He<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rod</ns0:hi> was pleased with <ns0:hi>Pilates</ns0:hi> Complement, and from that Day was reconciled to <ns0:hi>Pilate,</ns0:hi> tho there had been a former Enmity betwixt them, only as we shall hear hereafter, <ns0:hi>Herod</ns0:hi> Decreeing nothing against <ns0:hi>Christ, Pilate</ns0:hi> made some use of it, in his indea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vours to have delivered our Saviour.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:272" />15 Now at <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> feast, the governour was wont to release unto the people a prisoner whom they would.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 And they had then a notable prisoner called Barabbas.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 Therefore when they were gathered toge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, Pilate said unto them, whom will ye that I release unto you? Barabbas, or Jesus which is called Christ?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 For he knew that for envy they had delivered him.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 15. <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 6, 7, 8, 9, 10. <ns0:hi>Now at that Feast, he released unto them one Prisoner whomsoever they desired. And there was one Named Barabbas, which lay bound with them that had made insurrection with him, who had committed Murder in the Insurrection. And the Multitude crying aloud, begun to desire him to do as he had ever done unto them. But</ns0:hi> Pilate <ns0:hi>answered them, saying, will ye that I release unto you the King of the Iews? (for he knew that the Chief Priests had delivered him for Envy) but the Chief Priests moved the People, that he should rather release</ns0:hi> Barabbas <ns0:hi>unto them. Luke</ns0:hi> hath this passage of the History more fully, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 23.13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18. <ns0:hi>And</ns0:hi> Pilate <ns0:hi>when he had called together, the Chief Priests, the Rulers, and the People, said unto them, you have brought this Man unto me, as one that perverteth the People, and behold I having examined him before you, have found no fault in this Man, touching those things whereof you accuse him. No, nor yet</ns0:hi> Herod, <ns0:hi>for I sent you to him, and <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>o nothing worthy of Death is done unto him. I will there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore Chastise him, and Release him, for of necessity he must Release one unto them at the Feast. And they cryed out all at once, saying, Away with this Man, and release unto us</ns0:hi> Ba<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rabbas, <ns0:hi>who for a certain Sedition made in the City, and for Murder, was cast into Prison. Iohn Ch.</ns0:hi> 18.38, 39, 40. saith, that when he went out he told them, he found no fault in him at all. <ns0:hi>But you have a Custom, that I should Release unto you one at the Passover, will you therefore that I release unto you the King of the Iews. Then cryed they all again, saying, Not this Man, but</ns0:hi> Barabbas, <ns0:hi>now</ns0:hi> Barabbas <ns0:hi>was a Robber.</ns0:hi> The History is plain, <ns0:hi>Pi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />late</ns0:hi> discerned upon his before mentioned Examination of Christ, that our Saviour had done nothing amiss, but was only Loaded with the Malice, and Envy of the <ns0:hi>Chief Priests</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Scribes,</ns0:hi> this made him resolve to do what in him lay to deliver him. He first tells them that they had brought him before him, accused him of many things, but had proved against him nothing Criminal, That he had sent him to <ns0:hi>Herod,</ns0:hi> in whose Jurisdiction he had lived, but neither did <ns0:hi>Herod</ns0:hi> find any fault in him. Now there was a Custom that ever at the <ns0:hi>Passover,</ns0:hi> the Governour released a Prisoner at the request of the People: The People desired he would keep their old Custom in this particular, <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />poundeth to them, to release <ns0:hi>the King of the Iews.</ns0:hi> The <ns0:hi>Chief Priests</ns0:hi> influence the People to declare their Disatisfaction at that, and to Name one <ns0:hi>Barabbas,</ns0:hi> a Prisoner who was a <ns0:hi>Robber,</ns0:hi> and had been guilty of an Insurrection, and of Murder commit<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted in the Insurrection, accordingly the People cry out. <ns0:hi>Not this Man but Barabbas.</ns0:hi> This makes him again to return to the <ns0:hi>Iudgment Seat.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 When he was set down on the judgment seat, his wife sent unto him, saying, Have thou nothing to do, with that just man, for I hav<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                     <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                  </ns0:gap> suffered many things this day in a dream because of him.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 But the chief priests and elders persuaded the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Joh. 18.40. Act 13.14.</ns0:note> multitude, that they should ask Barabbas, and destroy Jesus.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> only mentioneth this passage of <ns0:hi>Pilates</ns0:hi> Wife, whe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther it was when <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> sate upon the <ns0:hi>Iudgment Seat</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cond time</ns0:hi> (the Story of which we have heard) or afterward is uncertain. Nor is it material, she doubtless referreth to some late Dream, which possibly she mig<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> have after her Husband was gone from her, for he was called <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. Whether this Dream was caused by God for a further Testimony of Christ Inno<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cency, or were meerly natural cannot be determined. But still the cry holdeth. <ns0:hi>Not him, but</ns0:hi> Barabbas. So much Influ<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ence had the <ns0:hi>Wicked Priests</ns0:hi> upon the People.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 The governour answered, and said unto them them, Whether of the twain, will ye that I release unto you? They said Barabbas.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 Pilate saith unto them, What shall I do then with Jesus, which is called Chirst? They all say unto him, let him be crucified.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 And the governour said, why? what evil hath he done. But they cryed out the more, saying, Let him be crucified.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> hath the same, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 15. <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 12, 13, 14. So also, <ns0:hi>Luk. Ch.</ns0:hi> 23.20, 21, 22, 23. saith <ns0:hi>Pilate, therefore willing to rease Iesus, spake again to them: But they cryed, saying, Crucifie him, Crucifie him. And he said unto them, the third time, why what Evil hath he done? I have found no Cause of Death in him, I will therefore Chastise him and let him go. And they were instant with loud Voyces, requiring that he might be Crucified, and the Voyces of them, and of the Chief Priests pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vailed. Iohn, Ch.</ns0:hi> 19. from <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 1.13. hath yet more Circum<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stances relating to the latter part of this <ns0:hi>Tryal,</ns0:hi> which follow. <ns0:hi>Then Pilate therefore took Iesus, and scourged him. And the Soldiers platted a Crown of Thorns, and put it on his Head, and they put on him a Purple Robe: And said, Hail King of the Iews, and they smote him with their Hands. Pilate therefore went forth again, and said unto them: Behold I bring him forth unto you, that you may know I find no fault in him. Then came Iesus forth, wearing the Crown of Thorns, and the Purple Robe. And Pilate saith unto them: Behold the Man! When the Chief Priests therefore, and Officers saw him, they Cryed out, saying, Crucifie him, Crucifie him? Pilate saith unto them, Take ye him and Crucifie him, for I find no fault in him. The Iews answered him: We have a Law, and by our Law he ought to dye, because he made himself the Son of God. When Pilate there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore heard that Saying, he was the more afraid. And went again into the Iudgment Hall, and saith unto Iesus, whence art thou? But Iesus gave no Answer: Then Pilate saith unto him, speak<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />est thou not unto me? Knowest thou not, that I have Power to Crucifie thee, and have Power to release thee? Iesus saith, thou could'st have no Power at all against me, except it were given thee from above: Therefore he that hath delivered me unto thee, hath the greater sin. And from thenceforth Pilate sought to release him, but the Iews Cryed out, saying, If thou lettest this Man go, thou art not Cesars Friend: He that mak<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth himself a King, speaks against Cesar.</ns0:hi> I have not given the <ns0:hi>Reader</ns0:hi> at one view, what all the Evangelists say, as thinking it scarce possible from them all, to set down the Order, how things passed at this Tryal; but only that I might take notice of what was remarkable in it, related from one or other of them. The reason of our reading so often of <ns0:hi>Pilats going out,</ns0:hi> and then again <ns0:hi>com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing on to the Iudgment Seat,</ns0:hi> seemeth to be, because as we heard before, the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> would not come into <ns0:hi>Pilates</ns0:hi> House, but stood at the Door; and on the other side I conceive, that he could not proceed judicially, but <ns0:hi>sitting upon the Tribunal, or Seat of Iudgment.</ns0:hi> So as, tho he could proceed in Judgment within the House, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ith the Attendance of his own Servants, Souldiers, and Officers: Yet, when he had any thing to propound to the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> he went out; we cannot think, that the <ns0:hi>Evangelists</ns0:hi> report all the things the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> objected against our Saviour, nor all the Que<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stions by <ns0:hi>Pontius Pilate</ns0:hi> propounded to him. For the Evan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gelists tells us, Summarily. That they accused him of many things, and <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>Hearest thou not, how many things they Witness against thee?</ns0:hi> There was it seems, but one thing that they most insisted upon, that was, his making himself a <ns0:hi>King,</ns0:hi> as to which we heard before, how our Lord cleared himself. In the whole Process of this Tryal, these things are remarkable. 1. <ns0:hi>Our Saviours Silence.</ns0:hi> 2. <ns0:hi>Pilates Equity.</ns0:hi> 3. <ns0:hi>The Rage and Madness of the Chief Priests, Scribes and People.</ns0:hi> Our Savi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ours <ns0:hi>Silence</ns0:hi> confirms to us, that piece of the Law of Nature. <ns0:hi>That no Man is bound to accuse himself. Pilates Equity</ns0:hi> appears in many things, 1. He would not Condemn him, without a particular hearing of his Cause himself, he would not force him to accuse himself; he accepts our Saviours Vindication of him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self, as to the great thing wherewith he was Charged, he twice declares, that he found no fault in him, he studies Expedients, to deliver an innocent Person from their Rage: He sends him to <ns0:hi>Herod,</ns0:hi> and obtains his Concurrent Suffrage to his innocency, he offer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth to release him according to a Custom, they had at the Passover<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> to deliver one, whomsoever they desired, when this would not do, he caused him to be Scourged, then brings him out to them again, hoping to have moved them to Compassion, by that lighter Punishment of him.                   </ns0:note> spit upon him, and took the reed, and smote him on the head.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="31">31 And after they had mocked him, they took the robe off from him, and put his own rayment on him, and led him away to crucify him.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> hath the same, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 15.17, 18, 19, 20, only he saith, they put upon him a <ns0:hi>Purple Robe, Iohn</ns0:hi> seemeth to mention this a little out of order, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 19.1, 2, 3, 4. as done before his Condemnation, for tho some t<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ink that <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> rather mention these things out o<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> their due order, yet the abuses seem more likely to be done to a Person, who was Condemned, and so De<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>d in Law, than while he was upon his Tryal. Writers tell us that none might be Crucifyed before he was <ns0:hi>Scourged,</ns0:hi> and that not with <ns0:hi>Rods</ns0:hi> (which was the Jewish manner, but with <ns0:hi>Whips</ns0:hi> (far more cr<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>e<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ly) but whether it was before, or af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter Condemnation we are not certain: He was Condemned upon that <ns0:hi>Article.</ns0:hi> That he should say, <ns0:hi>he was the King of the Iews.</ns0:hi> To mock him therefore, they set a <ns0:hi>Crown on his Head,</ns0:hi> but <ns0:hi>of Thorns,</ns0:hi> they put a <ns0:hi>Scepter</ns0:hi> into his Hand, but it was <ns0:hi>of a Reed,</ns0:hi> they bowed <ns0:hi>the knee before him,</ns0:hi> as was wont to <ns0:hi>Princes.</ns0:hi> They put on him a <ns0:hi>Robe</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Purple,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Scarlet,</ns0:hi> both which were us<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed by Princes. In short they put upon him all the Indignities, and marks of Scorn imaginable. When they had thus glutted themselves, they restore his own Garment to him, and lead him away to the place of Execution. Who can Read these things with a believing Heart, and dry Eyes? if he remembers, that our Sins platted the Crown of Thorns set upon our Saviours Head, and made the Whips with which he was Scourged? Our Sto<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />macks (when we read these things) are ready to rise against the <ns0:hi>Pagan</ns0:hi> Souldiers, but how little did they do in Comparison of what Christ suffered for our Sins? Who can read these things, and not be fortifyed against Temptations, from suffering if we will own the Gospel, and cause of Christ? Our sufferings will come much short of what Christ hath suffered for us.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="32">32 And as they came out, they found a man of Cyrene Simon by name, him they compelled to bear his cross.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="33">33 And when they were come to a place called Golgotha, that is to say A place of a skull.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="34">34 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>9. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                  </ns0:note> They gave him vinegar to drink, mingled with gall: and when he had tasted <ns0:hi>thereof,</ns0:hi> he would not drink.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 15.21. <ns0:hi>And they compelled one Simon a Cyrenian, who passed by coming out of the Country, the Father of Alexander, and Rufus, to bear his Cross. And they bring him unto the place Golgotha, which is, being interpreted the place of a Skull. And they gave him to drink Wine, mingled with Myrrh; but he received it not. Luke</ns0:hi> is larger in his Account of the passages, betwixt his Condemnation and Crucifixion, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 23.26. to <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 33. <ns0:hi>And as they led him, they laid hold on one Simon a Cyrenian coming out of the Country, and on him they laid the Cross, that he might bear it after Iesus. And there followed him a great Company of People, and of Women, which also bewailed, and lamented him. But Iesus turning unto them, said, Daughters of Ierusalem, weep not for me, but for your selves, and for your Children: For behold the days are coming, in the which they shall say, Blessed are the Barren, and the Womb that never bare, and the Paps which never gave Suck. Then shall they begin to say to the Mountains fall on us, and to the Hills cover us. For if they do thus, in a Green Tree, what shall be done in the dry? And there were also two other Male<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />factors led with him <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>e put to Death. Iohn, Ch.</ns0:hi> 19.17. saith no more then, <ns0:hi>And <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> bearing his Cross, went forth into a place, ca<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>led the place of a Skull, which is called in the Hebrew Golgotha. Matthew</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> say, That a Country<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />man, one <ns0:hi>Simon</ns0:hi> a <ns0:hi>Cyrenian,</ns0:hi> (compelled to it by the Soldiers) carried the Cross after Christ. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> saith, that he <ns0:hi>himself bare it.</ns0:hi> Both were doubtless true, some say that Christ himself did carry it through the City, and when he was out of the City, this <ns0:hi>Simon</ns0:hi> carried it. Others think, that Christ being wearied, <ns0:hi>Simon</ns0:hi> took it, but reason will tell us, that the <ns0:hi>Cross</ns0:hi> was too hea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vy a piece of Timber for one to bear, and therefore <ns0:hi>Simon</ns0:hi> was compelled to bear the hinder part, therefore <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> saith, he <ns0:hi>bare it after Iesus</ns0:hi>: The Dispute, whether this <ns0:hi>Simon</ns0:hi> was a <ns0:hi>Native Iew,</ns0:hi> tho an inhabitant of <ns0:hi>Cyrene,</ns0:hi> or a <ns0:hi>Proselyted, Cyrenian,</ns0:hi> or as yet a <ns0:hi>Pagan,</ns0:hi> and whether this <ns0:hi>Cyrene</ns0:hi> was one of the <ns0:hi>ten Cities,</ns0:hi> comprehended in the Name <ns0:hi>Decapolis,</ns0:hi> is not worth spending any Words about: All the Evangelists agree, that he was Cru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cified at <ns0:hi>Golgotha, Luke</ns0:hi> calls it <ns0:hi>Calvary,</ns0:hi> they are both Names of the same Signification. <ns0:hi>The place of a Skull,</ns0:hi> the one is the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> term, the other <ns0:hi>Latine: And they gave him Vinegar to drink, mingled with Gall. Mark</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>Wine mingled with Myrrh:</ns0:hi> There is so great a Cognation between <ns0:hi>Wine,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Vi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />negar,</ns0:hi> that it is no wonder if one Evangelist calls it <ns0:hi>Vinegar,</ns0:hi> another <ns0:hi>Wine,</ns0:hi> which, if it be acid, is <ns0:hi>Vinegar.</ns0:hi> The word tran<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />slated <ns0:hi>Gall,</ns0:hi> signifies all <ns0:hi>Bitterness</ns0:hi>; w<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ether it be caused from <ns0:hi>Gall,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Myrrh.</ns0:hi> Some think, th<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>t some good People gave him <ns0:hi>Wine,</ns0:hi> and the Soldiers added <ns0:hi>Myrrh</ns0:hi> to it. But this is a great incertainty: Certain it is, that it was an ordinary Favour they shewed to dying Persons, to give the<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> some Intoxicating Potion, to make them less sensible of their Pain: It is probable, it was something of this Nature; but our Saviour was not afraid to dye, and so had no need of suc<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> an Antidote ag<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>inst the Pain of it, he <ns0:hi>refused</ns0:hi> it: We shall <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ind they afterward gave him some<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thing to drink also. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> tells us, that gre<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>t multitudes fol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lowed him to the <ns0:hi>place of Execution</ns0:hi> (which is still very ordi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nary) Lamenting him, to whom our Saviour saith, <ns0:hi>Daughters of Ierusalem, Weep not for me, bu<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> for <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>our selves, and for your Chil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dren</ns0:hi>; and then prophesiet<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> the Miseries that should follow his Death, to that degree, that <ns0:hi>the Barren</ns0:hi> should <ns0:hi>bless themselves</ns0:hi>; and they all should say to <ns0:hi>the Mountains fall on us,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>to the Hills cover us.</ns0:hi> He bids the women Weep only for themselves and for their Children: For how much better is it, for Persons of any Tenderness to have no Children, then to have Children, and to see them dashed against the <ns0:hi>Stones,</ns0:hi> as was threatned to <ns0:hi>Babylon, Psal.</ns0:hi> 137.9. or to <ns0:hi>Kill them</ns0:hi> for the Parents Sustenance, as it hap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pened in <ns0:hi>Ahab's</ns0:hi> time, or to see them slain before the <ns0:hi>Parents Fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ces,</ns0:hi> as it happened to <ns0:hi>Zedekiah,</ns0:hi> when the Enemy took <ns0:hi>Ierusalem, Ier.</ns0:hi> 52.10. The People also, he saith, should (as it was of old Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phesied of those of <ns0:hi>Samaria) Hos.</ns0:hi> 20.8. <ns0:hi>Cry to the Moun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tains to cover them, and to the Hills to fall on them:</ns0:hi> A Prover<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bial Expression, to signifie their wishing themselves dead and under Ground, or expounded by <ns0:hi>Isaiah</ns0:hi> 2.19. <ns0:hi>And they shall go into the Holes of the Rocks, and into the Caves of the Earth, for Fear of the Lord, and for the Glory of his Majesty, when he shall arise to shake Terribly the Earth.</ns0:hi> See the like Expressions, <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 6.16. <ns0:hi>&</ns0:hi> 9.6. <ns0:hi>In those days, Men shall seek Death, and shall not find it, and shall desire to dye, and Death shall flee from them.</ns0:hi> For <ns0:hi>if they do thus to the green Tree, what shall be done to the dry</ns0:hi>? It is another Proverbial Expression, which may either be understood Impersonally. <ns0:hi>If they do,</ns0:hi> that is, if it be thus done to. If God suffers them thus to do to me, who am his Son, what shall be done to you? Who are but as dry Sticks, and so fitter for the Fire. <ns0:hi>If Iudgment begin at the House of God, where shall the Wicked and ungodly appear?</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 4.17.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="35">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:273" />35 And they crucified him, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 22.18.</ns0:note> parted his gar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments, casting lots: that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet, They parted my garments amongst them, & upon my vesture did they cast lots.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="36">36 And sitting down, they watched him there:</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="37">37 And set up over his head, his accusation written, THIS IS JESUS THE KING OF THE JEWS.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Mark, Ch.</ns0:hi> 15.24, 25. <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>W<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>en they had Crucified him, they parted his Garments, casting Lots upon them, what every one should take, and it was the third hour, and they Crucified him: And the Superscription of his Accusation was written over, The King of the Iews. And with him they Crucified two Thieves, the one on his right Hand, and the other on his left. And the Scripture was fulfilled, which saith, And he was numbred with the Transgressors. Luke</ns0:hi> 23.33. saith, <ns0:hi>And when they came to a place called</ns0:hi> Calvary, <ns0:hi>there they Crucified him, and the Malefactors, one on the right Hand, and the other on the left. Then said Iesus, Father forgive them, for they know not what they do. And they parted his Rayment, and cast Lots. Iohn</ns0:hi> telleth us some further Circumstances, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 19.18. <ns0:hi>Where they Crucified him, and two others with him, on either side one, and Iesus in the midst.</ns0:hi> And <ns0:hi>Pilate wrote a Title, and put it on the Cross, and the Writing was Iesus of</ns0:hi> Nazareth, <ns0:hi>the King of the</ns0:hi> Jews: <ns0:hi>This Title then read many of the</ns0:hi> Jews, <ns0:hi>for the place where Iesus was Crucified was nigh to the City, and it was written in Hebrew and Greek, and La<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tine. Then said the Chief Priests of the</ns0:hi> Jews <ns0:hi>to</ns0:hi> Pilate, <ns0:hi>write not the King of the</ns0:hi> Jews. Pilate <ns0:hi>answered, what I have writ<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ten, I have written. Then the Souldiers, when they had Cruci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fied him, took his Garments, and made four parts, to every Souldier a part, and also his Coat, now the Coat was without Seame woven from the top to the bottom: They said therefore amongst themselves, Let us not rend it, but cast Lots for it, whose it shall be: That the Scripture might be fulfilled, which saith, They parted my Rayment amongst them, and for my Vesture did they cast Lots. These things the<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>efore the Souldiers did. And they Crucified him.</ns0:hi> That is, four Souldiers, as we learn from <ns0:hi>Iohn's</ns0:hi> narration of this matter of Fact; it seemeth this business was assigned to four more especially: This <ns0:hi>Crucifying</ns0:hi> was a bitter, & shameful kind of Death, not in use amongst the Jews, but among<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>t the <ns0:hi>Romans,</ns0:hi> the manner of it is not particularly known to us: But as it is described by Writers, a piece of Wood was erected, which was crossed with a Bar upon the top. The Body of the Person being fastned to the main piece of Wood, his Arms were extended, and nailed to the cross Bar, or piece of Tim<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ber, and his hands and Feet were nailed. <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>It was about the third hour,</ns0:hi> which with us was about nine of the <ns0:hi>Clock</ns0:hi>: So hasty they were, in destroying this <ns0:hi>just Person,</ns0:hi> that betwixt Midnight and nine of the Clock in the Morning, they <ns0:hi>apprehended him, Tryed, and Condemned him in the Sanhedrim,</ns0:hi> or at least, in a <ns0:hi>Court of High Priests, and Elders,</ns0:hi> and then before <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Roman</ns0:hi> Governour, and led him to be Crucified, and nailed him to his Cross. The Evangelists tell us, he was crucified in the mid<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dle, betwixt two Thieves (of whom we shall read more afterward) several Scriptures of the old Testament, were fulfilled in this Cruci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fixion of Christ. <ns0:hi>They pierced my Hands, and my Feet, Psal.</ns0:hi> 22.16. was fulfilled in his nailing to the Cross. In his being Crucified betwixt two Theeves, was fulfilled that <ns0:hi>Isaiah</ns0:hi> 53.12. <ns0:hi>He was numbered with the Transgressors.</ns0:hi> That of the Psalmist, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 22.18. <ns0:hi>They parted my Garments amongst them, and upon my Vesture did they cast Lots,</ns0:hi> was fulfilled, in the Soldiers parting of our Saviour's Garments (as their Fee) but how could they part them, and yet not rend them? po<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>sibly they parted his other Garments, and only did cast Lots for his <ns0:hi>Coat,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>upper Garment.</ns0:hi> Or, it may be they valued it, and agreed each Mans share, and then cast Lots for the whol<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. I see no Ground for their Assertion, who say, that in such Cases they only stripped the Con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />demned Person of his upper Garment, <ns0:hi>Iohn's</ns0:hi> Relation seemeth to oppose it, he saith, <ns0:hi>And also his Coat. Matthew, Mark,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Iohn,</ns0:hi> all agree in the <ns0:hi>Inscription,</ns0:hi> which <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> drew to be put upon his Cross, signifying the Crime for which he died, on<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> puts in those words (of <ns0:hi>Nazareth.</ns0:hi>) Thus Christ died in the Attestation of his <ns0:hi>Kingly Office.</ns0:hi> This <ns0:hi>Inscription</ns0:hi> angred the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> they sollicit <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> to alter it, and that it might be, <ns0:hi>Who said he was the King of the</ns0:hi> Jews. But <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> refused, saying, <ns0:hi>What I have written, I have written.</ns0:hi> There was nothing more pleasing to <ns0:hi>Pilate,</ns0:hi> than this, (as he thought) to deride the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> as having such a despicable Person (as he judged him) their <ns0:hi>King:</ns0:hi> In the mean time the Counsels of God have their Effect; Christ in his Death, is declared to be the King of the <ns0:hi>Iews. Luke</ns0:hi> saith, that Christ said, <ns0:hi>F<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ther forgive them, for they know not what they do.</ns0:hi> Whether these Words were spoken, when our Lord was first <ns0:hi>Nailed to the Cross,</ns0:hi> or afterward is not much Material. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> relates them before the Soldiers<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                     <ns0:hi>parting his Garments.</ns0:hi> Our Saviour by them declares himself a true Pastor, and Shepherd of Souls, teaching his Disciples no more, than he himself did Practice, <ns0:hi>Cahp</ns0:hi> 5.44. <ns0:hi>He had taught his Disciples to pray for them, who despitefully used<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and Persecu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted them.</ns0:hi> Himself here practiceth it: The Malice of Men ought not to quench in Christians, the Grace of God. Let us now consider the passage that happened, from the time he was nailed to the Cross, until the time of his Expiration, which was more than three entire hours.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="39">39 And they that passed by, reviled him, wagg<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing their heads.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="40">40 And saying, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 26.61. Joh. 2.19.</ns0:note> Thou that destroyest the tem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple, and buildest <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> in three days, save thy self: If thou be the Son of God, come down from the cross,</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="41">41 Likewise also the chief priests mocking him, with the scribes and elders, said,</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="42">42 He saved others, himself he cannot save: If he be the King of <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                     <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                  </ns0:gap>srael, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="43">43 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 22.8.</ns0:note> He trusted in God; let him deliver him now, if he will have him: for he said, I am the Son of God.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="44">44 The theeves also which were crucified with him, cast the same in his teeth.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> relateth this part of the <ns0:hi>History,</ns0:hi> with no Material Cir<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cumstance differing from <ns0:hi>Matthew, Ch.</ns0:hi> 15.29, 30.31, 32. <ns0:hi>Luke,</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 23.39, 40. 41, 42, 43. <ns0:hi>And one of the Ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lefactors whcih were Hanged, Railed on him, saying, If thou be the Christ, save thy self and us. But the other answering, re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />buked him, saying, Doest thou not fear God, seeing thou art in the same Condemnation, and we indeed justly, for we have the due reward of our deeds, but this Man hath done nothing amiss. And he said unto Iesus, Lord remember me, when thou comest into thy Kingdom. And Iesus said unto him, Verily, I say unto thee. To day thou shalt be with me in Paradise.                <ns0:p n="46">46 And about the ninth hour, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Heb. 5.7.</ns0:note> Jesus cryed with a loud voice, saying, Eli, Eli, Lamasabachthani, that is to say, My God, my God, why hast thou for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />saken me.</ns0:p>

               <ns0:p n="48">48 And straightway one of them ran, and took a spunge,<ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 69.21.</ns0:note> and filled <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> with vinegar, and put <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> on a reed, and gave him to drink.</ns0:p>

               <ns0:p n="50">50 Jesus when he had cryed again with a loud voice yielded up the Ghost.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> hath the same, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 15. from <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 33. to <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 38. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 23, 44. <ns0:hi>That it was about the sixth hour, and there was a darkness over all the Earth, unto the ninth Hour. And the Sun was darkned, and the Vail of the Temple was Rent in the midst. And when Iesus had cryed with a loud Voice, he said, Father into thy Hands I commend my Spirit. And having said thus, he gave up the Ghost. Iohn</ns0:hi> saith no more, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 19.30. but that—<ns0:hi>he bowed his Head, and gave up the Ghost.</ns0:hi> It is said <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 19.14. <ns0:hi>It was about the sixth Hour,</ns0:hi> when <ns0:hi>Pi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />late</ns0:hi> brought forth Chirst to the Jews, how then could he be Cru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cified at the <ns0:hi>third Hour?</ns0:hi> and the Darkness begin at the sixth. The different ways the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Romans</ns0:hi> had of counting Hours, make us to be at a loss sometimes, as to Circumstances of time to reconcile some Scriptures. But as to the present difficulty, it is said that the Jews as they divided the Night into <ns0:hi>four Watches,</ns0:hi> so they also divided the Day into <ns0:hi>four parts,</ns0:hi> each part having his Denomination from the succeeding part, by which Name all the intermediate time was called. Thus when the third Hour (which with us is nine of the Clock) was past, they called all the sixth Hour till past twelve. Thus <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> Condemned Christ in the be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ginning of the sixth Hour, and the darkness began at the end of it, that is, after <ns0:hi>twelve,</ns0:hi> for dividing the day into <ns0:hi>Quadrants,</ns0:hi> the Hours had their Denomination from them. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> also saith no more, <ns0:hi>then about the sixth Hour,</ns0:hi> which is true if it were some small time after. <ns0:hi>There was darkness over all the Land, till the ninth Hour.</ns0:hi> That this darkness was caused by the <ns0:hi>E<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />clipse of the Sun</ns0:hi> at that time of the Day is plain enough, but that this was no <ns0:hi>Eclipse</ns0:hi> in the ordinary course of Nature is evi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dent, for 1. whereas all Eclipses use to be in the time of the New Moon, this was, when the Moon was at the Full, the fifteenth Day of the Month <ns0:hi>Nisan:</ns0:hi> 2. This <ns0:hi>Eclipse</ns0:hi> was not seen in one part or in another, but <ns0:hi>over all the Earth, that was under the same Hemisphear.</ns0:hi> 3. No <ns0:hi>Eclipse</ns0:hi> in a natural Course can last three Hours. So that plainly this was a Miraculous <ns0:hi>Eclipse,</ns0:hi> not caused by the Interpo<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ition of the Moon (as other Eclipses) but by the Mighty and Extraordinary Power of God, which made an Heathen <ns0:hi>Philosopher</ns0:hi> at a great distance cry out. <ns0:hi>Ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther the Divine being now suffereth, or Sympathizeth with one that suffereth,</ns0:hi> he is said to have seen this <ns0:hi>Eclipse</ns0:hi> in <ns0:hi>Egypt. And a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bout the ninth Hour,</ns0:hi> that is, about three of the Clock (as we reckon the Hours) Jesus <ns0:hi>cryed with a loud Voice, Eli, Eli,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Eloi, Eloi, Lamasabacthani.</ns0:hi> The Words are <ns0:hi>Hebrew,</ns0:hi> tho <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> reports them according to the <ns0:hi>Syriack</ns0:hi> Corruption of the Dia<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lect.                         <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>as a Type of Christ. He that was the Son of <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> useth <ns0:hi>Davids</ns0:hi> Words, po<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>sibly spoken by <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> in the Person of Christ. Gods forsaking any Person or places, must be understood with refe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rence not to his <ns0:hi>Essential Presence,</ns0:hi> for so he filleth all places, and is <ns0:hi>present</ns0:hi> with <ns0:hi>all Persons.</ns0:hi> But with reference to the <ns0:hi>Ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nifestations of his Providence for our good</ns0:hi>; thus when God witholds his good Providence to us, either with respect to our outward or inward Man, he is said to <ns0:hi>forsake us.</ns0:hi> A Total <ns0:hi>for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />saking</ns0:hi> either of our Bodies, or of our Souls, is not consistent with the being of our outward Man: or the Spiritual being or Life of our inward Man. All forsakings therefore in this Life, are <ns0:hi>Gradual,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Partial.</ns0:hi> The <ns0:hi>forsaking</ns0:hi> which Christ there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore here complains of, was not the <ns0:hi>Total withdrawing</ns0:hi> of Di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vine favour, and assistance from him (that was impossible) and incompetent with the first Words testifying his relation to God, and assistance in him, but it must be understood with respect to Gods <ns0:hi>Consolatory Manifestations,</ns0:hi> and that is testifyed by his other Words, related by <ns0:hi>Luke. Father into thy Hands I com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mend my Spirit.</ns0:hi> Which Words having said, <ns0:hi>he gave up the Ghost</ns0:hi> (say <ns0:hi>Matthew, Mark</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Luke) Iohn</ns0:hi> addeth, That he <ns0:hi>bowed his Head,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>yielded up the Ghost.</ns0:hi> Words added, to confirm what he elsewhere said. <ns0:hi>That he laid down his Life, none took it from him.</ns0:hi> His crying twice at this instant, with a loud Voice argued his Spirits not so spent, but he might have lived a few Minutes longer, but he freely laid down his Life. The People saying, <ns0:hi>he calls for Elias,</ns0:hi> when he said <ns0:hi>Eli, Eli,</ns0:hi> spake them to be <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> who to this day dream of an <ns0:hi>Elias</ns0:hi> to come, and <ns0:hi>restore all things.</ns0:hi> That they no better distinguished be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />twixt <ns0:hi>Eli</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Elias,</ns0:hi> must be attributed either to the Corrup<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion of their Dialect, he saying <ns0:hi>Eloi, Eloi</ns0:hi> (according to the Syriack Corruption of the Term) or their too great distance from him. Their mocking him upon it, was but Consonant to their former behaviour toward him, while he was upon the Cross. Their giving him the <ns0:hi>Spunge</ns0:hi> with <ns0:hi>Vinegar,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Hysope,</ns0:hi> we before gave an account of.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="51">51 And behold <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 span">
                        <ns0:desc>〈…〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 2 Chro 3.<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top, to the bottom, and the earth did quake, and the rocks rent.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="52">52 And the graves were opened, and many bo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dies of saints which slept arose.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="53">53 And came out of the graves, after his resur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rection, and went into the holy city, and appeared unto many.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Mark, Ch.</ns0:hi> 15.38. mentioneth o<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ly <ns0:hi>the rending of the Vail.</ns0:hi> No more doth <ns0:hi>Luke, Ch.</ns0:hi> 23.45. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> mentioneth none of these things. It pleased God to give a Testimony against this Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />digious piece of Wickedness, by <ns0:hi>Prodigious Signs,</ns0:hi> both in the <ns0:hi>Hea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vens,</ns0:hi> and on the <ns0:hi>Earth. In the Heavens,</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Sun,</ns0:hi> as we heard before, suffered an unusual Preter-natural <ns0:hi>Eclipse</ns0:hi> which lasted three hours. In the <ns0:hi>Earth,</ns0:hi> there was an <ns0:hi>Earthquake,</ns0:hi> to that degree, that the <ns0:hi>Rocks</ns0:hi> were rent by it. <ns0:hi>Earthquakes</ns0:hi> were sometimes no more than In<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dications of Gods Power, and Majesty; and some think, that by this Earthquak, Christ declared his Divine Power, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 68.8. <ns0:hi>Ioel</ns0:hi> 2.10. It is certain, that <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 54. the <ns0:hi>Centurion</ns0:hi> concluded from it, <ns0:hi>this was the Son ofGod.</ns0:hi> But <ns0:hi>Earthquakes,</ns0:hi> were some<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />times not only the <ns0:hi>Indications</ns0:hi> of the <ns0:hi>Divine Majesty and Power,</ns0:hi> but also of his <ns0:hi>Wr<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>th, Psal.</ns0:hi> 18.7, 8. <ns0:hi>Ioel</ns0:hi> 3.16. <ns0:hi>Nahum</ns0:hi> 1.6. And such doubtless was this: To shew that the Earth abhorred what these Men had done. Besides these, <ns0:hi>The Vail of the Tem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple was rent,</ns0:hi> three of the Evangelists mention it. It is not much Material, whether this were the outward <ns0:hi>Vail,</ns0:hi> or the <ns0:hi>inward Vail,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Hangings,</ns0:hi> which parted the most <ns0:hi>Holy Place</ns0:hi> from the <ns0:hi>oth<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>r part of the Temple,</ns0:hi> tho probably it was the <ns0:hi>inner Veil.</ns0:hi> By this rending of the Veil, God testifyed his wrath a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gainst the Jews, and that he was leaving his Temple amongst them. The Veil also was a Type of Christs Flesh, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 10.20. the Antitype being Rent, it was reasonable that the Type should also be so. By this also was shewed, that the <ns0:hi>Temple</ns0:hi>-Ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vice was now at an end, and to continue no longer, and the par<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tition-Wall betwixt <ns0:hi>Iew</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Gentiles</ns0:hi> was pulled down. For what <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> speaks, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 52, 53. of the <ns0:hi>Graves opening, and the Bodies of the Saints arising,</ns0:hi> &c. probably it was not till <ns0:hi>Christs Resurrection,</ns0:hi> only <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> puts it in here, reckoning up together all the <ns0:hi>Prodigious things</ns0:hi> that happened, for <ns0:hi>Mat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thew</ns0:hi> himself saith, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 53. <ns0:hi>They came out of their Graves af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter his Resurrection,</ns0:hi> and it is not likely that the Graves opened any considerable time before they came out of their Graves. These now were the Prodigies which attended the Death of our Saviour.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="54">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:274" />54 Now when the centurion, and they that were with him watching Jesus, saw the earth quake, and those things that were done, they feared greatly, saying, Truly this was the Son of God.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="55">55 And many women were there beholding afar off, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Luke 8.2, 3.</ns0:note> who followed Jesus, from Galilee, ministring unto him.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="56">56 Amongst which was Mary Magdalen, and Ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry the mother of James, and Joses, and the mother of Zebedees chlidren.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 15.39, 40, 41. <ns0:hi>And when the Centurion which stood over against him, saw that he so Cryed out, and gave up the Ghost, he said, Truly this Man was the Son of God. There were also Women looking on afar off, amongst whom was</ns0:hi> Mary Magdalen, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> Mary <ns0:hi>the Mother of</ns0:hi> James <ns0:hi>the less, and of</ns0:hi> Joses, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> Salome; <ns0:hi>who also when he was in</ns0:hi> Galilee, <ns0:hi>followed him, and Ministred unto him, and many other Wo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />men, which came up with him to</ns0:hi> Jerusalem, <ns0:hi>Luke, Ch.</ns0:hi> 23, 47, 48, 49. saith, <ns0:hi>Now when the Centurion saw what was done, he Glorified God, saying, Certainly this was a righteous Man. And all the People that came together to that sight, beholding the things which were done, smote their Breasts and returned. And all his A<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>quaintance, and the Women that followed him from</ns0:hi> Galilee, <ns0:hi>stood afar off beholding these things.</ns0:hi> We heard before, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 36. That the Soldiers <ns0:hi>sate down</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>watched Christ.</ns0:hi> The <ns0:hi>Centurion</ns0:hi> here mentioned, was the Captain of this <ns0:hi>Watch,</ns0:hi> he seeing the Earthquake, and all the other things that were done (saith <ns0:hi>Matthew) Mark</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>When he saw that he so Cryed out, and gave up the Ghost.</ns0:hi> He <ns0:hi>Glorified God</ns0:hi> (saith <ns0:hi>Luke) Matthew</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> tell us how he said, <ns0:hi>Truly this Man was the Son of God. Luke</ns0:hi> saith, he said, <ns0:hi>Certainly this was a righ<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />teous Man:</ns0:hi> he Glorified God by a <ns0:hi>Confession of the Truth,</ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>the Glory of God,</ns0:hi> saying, he was a <ns0:hi>Righteous</ns0:hi> Man, and such a Righteous Man, as was also the Son of God. It seems very pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bable, that this Captain living amongst the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> had learned from them their Expectation of a <ns0:hi>Messiah</ns0:hi>; and speaketh this with reference to that, and acknowledgeth that Christ was he. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> addeth, That all the People that came to see that sight returned, <ns0:hi>Smiting their Breasts,</ns0:hi> being convinced of the great Wickedness committed by their <ns0:hi>High Priests,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Chief Priests and Elders</ns0:hi>; and fearing that Vengeance which followed in less than forty Years <ns0:hi>(And many Women were there)</ns0:hi> these Women had followed Christ out of <ns0:hi>Galilee:</ns0:hi> Two only are named here, <ns0:hi>Mary Magdalen,</ns0:hi> who probably had her Name from <ns0:hi>Magdala</ns0:hi> a City in <ns0:hi>Galilee,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Mary the Mother of</ns0:hi> James and <ns0:hi>Ioses. Iames</ns0:hi> the less, saith <ns0:hi>Mark,</ns0:hi> to distinguish him from <ns0:hi>Iames</ns0:hi> the Son of <ns0:hi>Z<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>bedee,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>the Mother of</ns0:hi> Zebedees <ns0:hi>Children,</ns0:hi> these stood afar off, these three Evangelists say. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> told us, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 19. <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 25. That two of these were so near the Cross, with the Mother of our Lord, that he spake to them. Here we read no<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thing of the <ns0:hi>Mother of our Lord,</ns0:hi> probably she was gone with <ns0:hi>Iohn,</ns0:hi> to whom Christ had commended her, and the rest with<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />drew, and stood further off from the Cross at this time. <ns0:hi>Mat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thew</ns0:hi> goeth on now, describing the coming of <ns0:hi>Ioseph</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>Ari<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mathea,</ns0:hi> to beg the dead Body of Christ, so doth <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Luke, Iohn, Ch.</ns0:hi> 19.31, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 37. interposeth something tending to compleat the History. <ns0:hi>The</ns0:hi> Jews <ns0:hi>therefore, because it was the Preparation, that the Bodies should not re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />main upon the Cross, on the Sabbath day, for that Sabbath day was <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> High day, besought Christ that their Legs might be bro<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="3 letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•••</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>, and that they might be taken away. Then came the Soldiers, and brake the Legs of the first, and of the other which was Crucified with him. But when they came to Iesus, and saw that he was dead already, they brake not his Legs<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> But one of the Soldiers with a Spear pierced his side, and forthwith came there out Blood, and Water. And he that saw it bare Record, and his Record is true, and he knoweth that he saith true, that you might believe. For these things were done, that the Scriptures should be fulfilled. A Bone of him shall not be broken. And again another Scripture saith, They shall look upon him, whom they have pierced.</ns0:hi> The day upon which he was Crucified, was the fifteenth day of the Month <ns0:hi>Nisan,</ns0:hi> up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on the <ns0:hi>Friday,</ns0:hi> as we call it; this appeareth from this Text, which saith, It was the <ns0:hi>Preparation to the Iewish Sabbath,</ns0:hi> and that <ns0:hi>Sabbath</ns0:hi> the Evangelist saith, was an <ns0:hi>High Day,</ns0:hi> not because as some think the Jews put off their <ns0:hi>Passover</ns0:hi> to that Day, but because it was the second <ns0:hi>Day of the Feast of unlea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vened Bread.</ns0:hi> It is true, <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 19.14. it is called the <ns0:hi>Prepa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ration to the Passover,</ns0:hi> but we must remember, that all the se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven Days of unleavened Bread, were so called, as I before Noted, This Day was indeed the <ns0:hi>Preparation</ns0:hi> to the <ns0:hi>Sabbath</ns0:hi> in the <ns0:hi>Pas<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />chal Week,</ns0:hi> for otherwise we must say, that Christ did not Eat the <ns0:hi>Passover</ns0:hi> the same Day that the Jews did, which invovles us in many Inextricable difficulties, and could not be if the <ns0:hi>Pas<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />chal Lamb</ns0:hi> was to be killed by the <ns0:hi>Priests,</ns0:hi> for they would not have killed it the Day before. It is therefore most probable, that <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 19.14. must be expounded by <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 31. and the <ns0:hi>Prepara<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion of the Passover, v.</ns0:hi> 14. was <ns0:hi>the Preparation to the Sab<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bath,</ns0:hi> which falling within the compass of the seven days of un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />leavened Bread, was a great Day with them, especially being the day following the Eating of the <ns0:hi>Paschal Lamb.</ns0:hi> By the Law, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 21.23. The Body of none that was hang'd, was to abide all Night upon the Tree. It was betwixt three and four of the Clock in the Afternoon, before that Christ dyed, they used to set some hours apart for <ns0:hi>Preparation to the Sabbath,</ns0:hi> which that Night began as soon as the Sun was set, this therefore makes them to go to <ns0:hi>Pilate,</ns0:hi> and desire <ns0:hi>the Legs of them that suffered might be broken. Pilate</ns0:hi> grants their request. The Souldiers break the Legs of the two Thieves, but when they came to Christ, they found him dead, and brake not his Legs, but a Souldier with a Spear pierceth his side. The Evangelist takes notice of these minute things (and assureth us he saw them, that we might believe) that he might shew us how in every point, the things of old spoken concerning Christ, were fulfilled in him. Chri<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>t was the true <ns0:hi>Paschal Lamb,</ns0:hi> as to which the Law was: <ns0:hi>That a Bone of it should not be broken, Exod.</ns0:hi> 12.46. <ns0:hi>Num.</ns0:hi> 9.12. or else the <ns0:hi>Evangelist</ns0:hi> referreth to <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 34.20. where it is said of a <ns0:hi>Righteous Man: He keepeth all his Bones, that not one of them is broken.</ns0:hi> Our Saviours Side was pierced, and that also is recorded, to let us know the fulfilling of that Scripture, <ns0:hi>Zech.</ns0:hi> 12.10. <ns0:hi>They shall look on him, whom they have pierced.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="57">57 When the even was come, there came a rich man of Arimathea, named Joseph, who also himself was Jesus his disciple.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="58">58 He went to Pilate, and beg'd the body of Jesus, Then Pilate commanded the body to be delivered.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="59">59 And when Joseph had taken the body, he wrapt it in a clean linnen cloth.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="60">60 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa, 53.9.</ns0:note> laid it in his own new Tomb, which he had hewed out in the rock, and he rolled a great stone, to the door of the sepulcher, and departed.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="61">61 And there was Mary Magdalene, and the other Mary, sitting over against the sepulcher<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> hath it, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 15. from <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 42. to the end. <ns0:hi>And now when the even was come, because it was the Preparat<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

And</ns0:hi> Pilate <ns0:hi>marvelled if he were already dead, and calling un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to him the Centurion, he asked him whether he had been a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ny time Dead. And when he knew it of the Centurion, he gave the Body to</ns0:hi> Joseph. <ns0:hi>And he bought fine Linnen, and took him down, and wrapt him in the linnen, and laid him in a Se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pulcher, which was hewd out of a Rock<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and rolled a stone to the door of the Supulcher. Luke</ns0:hi> hath it, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 23, 50. <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> thus. <ns0:hi>And behold there was a Man Named</ns0:hi> Joseph, <ns0:hi>a Councellor, and he was a good Man, and a just. The same Man had not consented to the Counsel, and deed of them; he was of</ns0:hi> Arimathea <ns0:hi>a City of the Iews, who also himself wait<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed for the Kingdom of God. This Man went unto</ns0:hi> Pilate, <ns0:hi>and begged the Body of Iesus.                <ns0:p n="64">64 Command therefore that the sepulcher be made sure until the third day, lest his disciples come by night, and steal him away, and say unto the people, He risen from the dead, So the last error shall be worse then the first.</ns0:p>

               <ns0:p n="66">66 So they went, and made the sepulcher sure, sealing the stone, and setting a watch,<ns0:note place="bottom">This part of the <ns0:hi>History,</ns0:hi> is recorded by no other <ns0:hi>Evangelist,</ns0:hi> the recording it by <ns0:hi>Matthew,</ns0:hi> contributeth yet further to Evi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dence the Truth of Christs <ns0:hi>Resurrection.</ns0:hi> For here was all imagi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nable care taken to prevent a <ns0:hi>Cheat</ns0:hi> in the Case. The next day that followed the Day of the <ns0:hi>Preparation</ns0:hi> must be the <ns0:hi>Sabbath Day, Mark</ns0:hi> 15.42. These Superstitious Hypocrites, that quar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />relled with our Saviour, for his Disciples (being hungry) <ns0:hi>pluck<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing Ears of Corn on the Sabbath Day,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>for his healing</ns0:hi> him that had a <ns0:hi>Withered Hand, Chap.</ns0:hi> 12.13. can now themselves go to <ns0:hi>Pilate,</ns0:hi> to set him on Work, to command that the <ns0:hi>Sepulcher should be made fast to the third Day.</ns0:hi> They alledge that Christ, whom they impiously call <ns0:hi>that Deceiver,</ns0:hi> said, while he was a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />live, <ns0:hi>that he would rise again the third Day.</ns0:hi> to answer the Type of the Prophet <ns0:hi>Ionas, Chap.</ns0:hi> 12.39, 40. They were doubtless jealous that there was more Truth in those Words, then they were willing to believe. They pretend also a fear, lest his Disciples should come privately by Night, and steal his Body away, and then say he was risen. But was this a probable thing? that a Government should be afraid of a few, poor unarmed Men? they were doubt<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />less convicted in their own Consciences, that he would rise again from the Dead, and to prevent his coming out of the Sepulcher, they would have <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> Command, that the Sepulcher should be made sure. <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> tells them, that <ns0:hi>they had a Watch,</ns0:hi> a Band of Soul<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />diers, which he had commanded at this time to attend them, either for the Guard of the Temple, or other things, about which they would imploy them, they might make the Sepulcher as sure as they could <ns0:hi>So they went, and made the Sepulcher sure, seal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing the Stone, and setting a Watch.</ns0:hi> Vain Men! as if the same Power that was necessary to raise and quicken the Dead, could not also remove the Stone, and break through the Watch, which, they had set. But by this their Excessive Care, and Diligence, in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stead of preventing Christs Resurrection, as they intended they have confirmed the Truth, and Belief of it to all the World. So doth God take the wise in their own Craftiness, and turn their Wisdom into Foolishness, that he may <ns0:hi>set his King upon his Holy Hill of Zion.</ns0:hi>
